Understanding database internals is what separates a Staff Engineer from a senior engineer. When you say 'write to Postgres' — what actually happens on disk? When you add an index, why does writes get slower? When you read with a specific isolation level, how does the DB know what to show you?

Before the Engine: Choosing a Data Model

The storage engine question (“B-tree or LSM?”) comes second. The first question is how you model the data at all, because that determines which access patterns are cheap — and no storage engine rescues a model that fights your queries.

THE ONE QUESTION THAT DECIDES THE MODEL What do the RELATIONSHIPS in your data look like? one-to-many, self-contained → DOCUMENT a résumé: one person, many jobs, many skills → the whole thing is loaded together, always many-to-one, many-to-many → RELATIONAL orders → customers, products, warehouses → the same entity referenced from everywhere everything connects to everything → GRAPH social networks, road networks, recommendations → the JOINs would be arbitrarily deep
Not “SQL vs NoSQL”. The relationship shape picks the model, and the access pattern confirms it.
RelationalDocumentGraph
Wins atMany-to-many, joins, ad-hoc queries, constraintsTree-shaped data read as a whole; storage localityDeep or variable-length traversals
SchemaSchema-on-write — enforced up frontSchema-on-read — implicit, interpreted by the readerFlexible; edges added without migration
Weak atObject-relational mismatch; deep traversal needs recursive CTEsJoins (often emulated in application code); many-to-manyBulk aggregate scans
Real costMigrations on large tablesUpdate anomalies once data is duplicatedFewer engineers know the query language
⚠ Common misconception
“Document databases are schemaless, so we get flexibility for free.”

There is always a schema. The question is only whether it is enforced on write or assumed on read. “Schemaless” really means schema-on-read: the structure lives implicitly in every piece of code that touches the document.

The trade is about when you pay. Schema-on-write pays up front with a migration and gets a guarantee. Schema-on-read pays later, forever, in defensive code that handles every historical shape — and the shapes accumulate.

Document databases genuinely win on locality: if you always load the whole document, storing it contiguously is one disk read rather than a multi-table join. But note this only holds while you load most of the document. A large document from which you read one field is worse than relational, because most engines must load and rewrite the whole thing.

💡 The convergence worth knowing

The models are converging and the debate has largely dissolved. PostgreSQL has had excellent JSONB with indexing since 9.4; MongoDB added multi-document ACID transactions in 4.0. You can now get document locality inside a relational database and transactions inside a document database.

So the modern answer to “SQL or NoSQL?” is usually: start with PostgreSQL, use JSONB for the genuinely variable parts, and move only when a measured access pattern demands it.

🔍 Declarative vs imperative — why SQL survived everything

SQL says what you want; it does not say how to get it. That separation is why a query written in 1995 gets faster when you upgrade the database: the optimiser may now choose a hash join instead of a nested loop, use a new index, or parallelise across cores — without a line of your code changing.

An imperative implementation locks in the “how”. It also blocks parallelism, since the engine must preserve your stated order of operations.

This is the same argument as MapReduce vs SQL, and the same reason CSS beats hand-written DOM manipulation. Declarative interfaces leave room for the implementation to improve underneath you — a genuinely useful principle when designing any API.

How Data is Stored: B-Tree vs LSM-Tree

Every database uses a storage engine. The two dominant designs are B-trees (used by PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB) and LSM-trees (used by Cassandra, RocksDB, HBase, MongoDB's WiredTiger).

B-Tree

A balanced tree where every leaf page contains actual data rows. Tree height is O(log N). For 1 billion rows, that's about 30 levels. Each level = one disk seek.

B-tree: tree structure with data in leaves. Writes are in-place updates (random writes — slow on HDD).

LSM-Tree (Log-Structured Merge-Tree)

LSM-trees take the opposite approach: never modify data in place. All writes go to an in-memory buffer (MemTable) which is periodically flushed to disk as immutable sorted files (SSTs — Sorted String Tables). Background compaction merges SSTs.

LSM-tree: writes always go to MemTable (sequential). Compaction merges SSTs in background. No in-place updates.
B-TreeLSM-Tree
Write PerformanceSlower (random writes, page splits)Faster (sequential writes, batched)
Read PerformanceFaster (directly to leaf, O(log N))Slower (check MemTable + N SSTs)
Space AmplificationLow (in-place updates, no garbage)High (multiple versions during compaction)
Best ForRead-heavy, OLTP, joinsWrite-heavy, time-series, append workloads

Write-Ahead Log (WAL)

Every database uses a WAL (also called a redo log, commit log, or journal). Before any data is modified on disk, the change is written to the WAL first. The WAL is append-only and sequential — very fast.

Why: If the database crashes mid-write, the data pages might be partially updated — corrupted. On restart, the database replays the WAL to bring data pages to a consistent state. The WAL ensures durability: once written to WAL and fsync'd, the write is guaranteed even on crash.

MVCC — Multi-Version Concurrency Control

MVCC is how modern databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB, MongoDB) implement isolation without locking reads against writes. Instead of locking a row when writing, the database creates a new version of the row. Old versions remain visible to transactions that started before the write.

🎯 Scenario — Reading While Writing — Without Locks

Transaction A starts at T=100. It reads user row (version at T=80: name='Alice').

Transaction B starts at T=105 and updates: name='Alice Smith'. Creates new row version at T=105.

Transaction A reads user row again (still at snapshot T=100): still sees 'Alice' (T=80 version). No lock contention.

Transaction A commits. Transaction B's changes are now visible to new transactions.

Background vacuum process deletes old row versions that no transaction can see anymore (T=80 version).

💡 Key Insight

MVCC enables non-blocking reads alongside writes. Readers never block writers; writers never block readers. This is why PostgreSQL can handle high concurrency with many reads and writes simultaneously. The cost: storage for old versions, and vacuum overhead.

Indexes — When to Add, When to Remove

An index is a separate data structure that maps column values to row locations. Adding an index speeds up reads for that column but slows down every write (the index must be updated on insert/update/delete).

Index TypeBest ForExample Query
B-Tree (default)Equality + range queries, sortableWHERE age BETWEEN 20 AND 30
HashEquality only, faster than B-tree for =WHERE email = 'a@b.com'
GiST / GINFull-text search, array, geospatialWHERE content @@ 'distributed'
Partial IndexSubset of rows (saves space)WHERE is_active = true (index only active)
Composite IndexMulti-column queries (column order matters!)WHERE user_id = 1 AND created_at > X
Covering IndexInclude all columns needed in queryNo table access needed — "index-only scan"
⚠ Common Mistake

Composite index column order matters enormously. Index (user_id, created_at) can answer queries on user_id alone, or (user_id AND created_at), but NOT created_at alone. The leftmost prefix rule: only prefix columns can be used for filtering without a full scan.

Trace It End to End: One Write, One Read

If you can narrate these two paths out loud, you understand storage engines. Everything else is variation.

A SINGLE WRITE — UPDATE users SET name='Rishi' WHERE id=42 Client ▼ SQL over the wire Query parser → planner → executor ▼ Transaction manager assigns txn id, takes snapshot (MVCC) ▼ 1. WAL APPEND sequential write → fsync ↑ THIS is the commit. Everything after can be lazy. ▼ 2. BUFFER POOL modify the page in memory (marked dirty) B-tree: find leaf page, modify in place, maybe split LSM: insert into memtable (a skip list) — no page at all ▼ 3. ACK TO CLIENT ← we are done. Disk pages are still stale. ▼ 4. LATER, in the background B-tree: checkpoint flushes dirty pages (random writes) LSM: memtable fills → flush as an SSTable (sequential) → compaction merges SSTables Replication: the SAME WAL streams to followers CDC: the SAME WAL feeds search/cache/warehouse Notice: one log serves durability, replication AND integration.
A SINGLE READ — SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=42 B-TREE LSM-TREE root page (cached) memtable (RAM) ▼ ▼ miss internal page (cached) immutable memtables ▼ ▼ miss leaf page ← 1 disk read SSTable N bloom filter → "no" ▼ SSTable N-1 bloom filter → "no" row SSTable N-2 bloom → "maybe" ▼ block index → 1 disk read ~3–4 page reads, upper row levels always cached Bloom filters make ~99% of SSTables cost nothing to skip.
B-tree: bounded, predictable reads. LSM: reads depend on how many SSTables exist — which depends on whether compaction is keeping up.
💡 What changes under millions of operations

Writes: the B-tree's random page writes become the bottleneck once the working set exceeds RAM — every update is a read-modify-write of a random page. The LSM keeps absorbing writes sequentially, and the cost surfaces instead as compaction debt: background I/O, CPU, and latency spikes at inconvenient moments.

Reads: the B-tree stays flat and predictable. The LSM degrades as SSTable count grows — so if compaction falls behind, read p99 climbs. This is the real difference: the B-tree's cost is paid synchronously and visibly; the LSM's is deferred and shows up as an operational problem.

OLTP vs OLAP — Two Completely Different Machines

Everything above assumed OLTP: many small, keyed, latency-sensitive operations. Analytics is the opposite workload in every dimension, and running it on the same system is one of the most common architectural mistakes.

OLTP (transactional)OLAP (analytic)
Read patternA few rows, fetched by keyMillions of rows, a handful of columns
Write patternRandom, low-latency, from usersBulk load / event stream
Query shapeKnown, repeated, indexedAd-hoc, exploratory, aggregating
Sized byGB–TBTB–PB
BottleneckDisk seeksDisk bandwidth — a different problem entirely
LayoutRow-orientedColumn-oriented

Why column-oriented storage changes the economics

A typical warehouse query touches 3 columns of a 100-column table across a billion rows. Row storage must read every column of every row to get them — you read 100 columns' worth of bytes to use 3.

ROW STORAGE — all of a row together [id=1|date|product|store|qty|price|...95 more] [id=2|...] [id=3|...] ╱__________________________________________╲ must read ALL of this to get 3 columns COLUMN STORAGE — each column stored together date: [2024-01-01, 2024-01-01, 2024-01-02, ...] product: [31, 68, 69, 31, 31, 68, ...] ← read only these qty: [4, 1, 2, 7, 3, ...] ← ~30x less I/O store: (not read at all) AND THEN IT COMPRESSES BRILLIANTLY A column holds values of ONE type, often highly repetitive. Bitmap encoding: product_sk has 100k distinct values over 1B rows → one bitmap per value, 1 bit per row, then run-length encoded product_sk = 31: 0 1 1 0 0 1 0 ... → RLE → a few bytes WHERE product_sk IN (30,68,69) → bitwise OR of 3 bitmaps WHERE product=31 AND store=3 → bitwise AND of 2 bitmaps The query becomes CPU bitwise operations over compressed data that fits in L2 cache. This is why warehouses feel like magic.
Column stores win twice: they read less, and what they read compresses far better because a column is homogeneous.
⚠ A naming trap worth knowing

Cassandra and HBase have “column families” inherited from Bigtable, and this makes people call them column-oriented. They are not. Within a column family they store all of a row's columns together with the row key, and they do not use column compression. The Bigtable model is essentially row-oriented. If someone proposes Cassandra for an analytics workload on those grounds, that is the misunderstanding to correct.

✎ Mini exercise 8

Your product database is PostgreSQL, ~800GB, serving 12,000 QPS of user traffic at a p99 of 25ms.

The analytics team starts running dashboard queries against it: full-table scans with GROUP BY over 18 months of orders. Your p99 goes to 400ms and the on-call pager starts firing.

Work out: the three separate mechanisms by which their queries hurt yours, and what you would actually do.

Show the worked answer

Mechanism 1 — buffer pool eviction. A full scan of 18 months of orders pulls hundreds of GB through the buffer pool, evicting the hot working set your OLTP queries depend on. Those queries now hit disk instead of RAM. This is usually the largest effect and the least obvious.

Mechanism 2 — I/O and CPU contention. Sequential scans saturate disk bandwidth and burn CPU on aggregation, so transactional queries queue behind them.

Mechanism 3 — MVCC / vacuum starvation. A long-running analytic transaction pins every row version created since it started. VACUUM cannot reclaim them, the tables bloat, and plans degrade. This one persists after the query finishes, which is why the problem seems not to go away.

What I would do, in order:

  • Immediately: move the analysts to a read replica. Cheap, fast, and it fixes mechanisms 1 and 2 for the primary. It does not fix 3 on the replica (long queries there cause replication conflicts or lag), but the primary is protected.
  • Properly: stream changes via CDC (Debezium off the WAL) into a columnar warehouse — ClickHouse, BigQuery, Snowflake. Their queries then run on a system built for scans, typically 10–100x faster, and add zero load to the primary.
  • Not: adding indexes to make their queries faster. Analytic queries scan; indexes do not help scans, and every index you add slows every write on the OLTP path.

The transferable lesson: when two workloads have opposite access patterns, the answer is almost never to tune one system into serving both. It is to give each the storage layout it needs and connect them with a log. This is the same “derived data” pattern as materialised views, search indexes and caches — one source of truth, many purpose-built read models.

🎓 Understanding Check — Storage & Retrieval

Teaching questions with answers supplied.
Why can't a hash index answer range queries?

Because hashing deliberately destroys order — adjacent keys land in unrelated buckets, which is exactly what makes the distribution uniform. So “all keys between A and B” has no locality and degenerates into scanning every bucket.

Hash indexes also require the whole key space to fit in memory to be fast, and they handle collisions poorly on disk. The property that makes them fast for point lookups is the property that makes range scans impossible. B-trees and SSTables keep keys sorted precisely to preserve that ability.

Why do LSM-trees achieve higher write throughput than B-trees?

Because a B-tree write is a random write: find the leaf page holding that key, read it, modify it, write it back. Once the dataset exceeds RAM, each write costs a seek.

An LSM write is an append to a log plus an insert into an in-memory structure — no seek at all. The data reaches disk later as one large sequential write. The LSM does not do less work; it defers the work and reorganises it into sequential I/O, which even modern SSDs handle several times faster.

What is the real operational risk of running an LSM-based store?

Compaction falling behind. It is a background process competing with foreground traffic for I/O and CPU, and when it loses, SSTable count rises, read amplification rises, and read p99 degrades. In the worst case compaction cannot even start because it transiently needs free disk space comparable to the data being merged.

Practical consequences: never run an LSM store above ~70% disk, provision compaction throughput explicitly, and alert on SSTable count and pending compactions — not just on query latency, which tells you too late.

Why does adding an index slow down writes, and by how much?

Every index is a second copy of some of your data, kept sorted. A write to the table becomes a write to the table plus a write to each index — each with its own page location, its own potential split, and its own WAL records.

Roughly: each additional index adds meaningful write cost and, on a B-tree, its own random I/O. Five indexes on a hot table can easily halve write throughput. The right discipline is to audit for unused indexes — pg_stat_user_indexes shows scan counts, and production tables routinely carry indexes nothing has used in years.

Why is column storage so much better at compression than row storage?

Because compression exploits repetition, and a column is homogeneous: one type, often few distinct values, frequently sorted. A country column over a billion rows has maybe 200 distinct values — bitmap plus run-length encoding makes that almost free.

A row mixes an integer id, a timestamp, a string and a float side by side. There is little local repetition to exploit. And the compression pays off twice: less disk I/O, and the compressed column often fits in CPU cache, enabling vectorised processing over data that never leaves L2.

When would you deliberately choose a document model over relational?

When the data is genuinely a self-contained tree that you always load whole — a document, an event payload, a product with wildly varying attributes per category — and you do not need many-to-many relationships between the parts.

The moment you need “show me everyone who worked at company X”, you have a many-to-one relationship pointing the wrong way, and you are about to emulate a join in application code. That emulated join is slower, less correct and impossible to optimise. Document stores win on locality; they lose on relationships.

🎯 Matching the storage engine to the workload
User accounts, orders
B-tree OLTP (PostgreSQL/MySQL). Predictable reads, transactions, constraints.
Time-series / metrics
LSM with time-window compaction. Huge write rate; expiry drops whole files.
Chat message history
LSM (Cassandra). Write-heavy, read by recent range within a partition.
Analytics / BI dashboards
Columnar (ClickHouse, BigQuery, Snowflake), fed by CDC. Never the OLTP primary.
Full-text search
Inverted index (Elasticsearch), maintained from the log — not a database index.
Session / cache
In-memory (Redis). Durability is optional by design; speed is the point.
Social graph
Graph model or a purpose-built store. Recursive joins in SQL do not scale to deep traversal.
🌱 Takeaway — Storage & Retrieval

Every storage engine is a bet about your access pattern. There is no fastest engine, only an engine matched or mismatched to a workload.

  • Model first, engine second. Relationship shape picks relational / document / graph; the storage engine follows.
  • “Schemaless” means schema-on-read. You pay for the schema either at migration time or forever in defensive code.
  • The WAL is the centre of everything — durability, replication, and CDC are all the same log viewed differently.
  • B-tree = random writes, predictable reads. LSM = sequential writes, deferred cost as compaction. The LSM does not remove work; it moves it into the background where it becomes an operational concern.
  • OLTP and OLAP are opposite machines. Seeks versus bandwidth. Never make one database serve both — connect them with a log.
  • Column storage wins twice: reads only the columns needed, and compresses far better because columns are homogeneous.

📝 Interview Q&A

Why is Cassandra faster at writes than PostgreSQL for the same workload?

Cassandra uses an LSM-tree storage engine. Writes go to RAM (MemTable) first, then are periodically flushed to immutable SST files on disk as sequential writes. Sequential writes on SSD are 10-100× faster than random writes.

PostgreSQL uses B-tree. Every write must find the correct leaf page in the B-tree (random read), modify it (random write), update indexes (more random writes), and write to WAL. More I/O operations, mostly random.

Trade-off: Cassandra's LSM-tree makes reads slower (must check MemTable + multiple SST levels + Bloom filter). PostgreSQL's B-tree makes reads faster (O(log N) deterministic lookup). You choose based on write vs read ratio. Cassandra is designed for write-heavy workloads; PostgreSQL for read-heavy OLTP.

Explain MVCC and how it prevents the 'phantom read' anomaly.

MVCC assigns a transaction ID (xid) to each transaction. Every row version is tagged with xmin (the xid that created it) and xmax (the xid that deleted/updated it, or ∞ if still current).

A transaction with xid=100 sees only rows where xmin < 100 AND xmax > 100 (or xmax=∞). This is a snapshot of the database at the moment the transaction started.

Phantom reads: A phantom read is when you run the same query twice in a transaction and get different rows (because another transaction inserted a row). Under MVCC with Repeatable Read isolation, both queries use the same snapshot — new rows inserted by other transactions have xmin > current xid and are invisible. No phantom reads.

Note: PostgreSQL's Serializable Isolation goes further, using SSI (Serializable Snapshot Isolation) to detect write skew anomalies that even Repeatable Read allows.

🎯 Practice Design

Design a Time-Series Database for Infrastructure Metrics

You're building a system to store and query infrastructure metrics (CPU, memory, network) for 100,000 servers, each reporting 100 metrics every 10 seconds. Design the storage layer.

Hint areas to cover:
  • Calculate the write QPS: 100K servers × 100 metrics × 1/10 = how much?
  • Why is a traditional RDBMS wrong here? (Hint: think about access patterns and write amplification)
  • How would an LSM-tree storage engine (like Bigtable/Cassandra) handle this better?
  • What's your data model? Partition key? Clustering key?
  • How do you handle 'downsample' queries (avg CPU for last hour, per-minute resolution)?
  • How do you expire old data efficiently (keep last 90 days)?

Chapter 13
Microservices & Resilience Patterns
Making distributed services fail gracefully — circuit breakers, bulkheads, and service meshes.

Microservices take a monolith and split it into independent, deployable services. Each service owns its data, scales independently, and can be deployed without affecting others. The trade-off: you now have N services, all communicating over the network, all of which can fail independently.

📖 Analogy

A monolith is a single aircraft engine — if it fails, the plane crashes. Microservices are 4 engines — any one can fail without crashing the plane. But now you need 4× the mechanics, communication protocols between engines, and procedures for when one starts misbehaving.

The Cascade Failure Problem

The #1 failure mode in microservices is cascade failure: Service A calls Service B. B is slow. A's threads pile up waiting. A runs out of threads. A becomes slow. Service C calls A. C's threads pile up. C fails. Everything fails.

🎯 Scenario — The Thanksgiving Cascade

Order service calls Payment service. Black Friday. Payment service is under heavy load — responses take 10 seconds instead of 100ms.

Order service has 100 threads. Each thread waits 10 seconds for payment. After 10 seconds, 100 requests are in flight. Thread pool exhausted. New requests to Order service queue up. Order service times out for all clients. Frontend shows errors for everything — including unrelated features like browsing that don't need Payment at all.

One slow service took down an unrelated feature. This is cascade failure.

Circuit Breaker Pattern

Circuit breaker: after too many failures, 'trip' the circuit — fail fast without waiting. Test recovery gradually.

Bulkhead Pattern

Named after ship compartments that prevent flooding from sinking the whole ship. In microservices: isolate resources per downstream service. Service A has two thread pools: one for Payment calls, one for Inventory calls. If Payment slows down and fills its thread pool, Inventory calls are unaffected.

Without bulkheads: a single slow dependency consumes ALL threads → everything fails. With bulkheads: only the threads for that dependency are exhausted → all other features continue working.

Service Mesh

A service mesh is an infrastructure layer that handles all inter-service communication concerns: mTLS, load balancing, circuit breaking, retry, timeouts, observability. It runs as a sidecar proxy (Envoy) next to each service.

The key insight: instead of each service implementing retry logic, circuit breakers, and mTLS in its own language and framework, the sidecar handles all of it transparently. Services only write business logic.

PatternProblem SolvedImplementation
RetryTransient network failures3 retries, exponential backoff with jitter
TimeoutPrevent indefinite waitingPer-request timeout at each hop
Circuit BreakerPrevent cascade failureCount failures → trip → fail fast → probe
BulkheadIsolate failure domainsSeparate thread pools per dependency
Sidecar/MeshCross-cutting concernsEnvoy + Istio: handles mTLS, LB, observability
Health CheckRemove failed instancesLiveness (is it alive?) + Readiness (can it serve?)

📝 Interview Q&A

A service has a 99% success rate. It calls 5 downstream services in sequence, each with 99% success rate. What's the overall success rate?

0.99⁵ = 95.1%. A chain of 5 services, each individually reliable, produces a system that fails 5% of the time. This is why error rates compound in microservice chains.

With 10 services in the chain: 0.99¹⁰ = 90.4%. This is called the reliability tax of microservices. Mitigation: (1) Parallelize where possible — call all 5 simultaneously instead of sequentially, where the system fails only if ANY one fails... wait, that's worse for OR chains (0.99^5 = 95% for AND-chains). (2) Make operations optional — if inventory check fails, proceed with order and verify async. (3) Cache results — if catalog service is slow, serve cached data.

Your circuit breaker opens (trips) and starts failing fast. The client is now getting immediate errors instead of waiting 10 seconds. But the user experience is still broken — what do you do?

Failing fast is step 1. The real goal is a graceful degradation strategy:

(1) Fallback to cache: Return the last known good response from cache. User sees slightly stale data instead of an error.

(2) Default response: Return a sensible default. If payment service is down, show 'payment temporarily unavailable, try again' instead of a 500 error page.

(3) Feature flag: Disable the feature entirely but keep the rest of the app working. 'Recommendations are temporarily unavailable' — but the user can still browse and checkout.

The staff-level insight: design for failure modes upfront. Every call to an external service should have a defined fallback. This is a design review question: 'What does this feature do if Service X is down?'

🎯 Practice Design

Design a Resilient Payment Service

Your payment service calls 4 downstream services: Fraud Detection, Card Processor, Ledger Service, and Notification Service. Any of these can fail. Design the resilience patterns to ensure payment failures are handled gracefully.

Hint areas to cover:
  • Which services are on the critical path (payment fails if they fail) vs optional?
  • For each critical service: what's your timeout and retry strategy?
  • Where do you put circuit breakers? What are the thresholds?
  • Fraud detection takes 200ms on average but spikes to 5s during model reloads. Bulkhead?
  • If the Ledger Service is down, should you still charge the card? Outbox pattern?
  • Notification failure (email) should never fail a payment — how do you ensure this?

⚡ Quick reference
The failure you are trying to stop, and the mechanism that actually stops it. Each closes a different axis — they are not alternatives.
If you need…Reach forBecauseUsed in

Cascading Failure, Derived — and Why One Fix Is Never Enough

Every engineer knows the words “circuit breaker” and “exponential backoff”. Far fewer can say which failure each one actually prevents, which is why systems routinely have three of the five mechanisms and still fall over. Build the failure up and the answer becomes obvious:

🔨 Build it wrong first — deriving the full resilience stack
1
Service B slows down — a slow query, a GC pause, a cold cache. Service A calls B with a timeout and retries three times, the sensible default everyone ships with.
✗ A now sends 3× the traffic to a service that is already struggling. The retries are what finish B off.
→ Retries are a load multiplier applied at exactly the worst moment. That is the whole problem in one line.
2
Add exponential backoff. Wait 1s, then 2s, then 4s before retrying.
✗ Ten thousand clients failed at the same instant, so they all wait 1s together, retry together, wait 2s together, retry together. Continuous overload has become synchronised spikes, each big enough to re-break B.
→ Backoff controls when one client retries. It says nothing about what a population of clients does.
3
Add jitter. Randomise each wait between zero and the computed backoff.
✗ The spikes are gone; the total volume is not. Every client still eventually retries, and the sum still exceeds B’s capacity for as long as B is broken.
→ Jitter fixes timing. It cannot fix volume, because it never removes a retry — it only moves it.
4
Add a retry budget. A client may retry only while retries stay under roughly 10% of its recent request volume.
✗ Volume is bounded and B gets room to recover. But A still calls B on every request and waits out the timeout, so A’s threads are parked for the full duration each time.
→ The budget caps amplification. It does not stop A wasting its own capacity rediscovering, over and over, that B is down.
5
Add a circuit breaker. After a failure threshold, stop calling B at all for a cooling-off period, fail fast, and probe occasionally to see whether it recovered.
✗ A stops wasting threads on B. But A also calls C and D, and if they share one thread pool the requests already parked on B have starved those calls too.
→ The breaker protects the callee, and the caller’s latency. It provides no isolation between dependencies.
6
Add bulkheads. Give each dependency its own bounded concurrency pool, so calls to B can only ever exhaust B’s pool.
✗ Nothing further, for this failure. A degrades in exactly one feature and keeps serving everything else.
→ Isolation is the last axis. A failure in B is now a partial outage rather than a total one — which was the goal all along.
Five mechanisms, five different axes: jitter fixes timing, the budget fixes volume, the circuit breaker fixes duration, bulkheads fix blast radius, and timeouts bound each attempt. None substitutes for another, which is why “we have retries with exponential backoff” is an incomplete answer — it closes one axis out of five. Name the axis each mechanism covers and you have said something most candidates cannot.
WHAT EACH MECHANISM ACTUALLY FIXES failure axis mechanism without it ------------------ ------------------- ------------------------------ per-attempt time timeout threads parked indefinitely retry timing jitter synchronised retry spikes retry volume retry budget unbounded amplification failure duration circuit breaker capacity burned rediscovering the same outage repeatedly blast radius bulkhead one dep takes down all deps wasted work deadline propagation computing replies nobody wants who gets served priority shedding everyone fails equally A system with four of these seven has a specific, predictable way of falling over. Working out WHICH one is missing is usually the whole postmortem.
These are not alternatives to choose between. Each closes one axis, and an axis you leave open is the one your next incident goes through.
⚠ Common misconception
“We have retries with exponential backoff, so we are protected against cascading failure.”

Backoff closes one axis — when a given client retries. It does nothing about total retry volume, nothing about the caller burning its own threads rediscovering a known outage, and nothing about isolation between dependencies. Without jitter it actively creates a new failure mode by synchronising clients that failed together.

There is also a compounding trap: retries nest. If the client retries three times, the gateway retries three times, and the service retries its dependency three times, the bottom service sees up to 27× amplification. The rule that follows is counter-intuitive and worth stating plainly: retry at exactly one layer — the one closest to the user that can still make a meaningful decision — and pass failures straight through everywhere else.

The Circuit Breaker, Precisely

It is a three-state machine, and being exact about the states matters because the half-open state is where the value actually is:

  • Closed — calls pass through; failures are counted over a rolling window. Count a rate, not an absolute: 50 failures out of 50 requests is an outage, 50 out of 50,000 is background noise.
  • Open — calls fail immediately without touching the dependency. This is what frees the caller's threads and gives the callee room to recover.
  • Half-open — after a cooling period, allow a few trial requests. Success closes the breaker; failure reopens it. Without half-open you have built an outage detector that never recovers, and the probe must be limited to a handful of requests or reopening simply re-floods a service that had almost recovered.

The failure mode worth naming: a breaker with too sensitive a threshold trips on ordinary tail-latency noise and turns a healthy dependency into an unavailable one. A circuit breaker is a load-shedding device pointed at your own dependencies, and like all shedding it can shed too much.

✎ Mini exercise 16

A checkout service calls payments (critical), inventory (critical), recommendations (optional) and loyalty points (optional). All four share one 200-thread pool. Recommendations degrades to 8-second responses — slow, not down, so its health checks still pass. Checkout stops serving entirely, including pages that never used recommendations.

Work out: the mechanism of the outage, and which four changes you would make, in what order.

Show the worked answer

The mechanism is thread-pool exhaustion, and the fact that recommendations is optional is what makes it infuriating. At 8 seconds per call, even modest traffic parks threads for 8 seconds each: roughly 25 requests/sec to recommendations is enough to hold all 200 threads (25 × 8 = 200). Once the pool is empty, every endpoint blocks waiting for a thread — including checkout paths that never call recommendations at all. A slow dependency is more dangerous than a dead one, because a dead one fails fast and returns the thread immediately.

The order matters — cheapest and highest-impact first:

  1. Bulkhead. Cap recommendations at, say, 20 concurrent calls. This alone ends the outage: recommendations can be as slow as it likes and 180 threads remain for everything else. It is the single change that converts a total outage into a degraded feature.
  2. Aggressive timeout on the optional calls. Eight seconds is far beyond any sensible budget for a recommendation carousel. Give it 200 ms, then give up. A timeout is derived from what the caller can afford, never from what the callee usually takes.
  3. Circuit breaker on recommendations. Once it is reliably slow, stop calling it at all for a while and stop paying even the 200 ms.
  4. Graceful degradation. Render checkout with an empty recommendations panel. The optional dependency should never have been able to fail the page.

The transferable principle: an optional dependency that can fail your request is not optional — it is a required dependency you have not admitted to. The architectural question is not “is this call important?” but “what happens to the response if this call never returns?”, and the answer must be enforced by a bulkhead rather than by intent. Same reasoning as Ch 10's load shedding: decide in advance what you are willing to lose, because under pressure you will lose something.

🧠 Checking your understanding — resilience

Answers supplied. These separate people who have configured a resilience library from people who have debugged an outage.
How should you actually choose a timeout value?
From the caller's budget downward, never from the callee's observed latency upward. Start with what the user-facing request can afford end to end, subtract what the rest of the chain needs, and give this call the remainder. Setting a timeout at “p99 plus a margin” is the common error: it guarantees that whenever the dependency degrades you wait as long as it takes to fail, which is exactly the wrong moment to be patient. The timeout must also be shorter than your caller's, or you will be computing a response nobody is waiting for — which is what deadline propagation enforces automatically.
Why is a slow dependency more dangerous than a dead one?
A dead dependency fails immediately: connection refused, thread returned, breaker tripped on an obvious signal. A slow one holds resources for the full timeout on every call while continuing to pass shallow health checks. Concurrency is latency multiplied by rate, so an eightfold latency increase consumes eight times the threads at the same request rate. Almost every “the whole site went down because of one service” story is a slow dependency, not a dead one — which is why bulkheads and concurrency limits matter more than availability monitoring.
Where should retries live in a chain of five services?
At exactly one layer, and it should be the one closest to the user that can still make a meaningful decision. Retries nest multiplicatively, so three layers each retrying three times is 27× amplification against the bottom service. Everything else should propagate the failure immediately. A useful convention: retries are permitted at the edge or in the client, and every internal service fails fast so the decision is made once, by whoever knows what the user is waiting for.
What does a service mesh actually buy, and what does it cost?
It moves timeouts, retries, circuit breaking, mTLS and telemetry out of every application into a sidecar proxy, so policy is uniform and language-independent — genuinely valuable in a polyglot estate where otherwise every team reimplements the same five mechanisms differently and wrongly. The costs are real: an extra network hop each way, a sidecar's memory per pod, and a control plane now on the critical path for everything. Worth it with many services in many languages; overhead with six services in one. And note it does not decide what the timeouts should be — it only makes them consistent.
Your service is healthy but the user-facing request fails. How do you find the cause?
This is exactly what distributed tracing exists for: a trace ID propagated through every hop, producing a span tree that shows where the time went and which call failed. Without it you are correlating dashboards across a dozen services by eye and the causal link is guesswork. Note the ordering lesson — tracing is a design decision, not an operational one. It has to be threaded through the code before the incident, which is why it belongs here and not only in Ch 14.
When are microservices the wrong choice?
When the organisation cannot yet pay their operational cost, which is most of the time at the start. Splitting a system converts fast, reliable in-process function calls into slow, unreliable network calls — each of which now needs a timeout, a retry policy, a breaker and a trace. You take on distributed transactions, eventual consistency and versioned interfaces in exchange for independent deployability and team autonomy. A good trade when teams block each other on deploys; a bad one when three engineers are trying to ship a product. Microservices are an organisational solution with a technical cost, so “how many teams do you have?” is more diagnostic than any architectural argument.
🎯 Where each mechanism actually earns its keep
Optional enrichment calls
Bulkhead + short timeout + degrade. Recommendations, related items, social proof. The response must render without them, and only a concurrency limit makes that true under load.
Payments and other third parties
Circuit breaker + idempotency key. You do not control their capacity, and an ambiguous timeout must never become a double charge. Ch 7, D19
Client-to-edge traffic
Jitter + retry budget. Millions of independent clients failing simultaneously are the classic synchronised-retry population. Ch 10
Internal service-to-service
Deadline propagation + fail fast, no retry. Retry once, at the edge. Internal hops that each retry create multiplicative amplification.
Shared infrastructure (cache, database)
Concurrency limit + shed. Never let a caller send more concurrent work than the dependency can absorb — the cache-down stampede in Ch 9 is exactly this failure.
Fleet-wide changes
Staged rollout + automatic halt. Resilience against your own deploys, which cause more incidents than dependency failure does. D18
🌱 Takeaway — Microservices & resilience

Every mechanism here closes one axis of failure, and an axis you leave open is where your next incident goes.

  • Timeouts come from the caller's budget, not the callee's p99. Deriving them upward from observed latency guarantees maximum patience at the worst possible moment.
  • A slow dependency is worse than a dead one. It holds threads for the full timeout and passes shallow health checks. Concurrency is latency × rate.
  • Retry at exactly one layer. Nesting multiplies: three layers of three attempts is 27× against the bottom service.
  • Backoff, jitter, budget, breaker and bulkhead are not alternatives. They close timing, population timing, volume, duration and blast radius respectively.
  • An optional dependency that can fail your request is not optional. Enforce it with a bulkhead, not with good intentions.
  • Microservices are an organisational solution with a technical cost. “How many teams?” is the more diagnostic question.

Chapter 14 turns all of this into something you can see: none of these mechanisms is trustworthy unless you can measure whether it fired, and how often.

Chapter 14
Observability & SRE
If you can't measure it, you can't fix it — and you can't be on-call for it.
⚡ Quick reference
Measure what users feel, alert on what you would wake someone for.
If you need…Reach forBecauseUsed in
To know if users are having a bad timeSLIs on the four golden signalsLatency, traffic, errors, saturation — measured at the edge, where the user is.Google SRE, every mature on-call rota
To decide when to stop shipping featuresError budgetTurns reliability from an argument into arithmetic: budget spent means reliability work, budget left means ship.Google SRE, SLO-driven teams
Latency you can act onp99 and p99.9, never the meanOne slow dependency in a 100-call page affects most pages; averages hide exactly the tail that matters.Ch 1, D11
To find where a request went wrongDistributed tracingPer-request spans across services turn “the site is slow” into a specific call.OpenTelemetry, Jaeger, Ch 13
Cheap, high-volume numeric signalsMetrics, not logs~1.4 bytes per compressed datapoint against ~300 bytes per log line, for the same period.Prometheus, D11
To debug something you did not anticipateStructured logs + exemplarsMetrics answer questions you thought of in advance; logs answer the ones you did not.D11, Loki, Elasticsearch
Alerts people do not ignorePage on symptoms, not causes“Error rate above SLO” is actionable; “CPU above 80%” is usually noise.Google SRE alerting philosophy

Observability is the ability to understand what your system is doing from the outside, by examining its outputs. The three pillars are logs, metrics, and traces. At Google, this is formalized into the SRE (Site Reliability Engineering) discipline.

SLI, SLO, SLA — The Language of Reliability

These three terms define how you measure and commit to reliability:

  • SLI (Service Level Indicator): A specific measurement. Examples: request success rate, p99 latency, error rate.
  • SLO (Service Level Objective): A target for an SLI. Examples: 'success rate ≥ 99.9% over 30 days', 'p99 latency ≤ 200ms'.
  • SLA (Service Level Agreement): A legal contract with customers — SLO with consequences (usually credits/refunds if breached). Always weaker than your internal SLO — never set your SLA equal to your SLO.

Error Budgets — Making Reliability a Business Decision

Error budget = 1 - SLO. If SLO = 99.9%, error budget = 0.1% = 43.2 minutes/month of allowed downtime.

Error budgets make reliability a shared responsibility between SREs and developers: if the budget is full, no new risky features get deployed. If budget is healthy, the team can move fast. This removes the adversarial relationship between 'dev wants to ship' and 'SRE wants stability.'

The Three Pillars

PillarWhatBest ForTools
LogsTimestamped, structured events. "User 123 checked out at 14:32:01. Order ID: 456"Debugging specific incidents. Audit trails.Stackdriver, ELK, Splunk
MetricsNumeric aggregates over time. "99th percentile latency = 245ms"Dashboards, alerting, capacity planningPrometheus, Datadog, Cloud Monitoring
TracesEnd-to-end journey of a single request across servicesFinding latency bottlenecks across service boundariesDapper (Google), Jaeger, OpenTelemetry
🔬 Google-Level Depth — Google Dapper — The Paper That Defined Distributed Tracing

Dapper (2010 Google paper) introduced the trace context pattern: every request gets a globally unique trace ID. At each service boundary, a new span is created with the parent span's ID. All spans are reported to a central collector.

Critically, Dapper samples at 1/1024 of requests. At Google's scale (billions of requests/day), sampling everything would be petabytes of trace data. 1/1024 still gives thousands of samples per operation per minute — statistically meaningful for performance analysis.

The real insight: traces turn 'our API is slow' from a guess into a fact: 'the API is slow because Cart Service spends 180ms waiting for Inventory Service, which spends 150ms in a DB query for which no index exists.' Actionable in minutes, not days.

RED and USE Frameworks

Use these frameworks to know what to monitor:

FrameworkScopeMetrics
REDEvery service/endpointRate (requests/sec) + Errors (error rate %) + Duration (latency p50/p99/p999)
USEEvery resource (CPU, disk, network)Utilization (%) + Saturation (queue length) + Errors (hardware errors)

Percentiles — Why the Average Is Always the Wrong Number

This deserves its own section because getting it wrong is nearly universal, and because the fix costs nothing.

100 requests. 99 take 10ms. One takes 5,000ms. MEAN = (99×10 + 5000) / 100 = 59.9ms Describes NOBODY. No user experienced 59.9ms. It is not the typical case (10ms) or the bad case (5s). p50 = 10ms "half of users are faster than this" p99 = 5000ms "1 in 100 users has this experience" The mean hid both facts it was asked about.

And it gets worse, because the slow requests are systematically the important ones. The customer with the most data, the most orders, the largest cart — they have the most rows to process, so they are slowest. Your p99 is disproportionately your best customers. Amazon has noted that a 100ms latency increase measurably reduces sales, and that they specify latency targets at p99.9 for exactly this reason.

Tail latency amplification — the arithmetic that surprises people

A single page needs 100 parallel backend calls. Each backend has a 1% chance of exceeding 1 second. (p99 = 1s) The page is slow if ANY call is slow: P(all 100 fast) = 0.99100 = 0.366 P(page slow) = 1 − 0.366 = 63% A "1-in-100" backend event becomes a majority-of-pages event. Each service is individually healthy at 99% and the product is broken. This is why fan-out architectures must obsess over the tail, and why "our p99 is fine" is not a statement about user experience.
The parent request inherits the worst of its children, every single time.
⚠ Common misconception
“We average the p99 across our servers to get the overall p99.”

Percentiles do not average. The mean of ten servers' p99s is not the fleet's p99 — it is a number with no statistical meaning at all, and it is usually optimistic.

To aggregate correctly you must combine the distributions, not the summary values: keep histograms (Prometheus histogram buckets) or mergeable sketches (t-digest, HDRHistogram) and compute the percentile from the merged data.

This matters in practice: a dashboard averaging per-instance p99s will look calm while one instance is destroying real users' experience.

🔍 Describing load before you can describe performance

You cannot reason about scalability until you can state the load in numbers. DDIA's framing — load parameters — is the discipline of choosing the few numbers that actually drive your architecture.

The classic illustration is Twitter. The obvious parameters look like this:

  • Post tweet: ~4,600 requests/sec average, 12,000/sec peak
  • Home timeline reads: ~300,000 requests/sec

Those numbers are not the hard part. The load parameter that actually determines the architecture is the distribution of followers per user — because that decides how much work a single tweet creates under fan-out-on-write. A user with 100 followers is trivial; a user with 30 million is a different system.

The lesson generalises: the load parameter that matters is rarely the headline QPS. It is usually a distribution — followers per user, items per cart, rows per tenant, messages per conversation. Ask for the shape of the distribution, especially its tail, not just the average.

✎ Mini exercise 10

Your API dashboard shows: mean latency 45ms, p99 180ms. Both are within SLO and have been stable for months. Support insists some customers experience multi-second page loads. Engineering cannot reproduce it.

Work out: at least three reasons the dashboard can be simultaneously accurate and misleading.

Show the worked answer

1. You are measuring the wrong place. Server-side latency excludes DNS, TCP and TLS setup, network transit, and client rendering. A user on mobile in another region can experience 2s while your server honestly reports 45ms. Measure at the client, or at least at the edge.

2. Aggregation is hiding a subpopulation. A global p99 over all endpoints and all customers is dominated by your highest-volume, simplest endpoint. If 0.5% of traffic belongs to enterprise tenants with 1,000× the data, their experience is invisible — they are inside the 1% you are not measuring. Slice percentiles by endpoint, by tenant tier, and by region.

3. One page is many requests. If a page load makes 40 API calls, then a 180ms p99 per call means the probability that all 40 are fast is 0.9940 ≈ 67% — so a third of page loads contain at least one slow call. The user-facing SLI must be the page, not the request.

Also worth checking: the dashboard may average per-instance percentiles (statistically meaningless, see above); it may exclude failed or timed-out requests, which are the slowest ones by definition; and a 1-minute resolution can smooth away a 5-second stall entirely.

The transferable lesson: when metrics and users disagree, the users are right and the metric is measuring the wrong thing. The instinct to trust the dashboard over the support ticket is the instinct to correct.

🎓 Understanding Check — Measuring Systems

Teaching questions with answers supplied.
Why are tail latencies important when they affect so few requests?

Three reasons. First, the slow requests are systematically your most valuable users — slowness usually correlates with having more data. Second, fan-out amplification turns a 1% per-call event into a majority-of-pages event. Third, a single user makes many requests in a session, so the chance they hit the tail at least once approaches certainty.

A user who experiences one 5-second load in a session remembers the product as slow, regardless of the other 99 fast requests.

What does “scalability” actually mean, given it is not a property a system has?

It is not a yes/no attribute — “this system is scalable” is close to meaningless. It is a question about a specific growth path: “if load parameter X grows by factor N, what must change to keep performance metric P within its target?”

That phrasing forces the useful conversation: which parameter, growing how much, holding which metric fixed. A system that scales beautifully with more users may fall over when one user gets 1,000× bigger.

Why doesn't adding machines automatically make a system scale?

Because scaling out only helps the part of the work that is parallelisable and shared-nothing. Anything serialised — a single leader, a hot row, a global lock, a coordination round trip — does not get faster with more machines, and Amdahl's law caps your gains at the size of that serial fraction.

Worse, some things get worse as you add nodes: consensus commit latency grows with quorum size, scatter/gather tail latency grows with partition count, and gossip and repair traffic grow with membership. The real skill is identifying the serialised component, because that is your actual ceiling.

Why does maintainability get a whole third of DDIA's opening chapter?

Because the majority of a system's cost is incurred after it is first built — in operation, adaptation and debugging — and because unmaintainable systems become unreliable ones. A system nobody understands is a system where every change is a risk.

The three sub-goals are worth naming precisely: operability (make it easy to run — good telemetry, predictable behaviour, self-healing), simplicity (remove accidental complexity, which is complexity not inherent to the problem — abstraction is the main tool), and evolvability (make it easy to change, which is largely about schema evolution and loose coupling).

🌱 Takeaway — Measuring Systems Honestly
  • Never state performance as a mean. Use percentiles with an explicit window and measurement point.
  • Percentiles do not average. Merge histograms or sketches, never average p99s.
  • Fan-out amplifies the tail — a 1% slow-call rate over 100 calls means 63% slow pages.
  • Load parameters are usually distributions, not averages. Ask for the shape of the tail.
  • Scalability is a question, not a property: which parameter, growing how much, holding which metric?
  • When metrics and users disagree, the users are right.

📝 Interview Q&A

Your p99 latency SLO is 200ms. You're at 250ms p99. Walk me through how you'd diagnose this.

Step 1 — Is it all requests or a subset? Break down p99 by endpoint. Is it one slow endpoint or all of them? By user region? By request size?

Step 2 — Distributed trace. Pull a sample of slow traces (>200ms). The trace shows you which service hop is contributing the most latency. Is it your service? Downstream DB? Cache miss? Network?

Step 3 — Correlate with metrics. Is CPU high (compute bottleneck)? Is DB query time high (query problem)? Is cache hit rate low (cache miss → DB)?

Step 4 — Check recent changes. Was a deploy made recently? New feature that added a slow DB query? Index dropped?

Staff answer adds: 'I'd also check if p50 is also elevated — if only p99 is high but p50 is fine, it's a tail latency issue (GC pauses, lock contention, hot rows). If both are elevated, it's a systemic issue (slow new code path, resource saturation).'

Security & API Design
Protecting your system and making it a pleasure to use.
⚡ Quick reference
Push validation to the edge, and make every interface survive being versioned.
If you need…Reach forBecauseUsed in
To prove who a caller isOAuth 2.0 / OIDC + short-lived tokensShort expiry bounds the damage of a leak; revocation lists are the fallback, not the mechanism.Google Sign-In, Auth0, every modern API

Secrets that do not leakShort-lived credentials from a brokerA rotated secret in a config file is still a secret in a config file.Vault, KMS, workload identity

Authentication vs Authorization

Authentication (AuthN): Who are you? Verify identity. Username + password, OAuth token, certificate.

Authorization (AuthZ): What can you do? Once identity is confirmed, check permissions. RBAC (Role-Based), ABAC (Attribute-Based), or ACL.

The Rule: Never conflate them. Authenticate at the gateway. Authorize at every service (zero trust — just because the request came through the gateway doesn't mean it's authorized for this specific resource).

JWT — Inside the Token

JWT = 3 base64-encoded sections separated by dots. Payload is NOT encrypted — only signed. Don't put secrets in JWT claims.

API Design Principles

REST vs gRPC vs GraphQL

AspectRESTgRPCGraphQL
TransportHTTP/1.1 (HTTP/2 optional)HTTP/2 (required)HTTP/1.1+
FormatJSON (human-readable)Protobuf (binary, typed)JSON
TypingLoose (OpenAPI/Swagger)Strong (proto file)Schema (SDL)
StreamingLimited (SSE, chunked)Native bi-directionalSubscriptions (WebSocket)
Best forPublic APIs, browser clientsInternal service-to-serviceMobile with variable data needs
LatencyModerate (JSON parse)Low (binary, multiplexed)Moderate

Idempotency — Critical for Financial APIs

An operation is idempotent if calling it N times produces the same result as calling it once. GET is idempotent. DELETE is idempotent. POST is NOT by default.

For payment APIs: add an Idempotency-Key header. Server stores (key → response) for 24 hours. If the same key comes in again, return the stored response. Client can safely retry on network failure without double-charging.

API Versioning

  • URL versioning (/v1/users, /v2/users): Visible, easy to cache. Most common.
  • Header versioning (Accept: application/vnd.api+json;version=2): Cleaner URLs. Harder to test.
  • Never break backwards compatibility: Add fields; never remove. Never change field types. Deprecate over 12+ months.

Pagination — Cursor vs Offset

Offset pagination (?page=50&size=20) requires the DB to skip 1,000 rows — O(N) cost. Breaks when items are inserted/deleted during pagination. Never use at scale.

Cursor pagination (?after=eyJpZCI6MTAwMH0): the cursor encodes the last seen item (e.g., base64(id=1000)). Query: WHERE id > 1000 LIMIT 20. O(1) cost. Stable under writes. Always use at scale.

Encoding and Evolution — How Systems Change Without Downtime

🔗
This section is about the third pillar from Chapter 14: evolvability. Every system outlives its original schema. The question is not whether your data format changes, but whether it can change while the system is running.

The core problem: in any deployment large enough to roll gradually, old and new code run simultaneously, and old and new data coexist for years. That forces two distinct compatibility requirements, and mixing them up is the source of most deploy-time outages.

TWO DIRECTIONS — and you need BOTH BACKWARD COMPATIBILITY new code can read OLD data Usually easy: you know the old format, you wrote it. Required because old data lives forever in your database. FORWARD COMPATIBILITY old code can read NEW data Harder: the old code must ignore fields it has never heard of. Required because during a rolling deploy, un-upgraded nodes receive data written by upgraded ones. ⇩ THE CASE PEOPLE FORGET ⇩ ROLLBACK. Even a perfectly forward-compatible deploy must survive being reversed — the OLD code must tolerate data the NEW code wrote. If your rollback corrupts data, you do not have a deploy. You have a bet.
A rolling deploy is a period during which your system runs two versions at once, in both directions.
FormatHow it identifies fieldsSchema evolutionUse when
JSON / XMLBy name, in every message — verbose and repeatedAd-hoc; readers must be written defensivelyPublic APIs, human debugging, browser clients
Protocol BuffersBy field number. Names are compile-time onlyAdd optional fields with new numbers. Never reuse a numberInternal RPC, high volume
AvroBy position, using a writer schema and a reader schema resolved at read timeExcellent — designed for it. Great for dynamically-generated schemasData lakes, Kafka with a schema registry, big-data files
ThriftField IDs, like protobufSimilar to protobufLegacy; largely superseded
💡 Why field numbers rather than names

Protobuf's central trick: the wire format carries 2: "Rishi", not "name": "Rishi". That single decision gives you three things at once.

Size — typically 3–10× smaller than the equivalent JSON, because names are not repeated on every message. Renaming for free — change name to full_name in the schema and the wire format is unchanged, so nothing breaks. Forward compatibility by default — an old reader encountering field number 7 that it does not know simply skips it, because the wire type tells it how many bytes to jump.

And the corresponding rule: a field number is permanent. Reusing the number of a deleted field is the one truly catastrophic mistake, because old data will be silently reinterpreted as the new type. Mark removed numbers reserved.

The safe migration: expand and contract

Any schema change that looks like a rename or a type change must become a sequence of independently-deployable, independently-reversible steps:

THE UNSAFE VERSION (one deploy) ALTER TABLE users RENAME name TO full_name; → every un-upgraded node breaks instantly → rollback also breaks, because the column is gone THE SAFE VERSION (five deploys, each reversible) 1. EXPAND add full_name (nullable). Nothing reads it yet. old code unaffected — it does not know the column exists 2. DUAL-WRITE write BOTH name and full_name rollback still safe: name is still current 3. BACKFILL copy historical rows in batches throttled, resumable, no long transaction (see Ch 12: vacuum) 4. SWITCH reads move to full_name; keep dual-writing rollback STILL safe — this is why we keep writing both 5. CONTRACT stop writing name, then drop it (days later) Each step is safe on its own AND safe to reverse. That is the whole point — not five deploys for their own sake, but five points at which you can stop.
⚠ Common misconception
“Our deploy is backward compatible, so it's safe.”

Backward compatibility covers new code reading old data. It says nothing about the two situations that actually break deploys:

During the rollout, un-upgraded nodes receive data written by upgraded ones — that needs forward compatibility. During a rollback, the old code must handle everything the new code wrote — also forward compatibility, and often overlooked entirely because rollback is only exercised in an emergency.

The test that catches this: can you deploy version N+1 to half your fleet, and then roll it back, with zero data loss and zero errors? If nobody has ever tried, you do not know.

🔍 Three dataflow modes, three different lifetimes
  • Through databases. The writer may be long gone; data outlives every process that touched it. Data outlives code — so an unknown field written by a newer version must survive a read-modify-write by an older one, rather than being silently dropped. Many ORMs get this wrong and quietly erase fields they do not know about.
  • Through services (REST/RPC). Compatibility is bounded by how long old clients exist. You control server rollout; you do not control a mobile app installed on a phone that never updates. Server code must stay backward compatible essentially forever, which is why API versioning exists.
  • Through async messages. The most forgiving: producer and consumer are decoupled in time and neither blocks the other. But a message sitting in a queue during a deploy is read by whichever version happens to consume it, so both directions matter here too.
✎ Mini exercise 12

Your Order protobuf has int32 amount_cents = 4;. Finance now needs multi-currency, so you want Money amount = 4; with an amount and a currency code.

A junior engineer proposes changing the type in place, keeping field number 4, and deploying everything at once.

Work out: exactly what breaks, and what you would do instead.

Show the worked answer

What breaks: field number 4 currently has wire type varint (an int32). Money is a message, wire type length-delimited. Any reader that has not been upgraded will read field 4 with the wrong wire type — and depending on the library, either throw a parse error or, worse, silently produce garbage.

And this affects more than live traffic: every historical Order ever persisted or sitting in a Kafka topic still has an int32 in field 4. New code reading old records hits the same mismatch in reverse. “Deploy everything at once” is impossible anyway — you cannot atomically upgrade a fleet, and you certainly cannot upgrade the data already at rest.

What to do instead:

  • Add a new field number: Money amount_v2 = 17;. Leave field 4 exactly as it is.
  • Dual-write: populate both. Field 4 gets the cents value (assume the legacy currency); field 17 gets the full Money.
  • Migrate readers to prefer 17 and fall back to 4 when 17 is absent. Backfill historical records where feasible.
  • Much later, once no reader and no retained data depends on it, stop writing 4 and mark it reserved 4; so nobody can ever reuse that number.

The rule to carry away: field numbers are permanent identifiers, not labels. Reusing one is the single most destructive schema mistake, because it does not error — it silently reinterprets old bytes as a new type, and the corruption is discovered much later in data nobody was watching.

The wider principle: when a type must change, you never mutate — you add alongside, migrate, and remove. Same shape as expand/contract in SQL, and the same reason: you cannot change data and code at the same instant.

🎓 Understanding Check — Encoding & Evolution

Teaching questions with answers supplied.
Why does forward compatibility tend to be harder than backward compatibility?

Because backward compatibility is a problem you can solve with knowledge you already have — you know the old format and can write code to handle it. Forward compatibility requires code written today to behave sensibly when it meets data invented tomorrow.

The only way to achieve it is to build tolerance in from the start: ignore unknown fields rather than erroring, do not assume a closed set of enum values, and preserve unknown data through a read-modify-write. Formats like protobuf and Avro give you this by design; hand-rolled parsers usually do not.

Why is JSON a poor choice for high-volume internal service traffic?

Three reasons that compound. Size: field names repeat in every message, typically 3–10× the bytes of protobuf. Parse cost: text parsing and string allocation are far more expensive than reading length-prefixed binary. No schema enforcement: a breaking change is discovered at runtime in production rather than at compile time.

At a million internal calls per second, the size and CPU differences are measured in entire machines. The usual answer is protobuf/gRPC internally, JSON at the public edge where debuggability and browser support matter more than bytes.

Why does “data outlives code” change how you write database access code?

Because a row written five years ago by a version of your service that no longer exists must still be readable, and because a row written by tomorrow's version may be read by today's.

The concrete hazard is the read-modify-write cycle: old code reads a record containing a field it does not know, updates one attribute, and writes the whole record back — silently deleting the unknown field. The user's data is gone with no error anywhere. Preserving unknown fields through a round trip is a real requirement, not a theoretical one.

Why does the expand/contract migration keep dual-writing even after reads have switched?

Because that is the step that preserves rollback. If you stopped writing the old column at the same moment you switched reads, then rolling back would leave the old code reading a column that has been stale since the switch — silently serving wrong data rather than failing loudly.

Keeping the dual-write is what makes step 4 reversible, and reversibility is the entire purpose of the sequence. The old column is only dropped once you are confident you will never go back.

🌱 Takeaway — Encoding & Evolution
  • Rolling deploys mean two versions run at once, so you need backward and forward compatibility — and rollback needs the harder of the two.
  • Field numbers, not names, are what make binary formats evolvable. Numbers are permanent; reusing one silently corrupts data.
  • Expand → dual-write → backfill → switch → contract. Five reversible steps instead of one irreversible one.
  • Data outlives code. Preserve unknown fields through read-modify-write or you will silently delete users' data.
  • protobuf/gRPC internally, JSON at the edge is the standard, defensible split.

📝 Interview Q&A

A JWT expires in 15 minutes. How do you implement 'stay logged in for 30 days' without making the access token last 30 days?

Two-token strategy: Access token (JWT, 15 min TTL) + Refresh token (opaque, 30 day TTL, stored in DB).

Flow: Login → receive both tokens. Access token used for every API call (verified by signature — no DB lookup). At expiry (or 1 min before, proactively): send refresh token → auth service validates against DB → issues new access + refresh tokens → rotate refresh token (old one invalid).

If access token is stolen: expires in 15 min. Attacker has 15 min window. For high security, add IP binding or device fingerprint to refresh token.

If refresh token is stolen: 30 day window. Mitigated by refresh token rotation — if attacker uses the refresh token first, the legitimate user's next refresh fails, alerting them.

Design a URL Shortener (TinyURL / bit.ly)

Difficulty: Medium  .  Target: 45 min
[list] 1. Requirements
❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
What is the read-to-write ratio?
At 100:1 or higher this stops being a database problem and becomes a caching and CDN problem — which changes the entire design.
Are custom aliases allowed?
A yes introduces a global uniqueness constraint and a collision path that a pure counter design does not have.
Do links expire?
Decides whether you need TTL, garbage collection, and whether short codes can be safely reused.
Do we need per-click analytics?
This is what forces 302 over 301. A 301 lets browsers and the CDN absorb the redirect and you never see the hit.
Is it acceptable for codes to be guessable?
A sequential counter in base62 leaks your creation volume and lets anyone enumerate every link ever made.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.

Functional Requirements:

  • Given a long URL, generate a unique 7-character short code
  • Redirect short.ly/abc1234 -> original long URL (HTTP redirect)
  • Optional custom alias: user picks their own short code
  • Optional TTL: URLs expire after N days
  • Analytics: click count, referrer, geography (optional stretch)

Non-Functional Requirements:

  • Availability: 99.99% (52 min/yr downtime max)
  • Redirect latency: p99 < 20ms globally
  • Write latency: p99 < 200ms (less critical)
  • Scale: 100M new URLs/day, 10B redirects/day
  • Read/Write ratio: 100:1
[chart] 2. Capacity Estimation
⚖ Assumptions — and what breaks if each is wrong
100M new URLs/day, 10B redirects/day
If the ratio were closer to 1:1 the CDN and cache tier stop paying for themselves and this becomes a write-throughput design.
Short codes are 7 characters, base62
62^7 is ~3.5 trillion. At 100M/day that is ~95 years of headroom; at 10B/day it is under a year and the code length must grow.
Links are effectively permanent
If most links expired in 30 days, storage would plateau and a TTL sweep becomes a required component rather than an optional one.

Assumptions: 100M new URLs/day, 10B redirects/day

[plug] 3. API Design
POST /api/v1/urls Body: { long_url, alias?, ttl_days? } Response: 201 { short_code, short_url, expires_at? } Errors: 400 (bad URL), 409 (alias taken) GET /{short_code} Response: 301 Location: {long_url} (permanent, CDN-cacheable) 302 Location: {long_url} (if analytics tracking needed) Errors: 404 (not found), 410 (expired) GET /api/v1/urls/{short_code}/stats Response: { clicks, top_countries, referrers, created_at } DELETE /api/v1/urls/{short_code} Response: 204 (idempotent -- safe to retry)
[db] 4. Schema Design
-- Primary store (DynamoDB -- key-value, high read throughput) TABLE urls { short_code VARCHAR(10) PARTITION KEY, long_url TEXT, -- up to 2KB owner_id BIGINT, -- NULL = anonymous created_at TIMESTAMP, expires_at TIMESTAMP, -- NULL = never is_active BOOLEAN DEFAULT true } -- Click analytics (Cassandra -- time-series, append-only) TABLE clicks { short_code VARCHAR(10) PARTITION KEY, clicked_at TIMESTAMP CLUSTERING KEY DESC, country VARCHAR(2), referrer TEXT, ip_hash VARCHAR(64) -- hashed for privacy } -- Click counter (Redis, async flush to DynamoDB every 60s) KEY click_count:{short_code} -> INTEGER
[build] 5. High-Level Architecture
Redirect path — and the viral link that goes cold
request301 redirectlookupmiss
What is moving: a short code out, a 301 back. Because a 301 is permanent, browsers and the CDN cache it, so a popular link is served almost entirely at the edge and the origin never sees most of its traffic.
What goes wrong: a purge or a TTL expiry empties the edge just as a link goes viral. Every request now misses through to the service and the KV store, which was sized on the assumption that the edge absorbs ~95% of reads. The fix is not a bigger database — it is request coalescing so N simultaneous misses become one lookup (Ch 9), plus 301 rather than 302 wherever analytics permits.
Write path creates short code and caches. Read path: CDN -> Redis -> DynamoDB. Analytics on separate async path.
[search] 6. Component Deep Dives

ID Generation -- The Key Decision: The 7-character code needs to be unique globally without coordination overhead. Options:

  • Counter + Base62 (chosen): Each write server gets a range of counters (e.g., 1M IDs/batch from a central counter service). Convert to base62. 627 = ~3.5 trillion URLs. No collision. Predictable length. Pre-allocate ranges to avoid hot path to counter service.
  • Hash of long URL: MD5(long_url) -> first 7 chars. Same URL -> same code. But collision probability and no guaranteed uniqueness.
  • Random: UUID-like. High collision probability at scale without checking DB.

Caching Strategy: Write-through: on creation, immediately cache (short_code -> long_url) in Redis with 24h TTL. Redirect path: Redis O(1) lookup (~0.1ms). Cache miss -> DynamoDB (~5ms). Redis hit rate target: 99% (popular 1M URLs out of 100M cached).

301 vs 302: 301 (permanent) = browsers and CDNs cache it. Near-zero origin load for popular URLs. 302 (temporary) = every redirect hits your server. Use 301 for static URLs, 302 if you need to track every click or change destination later.

Expiration: Store expires_at in DynamoDB. Redis TTL = expires_at - now. On redirect: check expiry -> 410 Gone. Background sweeper job daily deletes expired entries.

[balance] 7. Trade-off Analysis
DecisionChosen vAlternative xReasoning
DB choiceDynamoDBPostgreSQLPure key-value access. No joins. Auto-scales. Managed. 100:1 read ratio means caching dominates -- DB is rarely hit.
ID generationCounter + Base62Random/HashNo collision handling. Predictable length. Pre-allocated ranges eliminate hot path to counter service.
Redirect code301 (popular URLs)302 always301 = CDN/browser cache = massive origin load reduction. 302 required for analytics. Use 301 for non-tracked, 302 for tracked.
AnalyticsAsync Kafka pipelineSync DB write on redirectZero added latency to redirect critical path. Analytics are eventually consistent -- acceptable.
[shield] 8. Fault Tolerance
DynamoDB node failure
Managed multi-AZ DynamoDB: automatic failover. Read from Redis during DB degradation -- cache continues serving popular URLs. On cache miss during outage: return 503 with Retry-After header.
Redis failure
Redis Cluster with replicas. On failure: read API falls through to DynamoDB directly (5ms vs 0.1ms, but correct). CDN cache continues serving popular URLs without any origin hit.
ID generator crash
Pre-allocated ranges stored per server. On crash: ID range is abandoned (some IDs wasted, no duplicates). New instance gets new range. No coordination needed on hot path.
CDN outage
DNS failover to origin. Higher latency (CDN miss -> origin). Multi-CDN strategy (CloudFront + Fastly) as mitigation for critical SLAs.
Analytics pipeline lag
Kafka durable (7-day retention). Consumer lag = analytics delayed, not lost. Zero impact on redirect service -- analytics consumer entirely decoupled.
[flag] 9. Conclusion — what I would say in the last three minutes
The dominant constraint

The 100:1 read-to-write ratio. Everything follows from it: a counter-based ID so writes never coordinate, and a CDN plus cache tier that absorbs almost all reads before they reach storage.

What I would build first

The KGS counter with pre-allocated ranges and the cache-in-front-of-KV read path. Analytics can be added later without touching either.

What I deliberately did not build

Real-time analytics, custom domains, and link previews. I would use 302 only for the small subset of links that need per-click tracking, and 301 for the rest so the CDN keeps absorbing them.

The biggest risk

The cache tier. At a 99% hit rate the origin sees 1% of 350K QPS; at 95% it sees five times that. I would alert on hit rate, not just on origin latency.

Design Twitter / Social Media Feed

Difficulty: Hard  .  Target: 45 min
[list] 1. Requirements
❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
What is the follower count at the 99th percentile?
This is the dominant constraint. A few accounts with tens of millions of followers is what breaks fan-out-on-write and forces a hybrid.
Is the timeline chronological or ranked?
Ranked puts a scoring service on the read path, which changes the latency budget and makes precomputation much harder.
How stale may a new post be before it appears?
Seconds allows fan-out-on-write; instant forces pull. This single number decides push versus pull.
Do we support edits and deletes?
Fan-out-on-write copies a post into millions of timelines, so retraction becomes an expensive distributed cleanup.
What is the read-to-write ratio?
Fan-out-on-write only pays off when reads dominate. If they do not, you have pre-computed work nobody reads.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.

Functional:

  • Post tweets (text <= 280 chars, optional media)
  • Follow / Unfollow users
  • Home timeline: tweets from followed users, reverse-chronological
  • User profile timeline: all tweets by a user
  • Likes, Retweets, Replies
  • Search: hashtags, full-text (stretch)

Non-Functional:

  • 500M DAU. Celebrities with 100M+ followers.
  • Timeline load p99 < 200ms
  • Post latency p99 < 500ms
  • Read >> Write (100:1)
  • Eventual consistency for timeline (2-5 sec lag OK)
