POST /v1/tweets Body: { text, media_ids?, reply_to? } Response: 201 { tweet_id, created_at } // returns as soon as the tweet is durable; fan-out is async GET /v1/timeline/home?cursor=&limit=50 Response: { items:[{tweet_id, author, text, ts}], next_cursor } // cursor is (ts, tweet_id), never an offset -- offsets skip // or repeat items when the feed mutates under the reader GET /v1/timeline/user/{user_id}?cursor=&limit=50 POST /v1/follow Body: { target_id } -> 202 // 202: following a celebrity may enqueue backfill work DELETE /v1/tweets/{id} -> 204 (idempotent)
[db] 4. Schema Design
-- Tweets (Cassandra -- write-heavy, time-series, no joins) TABLE tweets { tweet_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, -- Snowflake: time-sortable user_id BIGINT, content TEXT, media_ids LIST<UUID>, reply_to BIGINT, -- NULL for original tweets like_count BIGINT, -- eventually consistent Redis counter created_at TIMESTAMP } -- User timelines (Redis sorted set -- fast, ephemeral) KEY timeline:{user_id} -> ZSET { tweet_id: score=tweet_id } -- Capped at 800 entries. tweet_id = Snowflake = time-sorted. -- Social graph (separate service -- high read throughput) TABLE follows { follower_id BIGINT PARTITION KEY, followee_id BIGINT CLUSTERING KEY, created_at TIMESTAMP } TABLE followers { -- reverse: who follows a given user? followee_id BIGINT PARTITION KEY, follower_id BIGINT CLUSTERING KEY } -- Users (MySQL -- low write rate, strong consistency needed for uniqueness) TABLE users { user_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, username VARCHAR(50) UNIQUE, is_celebrity BOOLEAN, -- follower_count > 1M follower_countBIGINT }
[build] 5. High-Level Architecture
Fan-out on write — and the celebrity that stalls it for everybody
the posttimeline copies40M copies
What is moving: the post is written once and made durable, then — asynchronously — copied into every follower’s timeline. Reads afterwards are a single sequential fetch of a precomputed list, which is why this shape wins when reads vastly outnumber writes.
What goes wrong: an account with 40 million followers posts. The same loop now enqueues 40 million copies, saturating the fan-out workers, and every ordinary user’s post sits behind it — a queue delay that has nothing to do with those users. This is why production systems are hybrid: above a follower threshold, stop fanning out and merge the celebrity’s posts at read time instead.
Hybrid fan-out: write fan-out for regular users, read fan-out for celebrities. Both merged on timeline load.
[search] 6. Component Deep Dives

The Fan-out Decision (Most Important):

Three approaches to fan-out:

  • Fan-out on write (push): When tweet is posted, push tweet_id to all followers' Redis timelines immediately. Fast reads. Bad for celebrities: 100M Redis writes per tweet.
  • Fan-out on read (pull): No pre-computation. On timeline load, fetch last 20 tweets from each followed user. Read is slow if you follow 1,000 people: 1,000 Cassandra reads per timeline load.
  • Hybrid (Twitter's actual approach): Fan-out on write for regular users (<1M followers). Skip fan-out for celebrities -- their tweets are pulled on timeline load and merged in. Threshold tuned dynamically.

Timeline as sorted set: Redis ZADD timeline:{user_id} {tweet_id} {tweet_id}. Score = tweet_id (Snowflake is time-sortable). Fetch: ZREVRANGE -> get latest N tweet IDs. Cap at 800 to prevent unbounded memory. If user hasn't logged in for 30 days, delete their timeline (rebuild on next login from Cassandra).

Like counts: Redis INCR like:{tweet_id}. Async flush to Cassandra every 60s. Read likes from Redis (fresh) not Cassandra. Eventual consistency -- +/-60s accuracy on like count is fine.

[balance] 7. Trade-off Analysis
DecisionChosen vAlternative xReasoning
Fan-out strategyHybrid (write for regular, read for celebs)Pure write OR pure readPure write: 100M ops for one celebrity tweet impossible. Pure read: 1,000 Cassandra reads per timeline load for heavy followers. Hybrid balances both.
Tweet storageCassandraMySQLWrite-heavy, time-series access, no joins. Cassandra's LSM-tree excellent for append-heavy workloads. MySQL's B-tree would be slower for writes.
Timeline storageRedis sorted setCassandraSub-ms sorted reads. Volatile OK (rebuild from Cassandra on miss). ZRANGE is ideal for time-ordered tweet IDs.
ConsistencyEventual (seconds lag OK)StrongStrong consistency requires synchronous fan-out to millions of Redis nodes. Not feasible. 2-5 second timeline lag is invisible to users.
[shield] 8. Fault Tolerance
Redis timeline lost
Redis Cluster. On node loss: rebuild affected timelines from Cassandra on next request. Slow first load (~500ms), fast thereafter. Alert if rebuild rate is high (many nodes lost).
Fan-out service overwhelmed
Kafka back-pressure: fan-out workers pull at their own rate. Scale worker pods horizontally. Kafka retains messages for 7 days -- no loss during overload. Users see timeline lag, not errors.
Cassandra node failure
RF=3, quorum reads/writes. Node failure -> automatic reroute to replicas. Cassandra's gossip protocol detects failure in ~3s. No manual intervention.
Celebrity posts viral tweet (traffic spike)
Celebrity tweets use read fan-out -- no write spike. CDN caches user profile pages. Rate limit profile page fetches. Auto-scale read API pods on CPU metric.
[flag] 9. Conclusion — what I would say in the last three minutes
The dominant constraint

Follower-count skew. A handful of accounts with tens of millions of followers is what makes a single fan-out strategy impossible, so the design is a hybrid rather than a choice between push and pull.

What I would build first

Fan-out-on-write for the ordinary case, with a celebrity threshold above which posts are pulled and merged at read time.

What I deliberately did not build

Ranking, ads and notifications. A chronological timeline is a legitimate v1 and it keeps the read path free of a scoring service.

The biggest risk

Getting the celebrity threshold wrong. Too high and one account can stall the fan-out queue for everyone; I would make it a tunable and monitor fan-out lag per tier.

Design a Distributed Key-Value Store (like Redis / Amazon Dynamo)

Difficulty: Hard  .  Target: 45 min
[list] 1. Requirements
❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
Strong or eventual consistency?
The single biggest fork in the design. Strong means consensus on the write path and cross-region latency; eventual means quorums and conflict resolution.
Point lookups only, or range scans?
Decides hash versus range partitioning, and range partitioning brings hot-shard problems that hashing does not.
What is the value size distribution?
Multi-megabyte values need a different storage path from 200-byte ones, and change the memory overhead arithmetic entirely.
Single region or multi-region?
Determines whether an acknowledged write has to cross an ocean, which is a floor on write latency you cannot engineer away.
What must be durable when we acknowledge?
fsync-before-ack versus page-cache-and-hope is a correctness decision, not a tuning knob.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.

Build your own distributed KV store supporting:

  • get(key) -> value | null
  • put(key, value) -> OK
  • delete(key) -> OK
  • Tunable consistency: W=1/2/3, R=1/2/3, N=3
  • Horizontal scaling: add nodes without downtime
  • Automatic failover: if a node dies, system keeps working

Non-Functional:

  • 10M QPS total cluster
  • p99 < 1ms for get, < 5ms for put
  • Data survives N/2 node failures
  • Eventual consistency by default (Dynamo model)
[chart] 2. Capacity Estimation
⚖ Assumptions — and what breaks if each is wrong
Callers tolerate eventual consistency
If any caller needs linearizability, quorums are not enough and the write path needs consensus, roughly tripling write latency.
Access is by key, no range scans
Range queries would force range partitioning, which reintroduces hot shards that hashing avoids.
Values are small, order of kilobytes
Multi-megabyte values need a separate blob path; storing them inline destroys the memory model.

[plug] 3. API Design
GET /v1/keys/{key}?consistency=one|quorum Response: 200 { value, version_vector, coordinator } 404 not found // may return SIBLINGS when concurrent writes diverged -- // the client resolves and writes back PUT /v1/keys/{key}?w=2 Body: { value, context } // context = version vector from a prior read Response: 200 { version_vector } 503 insufficient replicas (when sloppy quorum is disabled) DELETE /v1/keys/{key} // writes a TOMBSTONE, not a removal -- // deleting outright lets a stale replica resurrect it // Admin: GET /v1/ring -- the token map, polled by smart clients
[db] 4. Schema Design
-- On each node (RocksDB or custom LSM-tree store) KEY -> { value: bytes, version: VectorClock | Timestamp, tombstone: bool } -- Metadata (gossip-distributed to all nodes) RING -> sorted([(hash_position, node_id, address)]) NODE_STATUS -> { node_id: { status, last_heartbeat, token_count } } -- Hint store (per node, for hinted handoff) HINTS -> { target_node: [(key, value, timestamp)] }
[build] 5. High-Level Architecture
Quorum write — and the sloppy quorum that trades consistency for uptime
client writereplica writeackhinted handoff
What is moving: the write goes to any node, which forwards it to all replicas and acknowledges as soon as W = 2 of them confirm. With R + W > N, any later read of 2 replicas is guaranteed to overlap this write.
What goes wrong: replica 3 is unreachable. A sloppy quorum accepts the write anyway and parks a hint on a healthy node to be handed off later — so the system stays available, but the R + W > N overlap guarantee no longer holds and a read can miss this value. Availability was bought with consistency, exactly as Ch 3 says it must be.
Consistent hash ring. Coordinator routes to N clockwise nodes. W=2 writes acknowledged = quorum satisfied.
[search] 6. Component Deep Dives

Consistent Hashing: key -> SHA256 -> position on ring -> next 3 clockwise nodes are the replicas. Adding/removing a node: only adjacent keys migrate.

Write path: Client -> any node (coordinator). Coordinator hashes key -> finds 3 replica nodes. Sends write to all 3 in parallel. Waits for W=2 ACKs. Returns success to client. 3rd replica catches up asynchronously.

Read path: Coordinator sends read to R=2 closest nodes. Takes latest by timestamp/vector clock. If versions differ -> read-repair: coordinator writes latest back to stale node.

Conflict resolution: Last-Write-Wins (LWW) by default (timestamp). For shopping cart use case: vector clocks + application-level merge (union of items). Cassandra uses LWW by default; DynamoDB's original design used vector clocks.

Anti-entropy: Background process (per node pair) compares Merkle trees. Find differing subtrees -> sync only different parts. Ensures all replicas converge even for cold keys that never get read-repaired.

Hinted handoff: If Node E is down during a write, coordinator stores the write with a 'hint: this belongs to E' on another node. When E recovers, the hint is delivered. Prevents permanent data loss from temporary failures.

[balance] 7. Trade-off Analysis
DecisionChosen vAlternative xReasoning
Consistency modelTunable quorum (R+W>N=strong, else eventual)Always strongTunable gives flexibility: low-latency apps use W=1,R=1; financial use W=3,R=2. One size doesn't fit all.
Conflict resolutionLWW (default) + vector clocks (opt-in)Reject conflicts (require re-read)Rejecting conflicts kills availability. LWW is simple. Vector clocks enable app-level merge for complex data types.
PartitioningConsistent hashing + vnodesRange partitioningConsistent hashing: smooth rebalancing. Vnodes: even distribution. Range: good for scans but creates hot partitions for sequential writes.
[shield] 8. Fault Tolerance
Node failure (permanent)
Detect via gossip heartbeat timeout (phi = 8 threshold). Remove from ring. Adjacent nodes inherit its key range. Replica count temporarily drops to 2; auto-repair brings it back to 3 via anti-entropy within minutes.
Network partition (split-ring)
Both halves continue serving with their available replicas. Writes with W=2 succeed on majority side, fail on minority (if only 1 replica there). On heal: anti-entropy detects divergence, repairs. LWW resolves conflicts.
Hot key (one key getting 1M QPS)
Detect via coordinator: if key appears in >10% of requests -> replicate to local cache. Or: key sharding -- append suffix (0-9), fan-out writes to 10 keys, fan-in reads with merge.
▶ Watch alongside this design
  • MIT 6.824 — Lecture 3: GFS ~80 min — the storage paper every Google interviewer assumes exists.
  • MIT 6.824 — Lecture 9: More Replication, CRAQ ~80 min — chain replication as an alternative to the quorum design used here.
[flag] 9. Conclusion — what I would say in the last three minutes
The dominant constraint

Whether the caller needs strong or eventual consistency. I designed for eventual with tunable quorums, because that is what buys availability during a partition; strong consistency would mean consensus on the write path and a different system.

What I would build first

Consistent hashing with virtual nodes, plus R + W > N quorums. Anti-entropy and hinted handoff come next, because without them eventual never actually converges.

What I deliberately did not build

Secondary indexes, transactions and range scans. Each of those pulls the design back toward a database.

The biggest risk

Silent divergence. Without Merkle-tree anti-entropy running and being monitored, replicas drift and nobody finds out until a read repair surfaces it years later.

Design WhatsApp / Messaging System

Difficulty: Hard  .  Target: 45 min
[list] 1. Requirements
❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
1:1 only, or groups — and how large?
Group size drives fan-out cost. A 100,000-member group is a completely different write amplification problem from a 1:1 chat.
Is ordering required per conversation or globally?
Per-conversation ordering lets you partition by conversation and avoid coordination. Global ordering does not.
Do we store history server-side?
Decides whether end-to-end encryption is possible, and whether server-side search can exist at all.
Is presence (online / typing) in scope?
Presence has a far higher write rate than messaging and is usually a separate system. Saying so is a scoping signal.
Multi-device per account?
Changes key management, read-state synchronisation and delivery semantics all at once.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.

Functional:

  • 1-to-1 and group messaging (max 256 members)
  • Message delivery: sent -> delivered -> read receipts
  • Online presence: show when user was last online
  • Push notifications for offline users
  • End-to-end encryption (Signal Protocol)
  • Media: images, videos, documents (up to 100MB)

Non-Functional:

  • 2B users, 100B messages/day
  • Message delivery: p99 < 500ms (online recipient)
  • High availability: 99.99%
  • Messages durable: survive sender/receiver being offline for weeks
[chart] 2. Capacity Estimation
⚖ Assumptions — and what breaks if each is wrong
Groups are bounded, order of hundreds
A 100,000-member group changes fan-out from a loop into its own subsystem.
Ordering is required per conversation only
Global ordering across conversations would force coordination and remove the partitioning that makes this scale.
Messages are not stored after delivery
If history must be retained server-side, end-to-end encryption becomes far harder and search becomes possible.

WebSocket servers: 2B users x 70% active daily x peak 30% online simultaneously = 600M concurrent connections / 50K/server = 12,000 WebSocket servers.

[plug] 3. API Design
// Long-lived WebSocket. HTTP is used only for auth and media. WS /v1/connect Header: Bearer <token> <- { type:"ack", client_msg_id, server_msg_id, seq } <- { type:"message", conversation_id, seq, from, ciphertext, ts } <- { type:"receipt", message_id, state:"delivered"|"read" } -> { type:"send", conversation_id, client_msg_id, ciphertext } // client_msg_id makes the send idempotent across reconnects POST /v1/media -> { media_id, upload_url } GET /v1/sync?since_seq= -> missed messages after reconnect POST /v1/keys/prekeys -> replenish the one-time prekey pool
[db] 4. Schema Design
-- Messages (Cassandra -- write-heavy, time-series) TABLE messages { conversation_id UUID PARTITION KEY, message_id BIGINT CLUSTERING KEY DESC, -- Snowflake sender_id BIGINT, content BLOB, -- encrypted ciphertext media_id UUID, -- reference to media service message_type ENUM(text, image, video, doc), created_at TIMESTAMP } -- Delivery receipts (separate table for performance) TABLE receipts { message_id BIGINT PARTITION KEY, user_id BIGINT CLUSTERING KEY, status ENUM(sent, delivered, read), updated_at TIMESTAMP } -- User presence (Redis -- ephemeral, frequently updated) KEY presence:{user_id} -> { status: online|offline, last_seen: timestamp } -- TTL: 30 seconds. Refreshed every 20s by client heartbeat. -- Message queue for offline delivery (Redis List per user) KEY inbox:{user_id} -> LIST [ message_ids... ] (max 1000)
[build] 5. High-Level Architecture
Message delivery — and the reconnect that can deliver twice
sendordered deliveryreceiptqueued while offline
What is moving: a message travels to the gateway holding the sender’s socket, is appended to the conversation’s ordered log with a sequence number, then pushed to the recipient. Ordering is guaranteed per conversation, which is what lets the system partition by conversation ID and coordinate nowhere.
What goes wrong: the recipient goes offline mid-delivery. Messages queue, and on reconnect the client asks for everything after its last acknowledged sequence. If the client acknowledged but the ack was lost, the server replays messages it already delivered — a duplicate. The fix is the client-supplied message ID: delivery is at-least-once and the client deduplicates on it (Ch 11).
Messages route through WebSocket servers. Connection registry (Redis) maps users to their current WS server.
[search] 6. Component Deep Dives

Connection Management -- The Hard Part: 600M concurrent WebSocket connections cannot all connect to one server. You have 12,000 WebSocket servers. When A sends a message to B, how does A's server know B is connected to Server C?

Connection registry: When a user connects, their WebSocket server writes {user_id -> server_id} to Redis. On message: sender's server looks up recipient's server -> forwards message over internal HTTP/gRPC -> recipient's server pushes to phone. Lookup: O(1) Redis get.

Offline delivery: Recipient not in connection registry -> store message in Redis inbox:{user_id} list. When user reconnects: flush inbox, deliver all queued messages, update receipts. Inbox in Redis, backed up in Cassandra for long-term storage (user offline for days).

End-to-End Encryption (Signal Protocol): Each device generates a key pair. Public keys uploaded to WhatsApp servers. Sender fetches recipient's public key, encrypts message locally. WhatsApp servers store and forward ciphertext -- they cannot read it. Key exchange happens via X3DH (Extended Triple Diffie-Hellman). Forward secrecy: ratchet keys for each message.

Read receipts: Two blue ticks. Receiver sends ACK -> delivered receipt. Receiver opens conversation -> seen receipt. Receipts stored in receipts table. Sender's server updates the message status and notifies sender over their WebSocket.

[balance] 7. Trade-off Analysis
DecisionChosen vAlternative xReasoning
TransportWebSocket (persistent)HTTP pollingPersistent connection = instant delivery, no polling overhead. Critical for sub-500ms delivery. Poll would require 1-5 req/sec x 2B users = billions of wasted requests.
Message storeCassandraPostgreSQLTime-series append workload. 100B msgs/day = 1.16M writes/sec. Cassandra's LSM-tree handles this. PostgreSQL B-tree would require enormous infrastructure for this write rate.
Group messagingFan-out on send (for small groups)Fan-out on receiveFor 256-member groups: fan-out on send = 256 DB writes + 256 WS pushes. Manageable. On receive = one write but N reads on timeline load. Fan-out on send is better for groups this size.
[shield] 8. Fault Tolerance
WebSocket server crashes
All connections on that server disconnect. Clients auto-reconnect to any WS server (load balancer with sticky session NOT required -- connection registry handles routing). Reconnect within 1-2 seconds. Messages in flight are re-delivered from Cassandra.
Connection registry (Redis) down
Short outage: WS servers cache recent {user->server} mappings locally (LRU, 5 min TTL). On cache miss: fan-out to all WS servers (expensive but rare). Redis Cluster + sentinels for HA.
Cassandra node failure
RF=3, W=2, R=1. Node failure -> writes still succeed (2 of remaining 4 nodes). Read: if returning stale data, read-repair brings it up to date. Hinted handoff for writes during node unavailability.
Message lost in transit
Message ID is Snowflake (globally unique). ACK from WS server means it received the message. If sender doesn't get ACK in 5s -> retry (idempotent: same message_id = same Cassandra row). Three retries, then store in outbox for async retry.
[flag] 9. Conclusion — what I would say in the last three minutes
The dominant constraint

Delivery ordering is required per conversation, not globally. That single relaxation is what lets me partition by conversation ID and avoid any cross-shard coordination on the hot path.

What I would build first

The WebSocket gateway plus per-conversation sequencing and the offline queue. Presence is deliberately a separate service.

What I deliberately did not build

Server-side search, which end-to-end encryption largely rules out, and global message ordering, which nobody needs.

The biggest risk

Presence. It has a far higher write rate than messaging and, if co-located, its load will take the messaging path down with it.

Design YouTube (Video Upload & Streaming)

Difficulty: Hard  .  Target: 45 min
[list] 1. Requirements
❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
Upload rate versus watch rate?
These size two completely different systems: transcoding capacity and CDN egress. They are rarely the same order of magnitude.
Live streaming, or video-on-demand only?
Live removes the batch transcode window and turns this into a latency problem instead of a throughput problem.
How many output renditions per video?
The transcode matrix — resolutions × codecs × bitrates — is the multiplier on your entire compute bill.
Must view counts be real-time and exact?
Counting at this scale is its own distributed problem. Approximate-and-eventually-correct is dramatically cheaper.
Is DRM or geo-restriction required?
Changes the delivery path and rules out simple CDN caching of a single artefact.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.

Functional:

  • Upload video (up to 10GB)
  • Transcode to multiple resolutions (360p, 720p, 1080p, 4K)
  • Stream video with adaptive bitrate (HLS/DASH)
  • Video metadata: title, description, tags, duration
  • Recommendations, search (stretch)
  • Like, comment, subscribe

Non-Functional:

  • 2B users, 500 hours of video uploaded every minute
  • Stream start latency < 2s
  • Streaming: smooth at varying bandwidth (adaptive bitrate)
  • Upload to availability: < 5 minutes after upload completes
  • Video storage: petabytes, 11-nine durability
[chart] 2. Capacity Estimation
⚖ Assumptions — and what breaks if each is wrong
Watch volume is orders of magnitude above upload volume
If uploads dominated, transcode capacity rather than CDN egress would be the binding cost.
Video-on-demand only
Live removes the batch transcode window and changes this into a latency-bound design.
A handful of renditions per video
Every extra rendition multiplies the transcode bill across the entire catalogue.

[plug] 3. API Design
POST /v1/uploads Body: { filename, size_bytes, content_type } Response: 201 { upload_id, chunk_size, upload_urls[] } // resumable: the client PUTs chunks directly to object storage PUT {upload_url}/chunk/{n} -> 200 { etag } POST /v1/uploads/{id}/complete -> 202 { video_id, state:"transcoding" } GET /v1/videos/{id}/manifest?profile=hls|dash Response: 200 HLS/DASH manifest of the available renditions // the player picks a rendition per segment; the server never decides POST /v1/videos/{id}/view -> 202 // fire-and-forget into a stream; counts are eventually correct
[db] 4. Schema Design
-- Metadata in a relational store; bytes in object storage. TABLE videos { video_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, channel_id UUID, title, description TEXT, state ENUM(uploading, transcoding, ready, failed), duration_s INT, published_at TIMESTAMP } -- INDEX: (channel_id, published_at DESC) for a channel page TABLE renditions { -- one row per output of the transcode DAG video_id UUID, height INT, codec VARCHAR, bitrate_kbps INT, object_key TEXT, state ENUM(pending, ready), PRIMARY KEY (video_id, height, codec) } TABLE view_counts { -- eventually correct, written from a stream video_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, count BIGINT, updated_at TIMESTAMP } -- Never incremented synchronously on the playback path.
[build] 5. High-Level Architecture
Upload and transcode — and the backlog users experience as “processing”
upload chunkstranscode jobrenditionsqueued jobs
What is moving: the client uploads chunks straight into object storage, then a transcode DAG fans each source out into a ladder of renditions, which are pushed to the CDN. Upload and transcode are deliberately decoupled: the upload succeeds long before the video is watchable.
What goes wrong: transcode is throughput-bound and uploads are bursty, so a spike fills the queue and every new video sits in processing. Nothing errors — which is what makes it insidious. The levers are to transcode lazily for the long tail (most uploads are never watched) and eagerly only for the low renditions, and to publish the source rendition immediately so the video is at least playable.
Upload -> raw GCS -> Kafka event -> transcode fleet -> HLS segments in GCS -> CDN streams to viewers.
[search] 6. Component Deep Dives

Resumable Upload: Large video files (10GB) cannot be sent in one HTTP request. Use chunked upload: split into 5MB chunks, upload each with offset. Server acknowledges each chunk. On failure: resume from last acknowledged chunk. Google Cloud Storage's XML API and TUS protocol implement this pattern.

Adaptive Bitrate Streaming (HLS): Transcoded video is split into 2-10 second segments (.ts files). A manifest file (.m3u8) lists all segments and their quality levels. The client player requests segments and monitors download speed. If downloading 720p segments is slow (bandwidth dropped), it switches to 480p manifest automatically. This gives smooth playback without buffering.

Transcoding pipeline: One Kafka event per upload. Transcoding worker pool: each worker fetches the raw video from GCS, transcodes one quality level (FFmpeg), uploads HLS segments to GCS, acknowledges Kafka. Multiple workers process different quality levels in parallel. Status tracked in PostgreSQL (video_id, status: transcoding/ready, progress %).

CDN strategy: HLS segments are immutable (content-addressed by segment hash). Cache-Control: max-age=31536000 (1 year). CDN naturally geo-distributes popular content. New videos: cold start -- first viewers get from GCS. After 100 views: cached at every CDN edge worldwide.

[balance] 7. Trade-off Analysis
DecisionChosen vAlternative xReasoning
TranscodingAsync Kafka pipeline (eventual availability)Sync (block upload until done)Sync transcode = wait 5-60 min for every upload. Terrible UX. Async = upload acknowledged immediately, video available in ~5 min. Acceptable.
Streaming formatHLS (HTTP Live Streaming)RTMP / WebRTCHLS works over standard CDN HTTP. RTMP requires special servers. WebRTC good for sub-second latency (live streaming) but overkill for pre-recorded video. HLS adaptive bitrate = optimal for variable bandwidth.
StorageGCS object storageHDFS / customGCS: 11-nine durability, petabyte scale, CDN integration, managed. HDFS: operational burden, no CDN, doesn't scale to exabytes easily.
[shield] 8. Fault Tolerance
Transcode worker crashes mid-job
Kafka offset not committed until job complete. Worker crash -> message re-delivered -> new worker picks up from beginning (idempotent: transcode is pure function, same input = same output). Partial segments discarded.
GCS regional outage
Multi-region GCS bucket (US + EU). If primary region down, read from secondary with minimal latency increase. Writes queued and replayed when primary recovers. CDN cache continues serving most traffic during outage.
CDN node failure
CDN routes around failed edge nodes automatically. Traffic shifts to next-nearest edge. Brief latency increase. Popular content likely cached on multiple edges.
[flag] 9. Conclusion — what I would say in the last three minutes
The dominant constraint

Upload volume and watch volume are different systems. Transcoding is a throughput problem sized by uploads; delivery is an egress problem sized by watches, and they scale independently.

What I would build first

Chunked resumable upload into object storage, then an asynchronous transcode DAG. Playback can serve the original rendition until the ladder is ready.

What I deliberately did not build

Live streaming, DRM and recommendations. Live in particular removes the batch transcode window and is a different design.

The biggest risk

Transcode cost. The rendition matrix multiplies your entire compute bill, so I would transcode lazily for the long tail rather than eagerly for everything.

Design a Distributed Job Scheduler (like AWS Lambda / Cron)

Difficulty: Medium-Hard  .  Target: 40 min
[list] 1. Requirements
❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
Exactly-once, or at-least-once with idempotent handlers?
Exactly-once execution is not achievable across a network, so the honest question is who absorbs the duplicate — you, or the handler.
What scheduling precision is required?
One second versus one minute changes the polling architecture completely, and precision is far more expensive than it sounds.
How long can a job run?
Long jobs need leases and heartbeats, and a lease that expires mid-run is the classic fencing problem.
Do jobs have dependencies on each other?
A DAG scheduler is a different system from a cron scheduler. This is worth scoping out loud.
What happens to a window missed during an outage?
Skip, or catch up? Catch-up creates a thundering backlog exactly when the system is already unhealthy.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.

Functional:

  • Schedule jobs: run at specific time (one-shot) or cron expression (recurring)
  • Each job has a handler (function/URL to call)
  • Exactly-once execution: a job must not run twice at the same scheduled time
  • At-least-once fallback: if execution fails, retry with backoff
  • Job status tracking: pending/running/succeeded/failed
  • 10M+ scheduled jobs, 100K jobs/sec at peak

Non-Functional:

  • Job fires within 1 second of scheduled time
  • No duplicate execution (critical)
  • Retry on failure (configurable: max retries, backoff)
  • HA: 99.99% -- scheduler failure must not cause missed jobs
[chart] 2. Capacity Estimation
⚖ Assumptions — and what breaks if each is wrong
10M scheduled jobs, 100K fires/sec at peak
If peak were 1M/sec the single-database claim loop breaks and the scheduler must shard by time bucket.
Jobs fire within 1 second of schedule
Relaxing to a minute allows a far simpler polling design with much lower database pressure.
Handlers are idempotent
Otherwise at-least-once delivery is unsafe and a deduplication store joins the execution path.

Assumptions: 10M scheduled jobs, 100K job fires/sec at peak, average payload 2 KB.

The number that shapes the design: at 100K fires/sec, a naive one-row-per-claim poll would be 100K transactions/sec against a single table — well past what one primary sustains. Workers therefore claim in batches and hold a lease, which cuts claim traffic by the batch factor and is why SKIP LOCKED matters: it lets N workers claim disjoint batches without blocking each other.

[db] 4. Schema Design
-- Jobs table (PostgreSQL -- ACID needed for scheduling locks) TABLE jobs { job_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(255), cron_expr VARCHAR(100), -- NULL for one-shot next_run_at TIMESTAMP, handler_url TEXT, payload JSONB, status ENUM(pending, running, succeeded, failed), retry_count INT DEFAULT 0, max_retries INT DEFAULT 3, last_run_at TIMESTAMP, locked_by VARCHAR(64), -- worker_id holding lock lock_expires TIMESTAMP -- fencing: lock expires if worker crashes } -- INDEX: (next_run_at, status) WHERE status = 'pending' -- This index allows efficient polling: 'give me pending jobs due now'
[build] 5. High-Level Architecture
Lease-based claim — and the paused worker that wakes up believing it still owns the job
claim + fencing tokenexecutionstale execution
What is moving: workers claim batches with SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED so they never block each other, each claim carries a monotonically increasing fencing token, and the worker heartbeats to extend its lease while it runs.
What goes wrong: worker 1 hits a long GC pause. Its lease expires, the scheduler hands the job to worker 2 with a higher token, and then worker 1 wakes up still believing it holds the lease — it cannot tell that time passed. Without fencing both would execute. The handler rejects token 41 because it has already seen 42, which makes the stale actor harmless rather than trying to prevent it. Ch 6
Scheduler polls DB with SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED -- atomic claim prevents double execution. Workers execute via Kafka.
[search] 6. Component Deep Dives

The Double Execution Problem -- Most Critical: Two scheduler instances both see a job due at T=1000. Both try to execute it. The job runs twice. For a payment job, this double-charges the customer.

Solution: SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
SELECT * FROM jobs WHERE next_run_at <= NOW() AND status='pending' LIMIT 100 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
This SQL atomically locks selected rows. A second scheduler running the same query will SKIP the already-locked rows and get different jobs. Completely prevents double-execution at the DB level. No application-level coordination needed.

Fencing against worker crashes: After claiming a job, set lock_expires = NOW() + 5 min. Worker must heartbeat every minute. If worker crashes, lock_expires passes -> background sweeper resets status to 'pending' -> job gets re-scheduled. Lock_expires is a fencing token: the crashed worker cannot complete the job after recovery (its lock has expired).

Scheduler high availability: Multiple scheduler instances. Only one is active (leader election via etcd/ZooKeeper/DB advisory lock). Follower schedulers are on hot standby. Leader failure -> follower takes over in <30s. With SELECT FOR UPDATE, even if two schedulers are briefly both active, no double execution.

[balance] 7. Trade-off Analysis
DecisionChosen vAlternative xReasoning
Job claimSELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKEDDistributed lock (Redis)DB-level locking eliminates network round-trip to external lock service. SKIP LOCKED allows concurrent schedulers without contention. Simpler -- no lock service dependency.
Exactly-onceDB lock + idempotent handler contractTransactionsFull exactly-once requires handler to be idempotent (we guarantee at-most-once delivery; handler must handle retries). Telling customers: 'your handler may run twice on failure -- make it idempotent' is standard practice.
DeliveryPull (DB poll every 1s)Push (DB triggers)DB triggers couple scheduler to DB internals. Poll is simple, predictable, scalable. 1-second poll granularity acceptable for most cron use cases. Sub-second scheduling needs a different architecture.
[shield] 8. Fault Tolerance
Scheduler leader crashes
Follower detects via etcd lease expiry (~15s). Takes over leadership. Jobs due during those 15s: lock_expires hasn't passed, so they're safe. After 15s: new leader picks up pending jobs. Max 15-second delay.
Worker crashes mid-execution
lock_expires passes -> sweeper resets job to pending -> re-executed. Handler MUST be idempotent (most are: send email with idempotency key, write to DB with upsert). Document this contract clearly.
DB (PostgreSQL) failure
Primary fails -> replica promoted (RDS Multi-AZ: ~30s). Schedulers lose DB connection, buffer job picks in memory (Kafka), retry DB connection. No jobs lost. Some delayed by up to ~1 min.
[flag] 9. Conclusion — what I would say in the last three minutes
The dominant constraint

Nobody can promise exactly-once execution across a network. So the design provides at-least-once delivery with fencing tokens, and requires handlers to be idempotent. Saying that plainly is the honest answer.

What I would build first

The leased-claim loop: SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, a lease with a heartbeat, and a fencing token so a resurrected worker cannot act on stale authority.

What I deliberately did not build

DAG dependencies between jobs. That is a workflow engine, and it is a different system worth scoping out explicitly.

The biggest risk

The catch-up stampede. After an outage, every missed window fires at once against a system that is already unhealthy; the backlog needs rate limiting, not just replay.

Design a Distributed Message Queue (Apache Kafka / Google Cloud PubSub)

Difficulty: Hard (Staff Expectation)  •  Target: 45 min
[list] 1. Requirements
❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
Ordering: per partition, or global?
Global ordering means a single partition, which caps your throughput at one machine. Almost nobody actually needs it.
At-least-once or exactly-once delivery?
Exactly-once needs idempotent producers plus transactions, and costs throughput. Most consumers are cheaper to make idempotent.
Retention: how long, and is replay required?
Replay turns the queue into a durable log and changes storage sizing by orders of magnitude.
How many consumer groups, and what lag is tolerable?
Decides fan-out cost and whether slow consumers can be isolated from fast ones.
What is the maximum message size?
Large payloads need a claim-check pattern — put the blob in object storage and send the pointer.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.

Functional Requirements:

  • Producers publish messages to named topics with optional partition keys.
  • Consumers subscribe to topics as part of Consumer Groups and consume sequentially.
  • Strict FIFO ordering within a single partition; total order across partitions is non-goal.
  • Configurable message retention (time-based e.g., 7 days, or size-based) independent of consumption status.
  • High throughput and low latency pub/sub delivery with replayability.

Non-Functional Requirements:

  • Throughput: 1,000,000 messages/sec write, 5,000,000 messages/sec read (fan-out 5x).
  • Latency: Produce p99 < 10ms, End-to-end consume latency < 50ms.
  • Durability: Zero data loss (RPO = 0) with multi-replica sync replication.
  • High Availability: 99.99% uptime (SLA), automatic partition leader failover < 5s.
[chart] 2. Capacity Estimation
⚖ Assumptions — and what breaks if each is wrong
Per-partition ordering is sufficient
Global ordering means one partition and caps throughput at a single machine.
Consumers can be made idempotent
Otherwise exactly-once semantics are required, which costs meaningful throughput.
Retention is measured in days, not years
Long retention turns this into a storage design and changes the cost model entirely.

-- Log Segment File Structure on Broker Disk -- File: /data/kafka/topics/{topic_name}-{partition_id}/{base_offset}.log -- Append-Only Binary Record Format: [Offset: 8B][Size: 4B][CRC: 4B][Magic: 1B][Attributes: 1B][Timestamp: 8B] [Key_Length: 4B][Key_Bytes][Value_Length: 4B][Payload_Bytes] -- Sparse Memory-Mapped Index: {base_offset}.index -- Every 4KB of log data, append entry (Relative Offset: 4B, Physical Byte Position: 4B) [Rel_Offset: 0 -> Pos: 0] [Rel_Offset: 120 -> Pos: 4096] [Rel_Offset: 245 -> Pos: 8192] -- Consumer Offset Tracking (__consumer_offsets internal compacted topic) KEY: (consumer_group_id, topic, partition_id) VALUE: (offset: int64, commit_timestamp: int64, metadata: string)
[build] 5. High-Level Architecture
Replication and leader election — why only the in-sync set may be elected
produced recordreplicationacknowledgement
What is moving: a record is appended to the partition leader, replicated to the followers, and acknowledged to the producer only once every replica in the in-sync set has written it. The lagging replica is deliberately excluded from that set — it is allowed to fall behind without slowing anybody down.
What goes wrong: the leader dies. Election must choose only from the in-sync set, because those replicas provably hold every acknowledged record. Electing the lagging replica — which some systems will do to stay available, called unclean election — means records the producer was told were durable simply vanish. That is the availability-versus-durability choice from Ch 3, made concrete in one config flag.
Zero-copy pagecache pipeline: writes bypass JVM heap into OS pagecache; reads stream directly from pagecache to NIC using sendfile()
[search] 6. Component Deep Dives

1. Why Kafka is blistering fast (The 4 Pillars of Performance):

  • Sequential I/O over Random Access: Disks (both HDD and NVMe) provide orders of magnitude higher throughput for sequential append operations vs random seeks. Kafka only appends to the active segment file.
  • PageCache Utilization: Kafka delegates caching to the Linux OS PageCache rather than maintaining an in-memory cache in the JVM heap. This avoids GC pauses, simplifies broker restarts (PageCache survives JVM restarts), and eliminates memory duplication.
  • Zero-Copy Data Transfer (sendfile): In standard architectures, reading from disk to network requires 4 context switches and 3 data copies (Disk -> OS PageCache -> JVM Heap -> Socket Buffer -> NIC Buffer). Kafka uses sendfile() syscall, transferring data directly from PageCache to NIC buffer (0 CPU copies, 2 context switches).
  • End-to-End Batching & Compression: Producers batch messages by partition and compress them (Zstandard/Snappy). Brokers store compressed batches untouched, and consumers decompress them. Network and disk bandwidth are reduced by 4x-10x.

2. In-Sync Replicas (ISR) and High Watermark (HW):

Each partition has 1 Leader and N Follower replicas. Followers continuously fetch messages from the leader. If a follower falls behind by more than replica.lag.time.max.ms (default 30s), it is dropped from the ISR. The High Watermark (HW) is the highest offset replicated to ALL nodes in the ISR. Consumers can ONLY read messages up to the HW. With acks=all and min.insync.replicas=2, no message is lost if a leader crashes.

3. Idempotent & Transactional Exactly-Once Semantics (EOS):

Each producer is assigned a 64-bit ProducerId (PID) by the broker coordinator. For every partition, the producer tracks a monotonically increasing SequenceNumber. The broker rejects any duplicate sequence number. For multi-partition atomic writes (Read-Process-Write cycle), a Two-Phase Commit Transaction Coordinator maintains a __transaction_state log and writes COMMIT/ABORT markers into topic partitions.

[balance] 7. Trade-off Analysis
DecisionChosen ✓Alternative ✗Reasoning
Storage EngineAppend-Only Segmented LogB-Tree / Embedded DB (RocksDB)Log gives O(1) disk writes, sequential reads, and instant zero-copy transfer. B-Trees incur random writes, write amplification, and complex locking.
Replication ConsensusISR with Quorum Controller (KRaft)Paxos / Raft per partitionISR allows dynamic quorum based on live replica speed, achieving maximum write throughput. KRaft manages cluster metadata with a single Raft quorum instead of ZooKeeper.
Consumption ModelPull (Long-Polling by Consumers)Push (Broker pushes to clients)Pull lets consumers pace themselves according to their processing capacity (eliminating consumer overload) and simplifies batch fetching and replay.
[shield] 8. Fault Tolerance
Leader Broker Crashes
KRaft controller detects heartbeat failure in <3s. Elects new leader from the ISR pool. No committed data is lost because ISR nodes are byte-for-byte in sync up to HW.
Slow / Stalled Follower
Controller evicts the lagging node from ISR so it does not block produce requests when acks=all. Once caught up, it rejoins the ISR.
Consumer Crashes during processing
Consumer group coordinator detects missed heartbeat (session.timeout.ms). Triggers Consumer Group Rebalance, reassigning crashed consumer's partitions to remaining workers from last committed offset.
Split Brain in Controller Quorum
KRaft uses Raft majority quorum (e.g. 3 of 5 nodes). A network partition cannot elect an illegitimate leader in the minority partition.
▶ Watch alongside this design
  • System Design Interview — Distributed Message Queue ~55 min — the closest match to this design anywhere on YouTube. Watch it after reading, and note where his choices differ from these.
[flag] 9. Conclusion — what I would say in the last three minutes
The dominant constraint

Sequential disk I/O plus the page cache is faster than most people assume. The whole design leans on it: an append-only log, zero-copy sendfile to consumers, and no per-message random access anywhere.

What I would build first

The partitioned append-only log with an ISR replication protocol. Ordering is per partition, which is the trade that makes throughput scale linearly with partitions.

What I deliberately did not build

Exactly-once semantics and global ordering. Both are available and both cost throughput; most consumers are cheaper to make idempotent.

The biggest risk

Partition count. It is effectively permanent once keys are hashed to partitions, and under-provisioning it caps your throughput in a way you cannot fix without a migration.

Design Google Drive / Dropbox (Distributed File Storage & Delta Sync)

Difficulty: Hard (Staff Expectation)  •  Target: 45 min
[list] 1. Requirements
❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
Sync only, or real-time collaborative editing?
These are different systems. Collaborative editing needs CRDTs or OT; file sync needs chunking and version vectors. Get this wrong and everything after it is wrong.
What is the largest file we must support?
Decides chunk size, resumable upload design, and whether a single file can exceed one machine.
Must offline edits merge, or is last-writer-wins acceptable?
Merging offline divergence is the hardest requirement in the design, and it is often not actually needed.
What is the sharing granularity — file, folder, or link?
Determines the ACL model and whether permission checks can be cached.
Do we deduplicate across users?
Cross-user dedup is a large storage win and a privacy leak: it lets someone test whether a file already exists.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.

Functional Requirements:

  • Users can upload, download, search, and delete files/folders across devices.
  • Automatic real-time file synchronization across desktop, mobile, and web.
  • Delta sync: When a file is modified, upload only the modified chunks (diffs), not the entire file.
  • File versioning (roll back to previous 30 versions) and soft delete / recovery bin.
  • Sharing permissions (view, comment, edit) with fine-grained ACLs.

Non-Functional Requirements:

  • Scale: 500M registered users, 100M Daily Active Users (DAU).
  • Storage: 100 PB active data, 100M file uploads/updates per day.
  • Consistency: Strong consistency for file metadata and chunk indexing (no stale directory tree).
  • Reliability: 99.999999999% (11 9's) data durability; 99.99% service availability.

If large files were the norm, chunk size and transfer scheduling would dominate the design.

Cross-user dedup saves more storage and leaks the existence of files between users.

[db] 4. Schema Design
-- Metadata DB (CockroachDB / Spanner for global ACID consistency) TABLE files { file_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, workspace_id UUID, parent_folder_id UUID, name VARCHAR(255), latest_version INT, is_deleted BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE, created_at TIMESTAMP, updated_at TIMESTAMP } TABLE file_versions { file_id UUID, version_number INT, total_size BIGINT, checksum_sha256 CHAR(64), created_by UUID, created_at TIMESTAMP, PRIMARY KEY (file_id, version_number) } TABLE file_chunks { file_id UUID, version_number INT, chunk_index INT, chunk_hash CHAR(64) REFERENCES chunks(chunk_hash), PRIMARY KEY (file_id, version_number, chunk_index) } TABLE chunks { chunk_hash CHAR(64) PRIMARY KEY, byte_size INT, storage_path VARCHAR(512), -- S3 / GCS object key ref_count BIGINT -- GC: deleted when ref_count == 0 }
[build] 5. High-Level Architecture
Chunked sync — and the offline edit that has no correct automatic answer
changed chunkschunk / deltametadataconflicting edit
What is moving: only changed chunks. The file is split by content-defined boundaries, each chunk is named by its hash, and the client uploads just the hashes the server has not seen — which is why a one-line change to a large document costs kilobytes.
What goes wrong: both devices edit the same file while offline. Neither version descends from the other, so the version vectors are concurrent — there is no correct automatic merge. Last-writer-wins is simple and silently destroys somebody’s work. The honest answer is to keep both and surface a conflicted copy, which is exactly what production file-sync products do. Ch 4
Content-defined chunking (Rabin Fingerprint) splits files into 4MB deduplicated blobs stored in S3; Spanner maintains atomic metadata; WebSockets notify sync clients
[search] 6. Component Deep Dives

1. Content-Defined Chunking vs Fixed-Size Chunking:

If you split files by fixed 4MB offsets, inserting 1 byte at the start of a 100MB file shifts all subsequent offsets, changing the SHA-256 hash of every single chunk (0% deduplication). Rabin Fingerprinting / FastCDC calculates a rolling polynomial checksum over a sliding window. When the checksum's lowest 13 bits equal a constant (e.g. hash & 0x1FFF == 0), a chunk boundary is set. Inserting data only changes 1 or 2 chunks surrounding the insertion; all remaining chunks retain identical hashes and are deduplicated.

2. Conflict Resolution (Two users edit simultaneously offline):

Google Drive uses Optimistic Concurrency Control with version numbers. When Client A commits version 2 of file_1, it succeeds. When Client B later attempts to commit version 2 of file_1, the DB detects a version mismatch (expected v1, currently v2). The server rejects Client B's commit and creates a branch: annual_report (Client B's conflicted copy 2026-09-07).pdf. For collaborative text docs (Google Docs), Operational Transformation (OT) or CRDTs (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types) resolve character-level conflicts in real time.

3. Garbage Collection for Chunks:

When files/versions are permanently deleted, chunks cannot be immediately removed from S3 because other files or users might share the same content-addressed hash. Each chunk row maintains a ref_count in the DB. When a version is purged, decrement ref_count. A daily MapReduce / Spark batch sweeper queries chunks with ref_count == 0 and deletes the underlying S3 objects.

[balance] 7. Trade-off Analysis
DecisionChosen ✓Alternative ✗Reasoning
Chunk SplittingClient-side Rabin ChunkingServer-side ChunkingClient-side saves huge upload bandwidth (never uploads chunks already in S3) and offloads CPU hashing from server infrastructure.
Metadata StoreSpanner / CockroachDB (NewSQL)Cassandra / DynamoDB (NoSQL)File tree operations (renaming a folder, moving 10,000 files) require atomic multi-row ACID transactions. NoSQL eventual consistency causes phantom or orphaned files.
Sync ProtocolDelta Sync with WebSocket notifyPeriodic Client PollingWebSockets deliver sub-second sync latency to all connected devices without hammering servers with millions of empty poll requests.
[shield] 8. Fault Tolerance
Upload Aborted Midway (Network drop)
Chunk uploads are idempotent. Client queries /upload/status with upload_id, receives list of already-persisted chunks, and resumes only the remaining chunks without re-uploading.
S3 / Cloud Storage Outage
Blob storage is multi-region replicated (e.g. S3 Cross-Region Replication). Read requests failover to secondary region CDN endpoint.
Metadata DB Primary Failure
Spanner / CockroachDB uses Multi-Paxos / Raft per range. Automatic leader election completes in <2s with zero data loss.
Zombie / Corrupt Chunks
Every downloaded chunk is verified against its expected SHA-256 hash by the client. If corrupted, client requests chunk from alternate replica.

The dominant constraint

Sync is not collaborative editing. I scoped this as file sync with versioning, which makes content-defined chunking and delta transfer the core, rather than CRDTs and operational transform.

What I would build first

Rabin-fingerprint chunking plus a chunk-hash manifest. Deduplication and delta sync both fall out of it for free.

What I deliberately did not build

Real-time co-editing, and cross-user deduplication. The second is a genuine storage win and a privacy leak, so I would keep dedup per-account.

The biggest risk

Conflict handling on offline edits. Last-writer-wins is simple and silently destroys work; the honest answer is to keep both versions and tell the user.

Design Uber / Lyft (Real-Time Geospatial Indexing & Ride Matching)

Difficulty: Hard (Staff Expectation)  •  Target: 45 min
[list] 1. Requirements
❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
What is the matching latency budget?
A few seconds allows a global optimisation over a batch; sub-second forces greedy local matching and a worse allocation.
How often do drivers report location?
This dominates total write volume — it is usually the largest number in the whole design.
Is pricing dynamic?
Surge is a separate feedback system with its own stability problems, and it interacts with matching.
One city or global?
Geo-sharding is natural here because demand is local; saying so early earns the partitioning discussion.
Are shared or pooled rides in scope?
Pooling turns matching into a routing optimisation that is NP-hard. Worth scoping out explicitly.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.

Functional Requirements:

  • Drivers broadcast their GPS location every 4 seconds when active.
  • Riders view real-time moving nearby drivers on the map (within 5km radius).
  • Rider requests a ride; system calculates upfront fare and ETA, then matches with the optimal driver.
  • Driver accepts/rejects ride dispatch within 15 seconds.
  • Trip lifecycle: Picked up -> In-transit with real-time routing -> Dropped off -> Payment processed.

Non-Functional Requirements:

  • Scale: 100M active riders, 5M active drivers globally.
  • Location Ingestion: 5M drivers × 1 update / 4s = 1,250,000 location writes/sec.
  • Matching Latency: Match driver within < 2 seconds from request.
  • ETA & Map Refresh Latency: < 100ms response time for nearby driver rendering.
  • Reliability: 99.99% availability. Zero duplicate ride bookings.

Demand is local to a city

Drivers report location every 4 seconds

Greedy matching is acceptable
If allocation quality mattered more than latency, batched global optimisation would be required.

[db] 4. Schema Design
-- Ephemeral Real-Time Geospatial Index (In-Memory Redis / Uber Ringpop H3) -- Redis Geospatial (GEOADD / GEORADIUS) or H3 Hexagonal Cell Sets: KEY: geo:h3:{h3_cell_index} -- e.g. geo:h3:8828308281fffff VALUE: SET of {driver_id} KEY: driver:{driver_id}:state VALUE: HASH { "lat": 37.7749, "lng": -122.4194, "status": "AVAILABLE", "h3_index": "8828308281fffff", "last_ping": 1725682910 } -- Trip State DB (CockroachDB / Cassandra for High Scale + ACID) TABLE trips { trip_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, rider_id UUID, driver_id UUID, status ENUM(requested, matched, arrived, in_progress, completed, canceled), pickup_lat DOUBLE, pickup_lng DOUBLE, dropoff_lat DOUBLE, dropoff_lng DOUBLE, fare_cents INT, created_at TIMESTAMP, updated_at TIMESTAMP }
[build] 5. High-Level Architecture
Geospatial matching — and the stale index that matches a driver who has gone
driver locationsride requestcandidates / matchbad match
What is moving: a continuous stream of driver positions into an in-memory H3 cell index, and — occasionally — a rider request that reads one cell plus its ring and greedily matches the best nearby driver. Demand is local, so no query is ever global.
What goes wrong: the location stream is by far the largest write volume in the design, so it is what saturates first. When the index falls behind, matching still works — it just matches against where drivers were 40 seconds ago, producing long pickups and cancellations. Nothing errors. Watch index staleness, not just matcher latency.
Location ingestion is buffered via Kafka into H3 in-memory spatial shards; Dispatch Engine computes 1-ring neighbors and queries OSRM routing engine for precise traffic ETA
[search] 6. Component Deep Dives

1. Spatial Indexing: Geohash vs Google S2 vs Uber H3:

  • Geohash (Rectangles): Encodes lat/lng into a base32 string (Z-order curve). Neighbor search has edge distortion at poles and cell boundaries vary drastically by latitude.
  • Google S2 (Spherical Hilbert Curve): Projects Earth onto 6 cube faces subdivided with a Hilbert curve. Great 1D index representation, but square cells have different distances to edge vs corner neighbors (factor of √2).
  • Uber H3 (Hexagonal Grid - Chosen): Subdivides the sphere into regular hexagons. Hexagons have the invariant that all 6 neighboring cells are equidistant from the center. This makes radius expansion (k-ring search: Ring 1 = 6 cells, Ring 2 = 12 cells) mathematically pure with zero corner distortion.

2. The Driver Matching Algorithm (DISCO):

Matching cannot just pick the nearest driver by Euclidean distance (they might be across a river or on a one-way highway).

  1. Lookup Rider's H3 cell (e.g. Resolution 8, ~460m).
  2. Fetch all AVAILABLE drivers in Rider's cell + k-ring(1) + k-ring(2) (total 1 + 6 + 12 = 19 hexagons).
  3. Batch call the Routing Engine (OSRM / Contraction Hierarchies) to calculate real street driving ETA considering traffic.
  4. Rank candidate drivers by ETA, driver acceptance rating, and supply-demand balance.
  5. Send dispatch offer to Top 1 driver with a 15-second TTL timer in Redis. If rejected/timed out, cascade to candidate #2.

3. Preventing Double Booking under Concurrency:

When two riders request a ride simultaneously in the same street corner, both may match with Driver D. To avoid double booking: The Dispatch Service executes a conditional atomic update on the driver's state in Redis/DB: UPDATE drivers SET status = 'DISPATCHED', active_trip_id = {trip_id} WHERE driver_id = {d_id} AND status = 'AVAILABLE'. If 0 rows updated, driver was already claimed; engine immediately selects next candidate.

[balance] 7. Trade-off Analysis
DecisionChosen ✓Alternative ✗Reasoning
Spatial GridUber H3 Hexagonal GridQuadtree / GeohashHexagons guarantee uniform neighbor distance in all 6 directions, drastically simplifying k-ring spatial smoothing and surge pricing calculations.
Location StorageIn-Memory Redis + TTL (Ephemeral)Persistent RDBMS / Disk DBDriver location pings are only relevant for ~30 seconds. Persisting 1.25M writes/sec to disk is wasteful. History is downsampled and written to cold analytics via Kafka.
Matching ArchitectureCentralized Dispatch (Batch Mini-Auction)Greedy First-Come-First-ServeBatching ride requests every 2-3 seconds achieves global optimization (minimizing total wait time for all riders) rather than greedily assigning the closest car to the first request.
[shield] 8. Fault Tolerance
Driver Loses Internet Mid-Trip
Driver app buffers GPS points in local SQLite. Upon reconnection, app uploads buffered breadcrumbs to reconcile route and compute accurate fare.
Dispatch Service Node Crashes during 15s offer
Driver offer is backed by Redis TTL key with an expiring lease. If dispatch node dies, heartbeat supervisor detects pending trip and re-dispatches to another driver.
Surge Traffic Spike (New Year's Eve 10x Load)
Rate limit nearby driver map refreshes from 4s to 8s per rider; drop unneeded background location telemetry while preserving dispatch pipeline.
Redis H3 Shard Failure
Redis Sentinel / Cluster promotes replica in <1s. Lost ephemeral driver pings are replenished within 4 seconds as drivers broadcast.
[flag] 9. Conclusion — what I would say in the last three minutes
The dominant constraint

Supply and demand are both intensely local. That is what makes geo-sharding correct here: a rider in one city never needs to be matched against a driver in another, so no query has to be global.

What I would build first

H3 hexagonal indexing over driver locations, with a greedy matcher inside a cell and its ring. It is not optimal, and it is fast enough to be right.

What I deliberately did not build

Pooled rides, which turn matching into an NP-hard routing problem, and dynamic pricing, which is a separate feedback system with its own stability failures.

The biggest risk

Location write volume. Drivers reporting every few seconds is the largest number in the design, and it is what will break first as the fleet grows.

Design a Distributed Web Crawler & Search Indexer (Googlebot Architecture)

Difficulty: Hard (Staff Expectation)  •  Target: 45 min
[list] 1. Requirements
❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
What politeness constraints must we honour?
This is the constraint that shapes the architecture: it forces partitioning by host so the rate limit becomes local instead of coordinated.
Freshness or coverage — which are we optimising?
Recrawling news hourly and archives yearly is a scheduling policy, and you cannot maximise both under a fixed budget.
Do we need to render JavaScript?
Headless rendering costs 10–100× more per page than fetching HTML, and changes your fleet size accordingly.
Exact duplicates only, or near-duplicates?
Exact is a hash. Near-duplicate needs SimHash or MinHash and a similarity threshold someone has to choose.
What is the crawl budget per domain?
Bounds both politeness and the risk of a spider trap consuming the entire fleet.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.

Functional Requirements:

  • Given a list of seed URLs, crawl billions of web pages across the public Internet.
  • Extract text content and outgoing hyperlinks to discover new URLs recursively.
  • Respect robots.txt rules and adhere to domain-level politeness (max 1 req/sec per host).
  • Deduplicate crawled content (avoid re-crawling identical or mirrored pages).
  • Store raw HTML / clean text in Document Store and update the Inverted Index for search.

Non-Functional Requirements:

  • Scale: Crawl 10 Billion pages per month (approx. 4,000 pages/sec continuous).
  • Storage: 10B pages × 100 KB avg clean text = 1 Petabyte storage per crawl cycle.
  • Freshness: Re-crawl dynamic sites (news) every few hours; static pages monthly.
  • Fault Tolerance: System must run 24/7 without deadlocks, handling spider traps and crashing hosts.
[chart] 2. Capacity Estimation
⚖ Assumptions — and what breaks if each is wrong
Politeness is defined per host
If it were per IP, hosts sharing an IP would need coordinated rate limiting across partitions.
Most pages are static HTML
If most required JavaScript rendering, fleet cost rises by one to two orders of magnitude.
Near-duplicate detection is good enough
Exact-duplicate-only detection would let templated content flood the index.

[plug] 3. API Design
// URL Frontier Internal RPC Protocol (gRPC) rpc FetchUrlsToCrawl(FetchBatchRequest) returns (FetchBatchResponse); message FetchBatchRequest { string crawler_worker_id = 1; int32 max_urls = 2; // e.g. 500 URLs } message FetchBatchResponse { repeated CrawlTask tasks = 1; } message CrawlTask { string url = 1; string domain = 2; int32 crawl_delay_sec = 3; // parsed from robots.txt int32 depth = 4; } // Inverted Index Search RPC rpc SearchIndex(SearchQuery) returns (SearchResponse); message SearchQuery { string query_text = 1; // "distributed consensus raft" int32 limit = 2; int32 offset = 3; }
[db] 4. Schema Design
-- URL Frontier State (Distributed Bigtable / Cassandra) TABLE url_frontier { url_hash CHAR(64) PRIMARY KEY, -- SHA-256(canonical_url) url TEXT, domain_hash CHAR(32), status ENUM(discovered, queued, fetching, crawled, error), priority_score FLOAT, -- PageRank + Domain Authority last_crawled_at TIMESTAMP, etag VARCHAR(128), content_simhash BIGINT -- 64-bit SimHash for near-duplicate detection } -- Inverted Index (Distributed Sharded Posting Lists - MapReduce / Lucene) TABLE inverted_index { term VARCHAR(128) PRIMARY KEY, -- e.g. "raft" posting_list BLOB -- Compressed list of (doc_id, term_frequency, [positions]) } -- Example Posting List: -- "raft" -> [Doc#12: TF=5, Pos=[12,45,89]], [Doc#99: TF=2, Pos=[3,120]]
[build] 5. High-Level Architecture
Crawl loop — and the spider trap that consumes the whole fleet
URL to fetchpage / contentfingerprinttrap URLs
What is moving: URLs out of per-host queues, pages back, and freshly discovered links returning to the frontier. Partitioning by host is the load-bearing decision: it makes the politeness delay a local constraint instead of a distributed rate limiter.
What goes wrong: a calendar page generates a link to the next month, forever. The frontier grows without bound and the fleet spends itself on one domain producing no new content. Defences: a per-domain crawl budget, a depth cap, and near-duplicate detection before indexing so the trap is visible as thousands of nearly identical pages rather than as growth.
URL Frontier uses 2-tier Priority & Politeness Queues; Bloom Filters discard already-seen URLs; Parser indexes text and loops discovered URLs back into Frontier
[search] 6. Component Deep Dives

1. The Mercator URL Frontier Architecture (Politeness + Priority):

To avoid hitting a single website (e.g. wikipedia.org) with 1,000 req/sec and causing a Denial of Service, the URL Frontier separates prioritization from politeness:

  • Priority Queues (F-Queues): Prioritizes URLs based on PageRank, domain authority, and freshness needs. High priority URLs are dequeued first into an intermediate router.
  • Politeness Queues (B-Queues): Each B-Queue contains URLs exclusively from a SINGLE host domain (e.g. Host #42 = nytimes.com). A scheduler maintains a min-heap of (next_allowed_fetch_time, B_queue_id). It only pops a queue if now() >= next_allowed_fetch_time (enforcing 1 req/sec per host), completely preventing DoS.

2. URL & Content Deduplication:

  • URL Dedup: A cluster Bloom Filter (stored in Redis or RAM) with 200B URLs at 1% false positive rate requires only ~240 GB RAM. If Bloom filter says 'Not Found', URL is 100% new. If 'Found', check Bigtable.
  • Near-Duplicate Content Detection (SimHash): 30% of web pages are duplicates or scrapers. Standard MD5/SHA256 changes completely on 1 character diff. SimHash projects 64-bit token hashes into a single 64-bit vector. Near-duplicate pages have a Hamming distance ≤ 3 (differ by at most 3 bits out of 64), which can be queried in O(1) time using a 4-table pigeonhole index.

3. Spider Traps & Infinite Dynamic Loops:

Websites with infinite calendar loops (/calendar?year=2027&month=13...) or session IDs in URLs trap crawlers. Defenses include: Max URL length limit (e.g. 512 chars), max path depth ≤ 8, URL pattern frequency monitoring per domain, and anomaly detection if a single domain yields > 50,000 URLs without new unique SimHash content.

[balance] 7. Trade-off Analysis
DecisionChosen ✓Alternative ✗Reasoning
URL Seen TestBloom Filter + BigtableRDBMS Unique IndexBloom Filter answers 'seen' checks in 5 nanoseconds from memory, saving 4,000 expensive disk round-trips per second.
Near-Duplicate64-bit SimHash (Cosine distance)MinHash / Jaccard similaritySimHash produces a compact 8-byte fingerprint per document and enables bitwise Hamming distance comparisons with zero decompression.
Crawler StorageSSTable / Bigtable Sparse ColumnRelational DB / PostgresBigtable handles massive append throughput, automatic tablet sharding across petabytes, and compresses sparse web documents efficiently.
[shield] 8. Fault Tolerance
Fetcher Worker Freezes (Slow Server Response)
Fetchers use non-blocking asynchronous I/O (epoll/libuv) with hard 5-second socket read timeouts and 2MB response size caps.
DNS Resolution Bottleneck
Local custom caching DNS server with pre-fetching; eliminates 100ms DNS query delay per crawled page.
Frontier Master Node Failure
Frontier queue state is checkpointed to RocksDB / distributed log (Kafka). Standby master restores queue pointers in <5s.
Malicious Spider Trap / Zip Bomb
Decompression stream reader capped at 10MB; immediately aborts and blacklists the URL pattern if exceeded.
[flag] 9. Conclusion — what I would say in the last three minutes
The dominant constraint

Politeness is per host, so the partition key must be the host. Making the constraint local instead of coordinated is the entire architectural move; partition by URL and you need a distributed rate limiter you cannot afford.

What I would build first

The Mercator-style frontier with per-host queues and a politeness delay, plus SimHash near-duplicate detection before anything is indexed.

What I deliberately did not build

JavaScript rendering, which costs 10 to 100 times more per page, and the ranking system, which is a different problem entirely.

The biggest risk

Spider traps and infinite URL spaces. Without per-domain budgets and depth caps, one badly behaved site consumes the whole fleet.

Design a Metrics & Logging Pipeline (Observability at Fleet Scale)

Difficulty: Hard (Staff Expectation)  .  Target: 45 min
[list] 1. Requirements
❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
Are metrics and logs one system or two?
Ask this first. They have opposite cost curves, and building them as one prices metrics like logs. This question is most of the design.
What is the retention per tier?
Raw for days, rollups for months, is what makes 13-month retention affordable. It is a lossy decision someone must approve.
What query latency do alerting, dashboards and forensics each need?
Three very different budgets. Alerting needs seconds on recent data; forensics can take minutes over cold storage.
Push or pull ingest?
Pull gives free liveness detection but cannot reach short-lived jobs or cross NAT.
Is this multi-tenant, and do we need per-tenant limits?
Without a per-tenant series budget, one team’s cardinality bomb takes down everyone’s monitoring.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.

Functional:

  • Ingest from 100,000 hosts emitting two different kinds of telemetry: metrics (numeric time series) and logs (semi-structured events)
  • Data queryable within 60 seconds of being emitted
  • Serve three consumers: dashboards (range queries), alerting (continuous evaluation), ad-hoc log search (forensics)
  • Tiered retention: metrics 13 months downsampled, raw logs 30 days

Non-Functional:

  • Ingest availability must exceed query availability — you can tolerate not being able to look, never losing the data you will need to look at
  • Must degrade under load rather than collapse, and must never become the cause of an incident
  • Cost-bounded: at this volume, storage cost is the design constraint
💡 The framing move that separates L6 from L5 here

Say this in the first three minutes: metrics and logs are two different systems and building them as one is the classic mistake. Metrics are numeric, aggregatable, and bounded by cardinality — you can pre-compute almost everything. Logs are unbounded, not aggregatable, and read rarely but urgently. They have opposite cost curves, so they get different storage engines behind a shared ingest path.

[chart] 2. Capacity Estimation
⚖ Assumptions — and what breaks if each is wrong
100K hosts, ~1,000 series each
Cardinality, not host count, is the binding constraint; one bad label can multiply this by the user base.
Sub-minute freshness is required for alerting
Relaxing to five minutes would allow batch ingestion and remove the streaming tier.
Logs are read rarely but urgently
If log search were high-volume, label-only indexing would be too slow and a full inverted index would be justified.

Assumptions: 100K hosts; 1,000 active metric series per host at 10s resolution; 100 log lines/sec per host at 300 bytes.

100M
