The number that decides the architecture: a metric datapoint compresses to roughly 1.4 bytes using delta-of-delta timestamps plus XOR-encoded floats (the Gorilla scheme), against 16 bytes uncompressed. So 10M datapoints/sec is only ~14 MB/s — about 1.2 TB/day. Logs at 10:1 gzip are ~26 TB/day.

Logs are ~20× the cost of metrics for a fraction of the query volume. That ratio is the entire justification for treating them differently, and it is the number to lead with when someone asks why you did not just use one system.

[plug] 3. API Design
POST /v1/ingest/metrics // protobuf, batched, gzip Body: { series: [{ name, labels{}, points:[{t, v}] }] } Response: 204, or 429 + Retry-After when shedding Note: fire-and-forget from the agent; NO synchronous ack path POST /v1/ingest/logs Body: { stream_labels{}, entries:[{t, line}] } Response: 204 | 429 GET /v1/query_range?q=&start=&end=&step= Response: { series:[{ labels{}, values:[[t,v]] }] } Errors: 422 series_limit_exceeded // reject, never OOM GET /v1/logs/search?selector=&filter=&start=&end=&limit= Response: streaming NDJSON, bounded by scan-bytes budget
[db] 4. Schema Design
-- METRICS: the label set IS the identity. Hash it once, store the mapping. TABLE series_index { series_id UINT64 PRIMARY KEY, -- hash(name + sorted labels) metric_name VARCHAR, labels MAP<str,str>, first_seen TIMESTAMP, last_seen TIMESTAMP -- drives churn detection + expiry } -- inverted index: label_name=label_value -> roaring bitmap of series_id BLOCK tsdb_block { -- immutable, 2h of data, columnar series_id, t0, delta_of_delta_ts[], xor_encoded_vals[] } -- ~1.4 bytes/point. Blocks compact 2h -> 1d -> 1w with rollups attached. -- LOGS: index the LABELS only, never the message body. TABLE log_chunk_index { stream_id UINT64, -- hash(stream_labels) t_start TIMESTAMP, t_end TIMESTAMP, object_key TEXT -- gzip chunk in object storage } -- Query = narrow by labels to a few chunks, then brute-force grep them.
[build] 5. High-Level Architecture
Telemetry ingest — and the cardinality bomb the collector has to stop
metric pointstime serieslog chunksrejected
What is moving: agents batch metric points every 10 s and push them through stateless collectors into a durable log, which is the shock absorber — it decouples a producer spike from consumer capacity. Downstream, the same stream forks into two completely different stores: compressed series for metrics, gzip chunks plus a label index for logs.
What goes wrong: one deploy adds a user_id label to a request counter. Each distinct value becomes its own time series, so one metric becomes millions, and the TSDB’s memory-resident index grows without bound until the process is OOM-killed. Nothing about traffic changed — an application change did this. The defence is a per-tenant series budget enforced at the collector, so the blast radius is one team rather than everyone’s monitoring.
100,000 hosts -- each runs a local AGENT (batches 10s, disk-buffers on failure) | v REGIONAL COLLECTORS stateless, terminate TLS, authenticate, validate, REJECT high-cardinality label sets at the door | v DURABLE LOG (Kafka) partitioned by series_id / stream_id | this is the shock absorber -- it decouples a | producer spike from consumer capacity +---------------------------+ v v METRICS CONSUMER LOG CONSUMER in-memory head block batch into 5-min gzip chunks WAL for crash recovery write chunk -> object store flush 2h block -> object write (stream_id, t_range, key) -> index | | v v TSDB QUERY LOG QUERY head (hot, RAM) + blocks label selector narrows to N chunks, downsampled rollups parallel scan with a bytes budget
The durable log in the middle is the whole design. Everything upstream of it is optimised for never dropping data; everything downstream can be restarted, rebuilt, or temporarily out of capacity without loss.
[search] 6. Component Deep Dives

Cardinality is the failure mode — name it before you are asked. A metric series is identified by its full label set, so every distinct combination is a separate series with its own in-memory index entry and compression state. Adding one label with unbounded values — user_id, request_id, a raw URL with query parameters — turns one series into millions. The database does not slow down gracefully; the ingester's memory-resident index grows without bound and the process is OOM-killed. This is the single most common way a metrics system dies, and it is always caused by a well-meaning application change, never by traffic growth.

Defences, in order of effectiveness: reject at the collector with a per-tenant series budget so the blast radius is one team; alert on series churn (new series per minute) rather than absolute count, because churn is the leading indicator; and offer the escape hatch — if you need per-user granularity, that is a log or an exemplar, not a metric.

Why Gorilla compression matters so much. Timestamps in a scrape arrive at almost exactly fixed intervals, so the delta between consecutive deltas is nearly always zero and encodes in one bit. Values usually change slowly, so XOR-ing consecutive float64s leaves mostly leading zeros. Together this gives ~1.4 bytes/point — a 12× reduction that is what makes the entire recent window fit in RAM. A metrics system whose hot window is in memory answers dashboard queries in milliseconds; one that goes to disk cannot.

The log indexing decision. A full inverted index over log content (Elasticsearch-style) makes arbitrary text search fast and costs roughly as much as the raw data again in index size, plus heavy write-time CPU. Indexing labels only and brute-force scanning the matching chunks (Loki-style) makes ingest cheap and drops storage cost by an order of magnitude, at the price of slower unselective searches. Choose label-only indexing here: log search is rare, is nearly always already scoped by service and time, and the cost difference at 26 TB/day dominates the latency difference.

Rollups. Nobody queries 10-second resolution from six months ago; the dashboard would have more points than pixels. Compact blocks into 5-minute and 1-hour rollups carrying min/max/sum/count, and let the query layer pick resolution from the time range. This is what makes 13-month retention affordable, and it is a lossy decision you should state out loud.

[balance] 7. Trade-off Analysis
DecisionChosen ✓Alternative ✗Reasoning
Metrics vs logsTwo storage engines, one ingest pathOne unified storeOpposite cost curves. Logs are ~20x the bytes for a fraction of the queries. A unified store prices metrics like logs and makes 13-month retention unaffordable.
Ingest transportPush, via a durable logPull / scrapePull is simpler and gives free liveness detection, but cannot cross NAT or reach short-lived jobs. The durable log is non-negotiable regardless: it absorbs spikes that would otherwise reach the storage tier.
Log indexLabels only + brute scanFull inverted index~10x cheaper ingest and storage. Searches are almost always already narrowed by service and time window, so the unselective-query penalty is rarely paid.
Under overloadShed at the collector, 429Buffer indefinitelyUnbounded buffering converts an observability degradation into an observability outage, precisely when you need it. Shed low-priority tenants first and keep alerting metrics flowing.
Query safetyReject over series/byte budgetBest-effort executionOne unbounded query must not be able to OOM the node serving everyone's alerts. A fast 422 is a better answer than a slow death.
[shield] 8. Fault Tolerance
Kafka unavailable
Agents buffer to local disk with a bounded ring (e.g. 1 GB / 15 min) and resume on recovery. Beyond the bound they drop oldest first, because in an incident the newest telemetry is the telemetry you need. Collectors return 429 so agents back off with jitter.
Metrics ingester crashes
The in-memory head block is backed by a write-ahead log on local disk; on restart it replays the WAL to reconstruct the head. Kafka consumer offsets are committed only after the WAL write, so recovery is at-least-once. Duplicate datapoints are idempotent — same series, same timestamp, same value overwrites harmlessly.
Cardinality bomb from one team
Per-tenant series budget enforced at the collector: series beyond the budget are rejected with a named error and an alert to the owning team. Blast radius is one tenant instead of the cluster. This is the single most important safeguard in the design.
Object storage degraded
Recent data is still served from the in-memory head and local blocks, so dashboards and alerting for the last few hours keep working — which is the window that matters during an incident. Historical queries fail fast with a clear error rather than hanging.
The observability system causes an incident
Agents are hard-capped on CPU and memory via cgroups and drop telemetry rather than compete with the application they observe. Ingest endpoints are on separate capacity from query, so a dashboard stampede during an outage cannot block ingestion. This inversion — monitoring taking down production — is common enough that you should raise it unprompted.
▶ Watch and read alongside this design
  • CMU 15-445 — #05 Row vs. Column Storage + Compression ~75 min — the columnar and compression foundations a TSDB is built from.
This design has no good video match, which is itself informative — the infrastructure round is the under-served half of the free video landscape. The primary sources are the Gorilla paper (Facebook, VLDB 2015) and the Prometheus TSDB documentation.
[flag] 9. Conclusion — what I would say in the last three minutes
The dominant constraint

Metrics and logs have opposite cost curves. Logs are roughly twenty times the bytes for a fraction of the queries, so they get separate storage engines behind one shared, durable ingest path.

What I would build first

The durable log in the middle. It decouples a producer spike from consumer capacity, and everything downstream of it can be rebuilt or restarted without loss.

What I deliberately did not build

Tracing, and per-tenant query isolation beyond a simple budget. Both matter and both are separable.

The biggest risk

Cardinality. One well-meaning application change adding a user_id label can OOM the ingesters, which is why the per-tenant series budget is enforced at the collector rather than reviewed by humans.

Design a Distributed Cache (like Memcached / Redis Cluster)

Difficulty: Hard (Staff Expectation)  .  Target: 40 min
[list] 1. Requirements
❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
Is this a cache or a low-latency store?
The highest-value question in the round. If we may lose the data freely it is about locality and eviction; if not, you are designing something two orders of magnitude more expensive.
What is the value size distribution?
At 100-byte values, per-entry overhead is more than half your RAM. The fix is to change the workload, not to buy nodes.
How stale may a read be?
Determines whether TTL alone is sufficient or you need an explicit invalidation channel.
What happens if the whole tier restarts?
Forces the conversation about whether the origin survives a 0% hit rate — which is the failure that actually takes systems down.
Single region, or replicated?
Replicating a reconstructible cache doubles cost; that memory usually buys a better hit rate instead.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.

Functional:

  • GET, SET with TTL, DELETE, atomic INCR
  • 10 TB working set across the cluster; values from 100 B to 1 MB
  • Elastic: add and remove nodes without a full cache flush

Non-Functional:

  • 10M QPS aggregate, p99 under 1 ms at the cache (excluding network to caller)
  • Cache loss is survivable — this is not a database — but a mass simultaneous loss must not take the origin down
  • No strong consistency requirement; the cache may serve a stale value
💡 Scope the problem before designing it

The clarifying question that earns the most here: “is this a cache or a low-latency store?” If the answer is cache, you may lose data freely and the design is about locality and eviction. If the answer is store, you need replication and durability and you are designing something two orders of magnitude more expensive. Most candidates assume the first and never say so; saying it out loud is the staff signal.

[chart] 2. Capacity Estimation
⚖ Assumptions — and what breaks if each is wrong
Data is reconstructible from the origin
If it is not, this is a low-latency store and needs replication and durability.
Access is Zipfian
Under a uniform distribution a cache smaller than the working set thrashes and adds latency instead of removing it.
Values average around 1 KB
At 100 bytes, per-entry overhead exceeds the payload and the design must pack entries.

Assumptions: 10 TB working set, average value 1 KB, 10M QPS at 95:5 read:write.

~10B
keys resident
~64 GB
usable RAM/node
~200
nodes (with headroom)
50K
QPS per node avg
~10 GB/s

~1.4 TB

The overhead nobody estimates: every entry carries key bytes, a hash-table slot, LRU pointers, TTL and flags — roughly 50–120 bytes before your value. With 1 KB values that is ~10% waste; with 100-byte values it is more than half your RAM. If the workload is small values, the correct answer is to change the workload — pack many logical entries into one cache entry — not to buy more nodes.

Sanity check the network, not just the memory: 10M QPS × 1 KB ≈ 10 GB/s aggregate, or ~50 MB/s per node. Comfortable. But a single hot key at 1M QPS × 1 KB is 1 GB/s to one node — an 8 Gbps NIC saturated by one key. Hot keys are a bandwidth problem before they are a CPU problem.

[plug] 3. API Design
// Binary protocol over pooled, pipelined TCP. No HTTP -- header // parsing alone would dominate a sub-millisecond budget. GET key -> value, cas_token | MISS MGET key[] -> values[] // one RTT for N keys, same node SET key value ttl flags -> STORED CAS key value cas_token -> STORED | EXISTS // compare-and-swap: the ONLY concurrency primitive here, // and what makes read-modify-write safe without a lock DELETE key -> DELETED | NOT_FOUND INCR key delta -> new_value // server-side, atomic // Client-side: routing table + consistent hash ring, refreshed // from a config service. The client picks the node -- no proxy hop.
[db] 4. Schema Design
-- Per node: slab allocator, NOT malloc. Fixed-size classes in a -- growth factor (1.25x): 96B, 120B, 152B, 192B ... 1MB STRUCT item { next, prev PTR -- LRU list linkage h_next PTR -- hash chain expiry UINT32 -- lazy: checked on read, not swept nbytes, flags UINT32 cas_id UINT64 -- bumped on every mutation key[], value[] BYTES } -- Rounding to a slab class wastes up to 20% per item. That is the -- price of never fragmenting -- a cache that fragments dies slowly -- over weeks, which is far worse than a fixed 20% tax. -- Ring: 200 physical nodes x ~200 virtual nodes = 40,000 points. -- Virtual nodes are what make removal move 1/N of keys, not half.
[build] 5. High-Level Architecture
Read path — and what a dead cache node does to the origin
request / hitmiss reaching the origin
What is moving: a key lookup out, and either a cached value back in ~0.2 ms, or — on a miss — a read that continues to the origin. The client hashes the key itself and talks to exactly one node, so there is no coordinator anywhere on this path.
What goes wrong: node B dies and its share of keys is rehashed onto the survivors — where they are not present. Every one of those reads is now a miss travelling to an origin sized for about 1% of read traffic. With consistent hashing that is ~1/N of keys and survivable; with hash mod N it is 99.5% of keys at once, a cold-start stampede the origin will not survive.
APPLICATION + smart client library | | 1. hash(key) -> position on the ring | 2. walk clockwise to the owning virtual node | 3. connect DIRECTLY -- no proxy, no extra hop v CONSISTENT HASH RING 200 nodes x 200 vnodes = 40,000 points | +-------------+-------------+-------------+ v v v v node 1 node 2 node 3 ... node 200 slab alloc slab alloc slab alloc hash table hash table hash table LRU chains LRU chains LRU chains CONFIG SERVICE (small, strongly consistent -- etcd/Zookeeper) holds the authoritative ring; clients poll and cache it. Only membership needs consensus. Ch 6's expensive machinery is bought for a few KB of topology, never for the 10M QPS data path. HOT KEY PATH: keys above a QPS threshold are promoted to a client-local L1 (a few ms TTL) and replicated to R nodes, with the client picking one at random.
The single most important structural decision is that the data path touches no coordinator. Consensus is confined to membership, which changes a few times a week; the 10M QPS path is a hash computation and one round trip.
[search] 6. Component Deep Dives

Why consistent hashing, in one number. With plain hash(key) mod N, changing N from 200 to 201 remaps roughly 99.5% of keys — a total cache flush and an instant origin stampede. Consistent hashing remaps only the keys owned by the departing node, about 1/N ≈ 0.5%. Virtual nodes are what make that share even: with one point per node, hash positions cluster and a removal dumps its whole range onto a single neighbour, which then falls over. Roughly 200 virtual nodes per physical node brings load variance under about 5%.

The hot key problem, which is where this interview actually goes. Consistent hashing distributes keys evenly; it cannot distribute traffic evenly, because traffic is Zipfian. One celebrity key can take 1M QPS to a single node while the other 199 idle. Three defences, and they compose:

  • Client-side L1 with a very short TTL (5–50 ms). A hot key is by definition read constantly, so even a 10 ms TTL collapses 1M QPS into ~100 QPS per client. This is the highest-leverage fix and it costs almost nothing, because the staleness it introduces is bounded by a number you choose.
  • Replicate hot keys to R nodes under salted names (key#1 … key#R), with clients picking one at random. Divides load by R at the cost of R× the memory for those keys and R invalidations per write.
  • Detect, do not guess. Track approximate per-key request rates with a count-min sketch on each node — sublinear memory, tolerable error — and promote keys past a threshold automatically. Static hot-key lists are always stale by the time they matter.

Eviction at scale. Strict LRU needs a lock on the list head for every read, which is a global mutex on your hottest path and will not sustain 50K QPS per node. Real implementations approximate: bump an item's position only if it has not been bumped in the last ~60 seconds, or use a CLOCK/second-chance bit. You give up exact recency ordering — which was only ever a heuristic — and you get a lock-free read path. Approximating the approximation is free.

Expiry is lazy, not swept. Actively scanning 10 billion keys for expired entries would burn CPU proportional to cache size rather than to traffic. Instead, check the TTL on read and let LRU reclaim the rest. The consequence to state: expired-but-unread entries still occupy memory, so your usable capacity is always somewhat below your nominal capacity.

[balance] 7. Trade-off Analysis
DecisionChosen ✓Alternative ✗Reasoning
RoutingSmart client, direct connectProxy tierA proxy adds a network hop -- often 0.3-0.5 ms against a sub-1 ms budget -- plus a tier to scale and fail. A proxy wins only when you cannot control the clients or need many languages; then pay the hop deliberately.
PartitioningConsistent hashing + vnodeshash mod Nmod N remaps ~99.5% of keys when one node joins. That is a full flush and a guaranteed origin stampede at exactly the wrong moment.
ReplicationNone, except hot keysReplicate everythingDoubles cost to protect data that is by definition reconstructible. Spend that memory on a larger working set instead -- a bigger cache raises the hit rate, which is worth more than surviving one node loss.
EvictionApproximate LRUStrict LRUStrict LRU requires a lock on the list head per read. The recency ordering it buys was already a heuristic; the lock contention is real.
ConsistencyDelete on write, TTL backstopWrite-through updateUpdating races: two writers can land their cache updates in the opposite order to their database writes and leave the cache permanently stale. Delete has no such race. Ch 9
[shield] 8. Fault Tolerance
Single node dies
Its ~0.5% of keys become misses and are refilled from the origin on demand. Clients mark the node down after a short failure-detection window and skip it on the ring. Critically, the origin must have headroom for a 0.5% miss-rate increase -- which it does, because that is a rounding error against the normal miss rate.
Node flapping
Far worse than a clean death: each transition reshuffles key ownership, so keys ping-pong between nodes and the effective hit rate collapses while both copies go stale. Damp it -- require N consecutive failures to eject and a longer, hysteretic interval to re-admit. Slow, stable membership beats accurate, twitchy membership. Ch 1
Whole cache tier restarts
The genuine disaster: hit rate goes to 0% and the origin sees 20-100x its normal load, which is a metastable failure it will not recover from on its own. Mitigate with staggered restarts (never more than 10% of the fleet at once), a concurrency limit on origin fill so the cache cannot forward more than the origin can serve, and load shedding beyond it. Ch 10
Hot key saturates one node's NIC
Count-min sketch detects the key, the control plane promotes it to replicated + client-L1 mode automatically. Detection must be automatic: by the time a human has read the graph, the node has been dropping packets for ten minutes.
Ring disagreement between clients
During a config rollout, two clients may briefly hold different rings and write the same key to different nodes -- producing two divergent copies with no reconciliation. TTLs bound the damage, and the config service versions the ring so a client can detect and refuse a stale topology. This is why membership is the one thing that gets consensus.
▶ Watch alongside this design
  • System Design Interview — Distributed Cache ~40 min — the direct companion to this design, covering consistent hashing and eviction at interview depth.
  • MIT 6.824 — Lecture 16: Memcached at Facebook ~80 min — the production reality: what actually broke, and what they did about it. Read the paper too if you have time.
[flag] 9. Conclusion — what I would say in the last three minutes
The dominant constraint

It is a cache, so the data is reconstructible. That permission is what makes the rest cheap: no replication, no durability, no consensus on the data path, and a node loss costs 1/N of the hit rate rather than any correctness.

What I would build first

Consistent hashing with virtual nodes plus a smart client that connects directly. Consensus is confined to membership, which changes a few times a week.

What I deliberately did not build

Persistence and cross-region replication. Both would double the cost to protect data whose whole point is that losing it is safe.

The biggest risk

The cold-start stampede. If the tier restarts and the origin cannot survive a 0% hit rate, the cache is not an optimisation but an undeclared hard dependency.

Design Typeahead / Autocomplete (Search Suggestions at Google Scale)

Difficulty: Hard (Staff Expectation)  .  Target: 40 min
[list] 1. Requirements
❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
Are suggestions personalised or global?
Personalisation breaks the single precomputed table, because there is no longer one answer per prefix. This changes everything downstream.
What is the latency budget?
Above roughly 100 ms the suggestion arrives after the next keystroke and the feature stops feeling live. That number decides precompute versus live search.
How fresh must trending terms be?
Minutes forces a second, streaming lane on top of the batch table. Days does not.
How many languages and locales?
Each locale multiplies the size of the precomputed table and the safety review surface.
What are the safety and filtering requirements?
Suggestions are published editorial content. An offensive completion is a public incident, not a relevance bug.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.

Functional:

  • Given a prefix, return the top 10 completions ranked by likelihood
  • Fire on every keystroke; a 20-character query means up to 20 requests
  • Trending terms must appear within minutes, not days
  • Tolerate typos in the prefix; suppress offensive and unsafe suggestions

Non-Functional:

  • p99 under 100 ms end to end — above roughly 100 ms the suggestion arrives after the user has typed the next character, and the feature stops feeling live
  • Read-dominated to an extreme degree: essentially 100% reads on the serving path
  • Stale suggestions are acceptable; slow suggestions are not
💡 The reframe that carries the interview

This is not a search problem, it is a precomputation problem. You are not searching a corpus at request time — you are looking up an answer that was computed hours ago. Once you say that, every subsequent decision follows: the serving path does one lookup and no ranking, and all the interesting engineering moves offline into the pipeline that builds the lookup table.

[chart] 2. Capacity Estimation
⚖ Assumptions — and what breaks if each is wrong
Suggestions are global, not personalised
Personalisation removes the single precomputed answer per prefix and invalidates the whole serving model.
The prefix table fits in memory, about 150 GB
If it did not, the serving path gains a disk seek and the latency budget no longer holds.
Hourly freshness is sufficient for most terms
Only trending terms need the streaming lane; if everything needed minute freshness the batch build is pointless.

Assumptions: 5B searches/day; ~15 keystroke requests per search after client-side debouncing; 100M distinct queries worth suggesting.

~75B
suggestion reqs/day
~870K
QPS average
~2.6M
QPS peak (3x)
~500M

~150 GB

<100 ms
