The estimate that decides the architecture: 500M prefixes × 10 suggestions × ~30 bytes ≈ 150 GB. That fits in the RAM of a modest cluster — perhaps 8 machines with replication. The entire answer set fits in memory, which is why the serving path can be a hash lookup and why p99 under 100 ms is comfortably achievable.

Note the client-side saving: debouncing at ~50 ms and cancelling in-flight requests cuts request volume by roughly 60% for free, before any server-side work. Mention it — the cheapest capacity is the request you never send.

[plug] 3. API Design
GET /v1/suggest?q={prefix}&lang=&country=&n=10 Response: 200 { suggestions:[{ text, score, type }], ttl_ms } Headers: Cache-Control: private, max-age=60 Errors: returns 200 with [] -- NEVER an error. // A failed suggestion must look like "no suggestions", // never like a broken page. Fail invisibly. // Transport: keep-alive HTTP/2 or a persistent WebSocket. TCP+TLS // setup per keystroke would blow the entire latency budget. POST /v1/feedback // which suggestion was accepted Body: { prefix, shown[], selected_index, session } // This is the training signal that ranks tomorrow's table.
[db] 4. Schema Design
-- SERVING: a flat, immutable, precomputed map. No tree walk at read time. TABLE prefix_top_k { prefix VARCHAR(1..20) PRIMARY KEY, -- + lang, country suggestions BLOB -- packed [text, score] x 10 } -- Built offline. Served from RAM. Sharded by hash(prefix). -- OFFLINE: the trie exists only in the build pipeline, never at read time. NODE trie_node { children MAP<char, node>, top_k ARRAY[10] -- cached at EVERY node } -- Caching top_k at each node is the whole trick: it converts -- "walk the subtree and rank" into "read one array". TABLE query_counts { -- the ranking input query, lang, country, count_7d, count_1h, ctr, is_safe }
[build] 5. High-Level Architecture
Suggestion path — and the bad table that has to be one flip from rollback
prefixcached resultslookupempty result
What is moving: a prefix out, ten suggestions back — usually from the edge, because short prefixes are both the hottest and the most stable. On a miss it is a single hash lookup into a precomputed table, plus a small trending overlay merged at read time. No ranking happens on this path.
What goes wrong: a build publishes a partial table. Suggestions silently degrade to nothing — and because the endpoint returns 200 with an empty list by design, no error rate moves. That is why the swap must be gated: table size within a few per cent of the last build, canary prefixes unchanged, zero safety violations in a sample — and why versions are immutable so rollback is a pointer flip.
OFFLINE PIPELINE (hourly) SERVING PATH (per keystroke) query logs (last 7d) browser | | debounce 50ms, v | cancel in-flight aggregate + filter v (safety, spam, PII) CDN / edge cache | | ~40% hit on v | common prefixes build TRIE, cache top-k v at every node SUGGEST SERVICE | | hash(prefix) -> shard v v flatten -> prefix_top_k IN-MEMORY SHARDS | one hash lookup, no ranking v | ATOMIC SWAP into serving -------------------+ (version the whole table; flip a pointer. Never mutate in place -- a half-updated table serves incoherent suggestions.) REAL-TIME LANE (minutes): trending terms from a streaming count-min sketch, merged at read time as a small overlay on top of the hourly table.
Two lanes, deliberately. The hourly batch lane gives quality and safety review; the streaming lane gives freshness for breaking terms. Merging a small overlay at read time is far cheaper than rebuilding 150 GB every minute.
[search] 6. Component Deep Dives

Why not walk a trie at request time? A trie find-the-prefix is O(len), which is fine — but then you must traverse the entire subtree beneath it to collect and rank candidates. For the prefix “a” that subtree is essentially the whole corpus. Caching the top 10 at every node converts that traversal into a single array read, and it is the difference between a system that works and one that times out on the first character. The cost is memory and rebuild time, both of which you have.

Sharding: by prefix, not by node. Hash the prefix string and shard on that, so any single request is answered by exactly one shard with no scatter-gather. Sharding the trie structurally — by first letter, say — is the trap: it produces wildly unequal shards (far more queries start with s than with z) and forces multi-shard traversal. Replicate the entire table to every serving node instead if it fits, which at 150 GB it nearly does; full replication makes every node able to answer everything and eliminates the routing problem outright. Ch 5

The short-prefix problem. Single-character prefixes are requested orders of magnitude more often than long ones. These are perfect cache candidates precisely because they are both hottest and most stable — the top suggestions for “a” barely move hour to hour. Push the first two characters' worth of results to the CDN and the client, and a large fraction of traffic never reaches your service at all.

Typo tolerance without paying for it on every request. Full edit-distance search over the trie at request time is too slow. Instead, precompute: for known high-frequency misspellings, store the corrected prefix's results directly under the misspelling as an ordinary key. This turns fuzzy matching into an exact lookup and costs only offline build time. Reserve genuine edit-distance search for the tail, behind a stricter latency budget, and only when the exact lookup returned nothing.

Ranking is where the product lives. Raw frequency is a weak signal because it is dominated by yesterday's news and never surfaces anything rising. Blend: 7-day frequency for stability, 1-hour frequency for trend, historical click-through rate for quality, plus personalisation and locale. Then apply the safety filter last and hard — suggestion lists are published editorial content, and an offensive completion is a public incident, not a relevance bug. The safety filter must run at build time and again at serve time, because the streaming overlay bypasses the batch review.

[balance] 7. Trade-off Analysis
DecisionChosen ✓Alternative ✗Reasoning
Read pathPrecomputed prefix→top10 mapLive trie traversalTraversing the subtree under a one-character prefix means ranking the whole corpus. Precomputation moves all the work offline, where it has hours instead of milliseconds.
ShardingHash of prefix (or full replication)By first letterStructural sharding produces grossly unequal shards and multi-shard reads. At 150 GB, replicating everything to every node is both affordable and simpler.
FreshnessHourly batch + streaming overlayContinuous rebuildRebuilding 150 GB per minute is enormous waste for a handful of changed entries. A small merged overlay gets the freshness at a fraction of the cost.
TyposPrecomputed misspelling keysEdit distance at query timeFuzzy search over a large trie cannot fit a 100 ms budget. Precomputing the common cases converts it to an exact lookup; the long tail is not worth the latency.
On failureReturn empty, 200 OK5xx errorAutocomplete is an enhancement. Degrading to "no suggestions" is invisible; an error is a visible broken feature. Never let an optional component fail loudly.
[shield] 8. Fault Tolerance
Build pipeline fails
Keep serving the previous table version indefinitely. Suggestions age gracefully -- a day-old table is barely distinguishable to users -- so there is never a reason to swap in a partial build. Alert on table age, not on job failure, because a job that "succeeded" with 3% of the data is the more dangerous outcome.
Bad table published
Versioned tables and a pointer swap make rollback a single atomic flip. Gate the swap on automated checks: table size within 10% of the previous build, top suggestions for a fixed set of canary prefixes unchanged beyond a threshold, and zero safety-filter violations in a sampled scan.
Serving shard dies
Data is immutable and fully replicated, so any surviving replica answers identically -- no rebuild, no repartition, no state to recover. This is the payoff for making the serving tier stateless over a read-only snapshot: node failure is a routing event, not a data event.
Traffic spike (breaking news)
The spike concentrates on a few prefixes, which is the best possible shape for a cache -- CDN and client caching absorb the bulk of it. Beyond that, shed load by shortening result lists and raising client debounce via a server-pushed config, degrading quality before availability.
Offensive suggestion surfaces
Blocklist evaluated at build AND serve time, because the streaming overlay skips the batch review path. Serve-time filtering also gives a same-minute kill switch for a specific term without waiting for a rebuild -- which is the response time this class of incident actually requires.
▶ Watch alongside this design
  • System Design Interview — Top K Problem (Heavy Hitters) ~45 min — the ranking and count-min sketch machinery behind both the trending lane here and D11's hot-key detection.
  • CMU 15-445 — #09 Vector Indexes, Inverted Indexes, Filters, Tries ~75 min — tries as a database implementer builds them.
[flag] 9. Conclusion — what I would say in the last three minutes
The dominant constraint

It is a precomputation problem, not a search problem. The whole prefix-to-top-k table fits in memory, so the serving path is one hash lookup and every interesting decision moves offline into the build.

What I would build first

The offline trie build that caches top-k at every node, flattened into a versioned table that is swapped atomically.

What I deliberately did not build

Personalisation, which breaks the single precomputed table because there is no longer one answer per prefix.

The biggest risk

Publishing a bad table. Suggestions are editorial content, so I would gate the swap on canary prefixes and a safety scan, and keep serve-time filtering as a same-minute kill switch.

Design a RAG Q&A System (Retrieval-Augmented Generation over Private Data)

Difficulty: Hard (Staff Expectation)  .  Target: 45 min
[list] 1. Requirements
❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
Whose data is it, and what is the access-control model?
Ask this before anything else. It forces ACL filtering inside retrieval; post-filtering the answer is not a security control once a restricted passage is in the prompt.
How large is the corpus and how often does it change?
Decides index architecture and whether re-indexing can be incremental or must be a full rebuild.
Must answers carry citations?
Citation changes the whole pipeline — you must track provenance per chunk and validate that emitted citations point at retrieved text.
What is the latency budget, and can we stream?
Streaming makes time-to-first-token the number the user feels, rather than total generation time.
What should happen when nothing relevant is found?
“I don’t know” must be an acceptable answer, or the system will confidently invent one and nobody will be able to tell.
Is there a cost ceiling per query?
Token spend dominates everything else here, and it is the constraint most candidates never mention.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.

Functional:

  • Answer natural-language questions over a customer's private document corpus (10M documents, ~50 GB of text)
  • Every answer carries citations to the source passages it used
  • Respect per-user access control — a user must never see content from a document they cannot open
  • New and updated documents become answerable within 15 minutes

Non-Functional:

  • p95 under 3 seconds to first token; streaming thereafter
  • Cost per query is a first-class constraint, not an afterthought
  • Answers must be attributable; “I don't know” is a correct and required output
💡 Two things to say early that most candidates miss

First: this is two systems — an offline indexing pipeline and an online serving path — and almost all the quality lives in the offline half while all the latency lives in the online half. Second: access control must be enforced at retrieval time, not by filtering the answer. Once a restricted passage enters the prompt, the model may paraphrase it and no downstream filter can reliably catch that. Post-filtering a generated answer is not a security control.

[chart] 2. Capacity Estimation
⚖ Assumptions — and what breaks if each is wrong
The corpus is 10M documents, ~50 GB of text
Two orders of magnitude more and the vector index no longer fits one machine even quantised.
Query volume is low, around 1 QPS
This is cost- and quality-constrained, not throughput-constrained. High QPS would change the serving design entirely.
Permissions change rarely but must be respected immediately
This is why ACLs are resolved at query time rather than trusted from the index.

Assumptions: 10M documents averaging 5 KB of text; chunked at ~500 tokens with overlap; 1,536-dimension embeddings; 100K queries/day.

~100M
chunks
6 KB
per vector (fp32)
~600 GB
vectors, unquantised
~150 GB
int8 quantised
~1.2
QPS average
~4K
prompt tokens/query

The number that reframes the problem: 1.2 QPS is nothing. This system is not throughput-constrained — it is cost- and quality-constrained. Say that explicitly, because it inverts the usual instinct: the interesting engineering here is not sharding for scale, it is the index that fits in memory and the tokens you do not send.

Vector index sizing is the real capacity question. 600 GB of fp32 vectors does not fit one machine; 150 GB of int8 does, comfortably. Scalar quantisation to int8 costs a few percent of recall and 4× the memory — the single highest-leverage trade in the design. Note also that an HNSW graph adds roughly 30–50% overhead on top of the vectors for its edge lists.

Cost: at ~4K prompt tokens per query, token spend dominates everything else. Trimming retrieved context from 10 chunks to 5 nearly halves the bill and frequently improves answer quality.

[plug] 3. API Design
POST /v1/ask Body: { question, conversation_id?, filters{}, stream:true } Auth: user token -> resolved to an ACL group set Response: server-sent events { type:"retrieval", chunks:[{doc_id, score, snippet}] } { type:"token", text:"..." } // streamed { type:"citation", span:[s,e], doc_id, chunk_id } { type:"done", usage:{prompt_tokens, completion_tokens} } Errors: 422 no_relevant_context // retrieval found nothing 429 token_budget_exceeded // Emitting the retrieval event FIRST is a real design decision: the // user sees sources in ~300ms while generation runs, which makes a // 3-second answer feel responsive and makes the system auditable. POST /v1/documents // triggers async re-index POST /v1/feedback // thumbs + which citation was wrong
[db] 4. Schema Design
TABLE chunks { chunk_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, doc_id UUID, ordinal INT, -- position within the document text TEXT, -- the chunk itself heading_path TEXT, -- "Handbook > Leave > Parental" acl_groups ARRAY<UUID>, -- DENORMALISED from the document embedding VECTOR(1536), content_hash BYTES, -- skip re-embedding unchanged chunks updated_at TIMESTAMP } -- acl_groups is denormalised ON PURPOSE. The ANN index must filter -- during the graph walk; a post-hoc join cannot -- you would retrieve -- 10 results, discard 9 for permissions, and return almost nothing. -- Two indexes over the same chunks, queried together: -- HNSW over embedding (semantic / meaning) -- BM25 inverted over text (lexical / exact terms, IDs, error codes)
[build] 5. High-Level Architecture
Retrieval and generation — and why access control cannot be applied at the end
questionretrieved chunksanswerrestricted content
What is moving: the question is embedded and searched against a vector index and a lexical index together, the ACL predicate is evaluated during the graph walk so only permitted chunks are ever returned, and those chunks are assembled into a prompt with citations.
What goes wrong: if you filter after retrieval — or worse, filter the generated answer — a restricted passage has already entered the prompt. The model can paraphrase it, summarise it, or answer a question about it, and no output filter reliably catches that. Post-filtering is not a security control. This is why the ACL groups are denormalised onto every chunk: so the filter can run inside the search, not after it.
OFFLINE: INDEXING ONLINE: SERVING document source user question + auth | | v v parse + extract rewrite query (PDF, HTML, tables) (resolve "it", "that one", | expand acronyms) v | CHUNK ~500 tokens, +-----------+-----------+ 15% overlap, never v v across a heading VECTOR SEARCH BM25 SEARCH | HNSW, ACL-filtered lexical, exact v during graph walk terms and IDs EMBED (batched, skip | | unchanged content_hash) +-----------+-----------+ | v v FUSE (reciprocal rank) write vectors + BM25 top ~50 candidates + acl_groups | | v v RERANK cross-encoder ATOMIC INDEX SWAP 50 -> top 5 | v ASSEMBLE PROMPT -> LLM stream tokens + citations Two retrievers, then rerank. Vector search finds meaning; BM25 finds the exact error code or product name that embeddings routinely miss. Neither alone is enough.
The retrieve-wide-then-rerank-narrow shape is the core pattern: cheap recall over 50 candidates, then an expensive, accurate model over only those 50. Sending all 50 to the LLM would cost 10× as much and answer worse.
[search] 6. Component Deep Dives

Chunking is the highest-leverage decision and the one most often rushed. Chunk too small and you sever the context that makes a passage meaningful; too large and the embedding averages several topics into a vector that matches none of them well. Split on document structure — headings, sections, paragraph boundaries — never on a fixed character count that cuts mid-sentence. Overlap adjacent chunks by 10–15% so a fact spanning a boundary survives in at least one. And prepend the heading path to each chunk's text before embedding: a chunk reading “employees receive 12 weeks” is nearly useless in isolation, and decisive when it begins “Handbook > Leave > Parental”.

Why hybrid retrieval, concretely. Embeddings capture semantic similarity and are systematically bad at rare exact tokens — an error code like ERR_4021, a part number, an unusual surname. BM25 handles those and is helpless at paraphrase. Run both, then fuse with reciprocal rank fusion, which combines by rank position rather than by score and so needs no score normalisation between two incomparable scoring systems. This is a small amount of work for a large and reliable quality gain.

Access control must filter inside the ANN search. HNSW navigates a proximity graph; if you filter results after the walk, you may traverse to 10 neighbours and discard 9 for permissions, returning one weak result while better permitted chunks sat one hop away unexplored. The index must evaluate the ACL predicate during traversal so the walk keeps expanding until it has 10 permitted results. This is why acl_groups is denormalised onto the chunk — and it is the detail that separates a demo from a system you can sell to an enterprise.

Attributing failure — the question a good interviewer will ask. When an answer is wrong, was it retrieval or generation? These have opposite fixes, so you must be able to tell them apart. Instrument both: log the retrieved chunks with every answer, and evaluate them separately — retrieval by whether the passage containing the answer was in the top k on a labelled set, generation by whether the answer is supported by the passages actually supplied. A retrieval failure means fixing chunking, embeddings or the reranker; a generation failure means fixing the prompt or the model. Teams that measure only end-to-end accuracy cannot act on the number they have.

Cost and latency levers, in order of value: cache embeddings by content_hash so re-indexing an edited document re-embeds only changed chunks; cache whole answers for repeated questions, which in an enterprise corpus is a surprisingly large fraction; trim to 5 reranked chunks rather than 10; and stream tokens so time-to-first-token is what the user experiences rather than total generation time.

[balance] 7. Trade-off Analysis
DecisionChosen ✓Alternative ✗Reasoning
RetrievalHybrid vector + BM25, fusedVector onlyEmbeddings systematically miss rare exact tokens -- error codes, part numbers, names -- which are exactly what users paste into a search box. Cheap to add, large and reliable quality gain.
Vector storageint8 scalar quantisationfp324x memory reduction for a few percent of recall. Turns a 600 GB multi-machine index into a 150 GB single-machine one, which removes an entire distribution problem.
Access controlFilter during ANN traversalPost-filter resultsPost-filtering returns too few results and, worse, is not a security boundary: once a restricted passage is in the prompt the model can paraphrase it past any output filter.
RerankingCross-encoder over top 50Send all 50 to the LLM10x the token cost for worse answers -- long contexts dilute attention and degrade quality. Retrieve wide, rerank, then send narrow.
FreshnessIncremental by content_hashNightly full re-indexRe-embedding 100M unchanged chunks nightly is enormous waste and cannot meet a 15-minute freshness target.
[shield] 8. Fault Tolerance
Retrieval returns nothing relevant
Threshold on the reranker score and return an explicit "I could not find this in your documents" rather than generating from the model's parametric memory. An unsupported answer that looks confident is worse than no answer, because the user cannot tell the difference -- and this is the single most damaging failure mode of the whole class of system.
LLM provider slow or unavailable
Timeout and fall back to returning the retrieved passages with highlights -- degraded to search, but still useful, and still cited. Circuit-break on sustained failure rather than queueing requests that will time out anyway. Ch 10
Vector index corrupt or mid-rebuild
Build into a new index version and swap atomically; never mutate the serving index in place. Keep the previous version on disk for instant rollback. Until the swap, BM25 alone still answers -- degraded recall on paraphrase, but the system stays up.
Document permissions change
This is a correctness AND security issue: revocation must propagate faster than re-indexing. Resolve ACLs at query time against the live permission service for the candidate set, using the denormalised acl_groups only as a pre-filter. Slightly slower, and it means a revoked user stops seeing content within seconds rather than at the next index build.
Prompt injection from document content
Retrieved chunks are untrusted input, not instructions -- a document containing "ignore previous instructions" must not be obeyed. Keep retrieved content in a clearly delimited region of the prompt, instruct the model to treat it as data, and validate that emitted citations actually point at retrieved chunks. Treat this as an injection class alongside SQL injection, not as an AI curiosity. Ch 15
▶ Watch alongside this design
  • Andrej Karpathy — Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT 3h 31m — the full training stack. The best single grounding if an AI round comes up; watch at 1.5× if time is short.
  • Andrej Karpathy — Intro to Large Language Models ~60 min — the shorter version if 3.5 hours is not available to you.
  • 3Blue1Brown — Attention in transformers, step-by-step ~26 min — the fastest route to real intuition for the mechanism rather than the vocabulary.
  • 3Blue1Brown — Large Language Models explained briefly ~8 min — worth watching first if the whole area is new.
  • CMU 15-445 — #09 Vector Indexes, Inverted Indexes, Filters, Tries ~75 min — vector indexes and inverted indexes in one lecture, which is exactly the hybrid retrieval this design uses.
[flag] 9. Conclusion — what I would say in the last three minutes
The dominant constraint

Access control has to be enforced during retrieval. Once a restricted passage is in the prompt the model can paraphrase it past any output filter, so post-filtering is not a security control. This constrains the index design more than latency does.

What I would build first

Hybrid retrieval (vector plus BM25) with ACL filtering inside the ANN traversal, then a cross-encoder rerank down to a handful of passages.

What I deliberately did not build

Fine-tuning, and agentic multi-step retrieval. Both are tempting and neither is needed to answer grounded questions with citations.

The biggest risk

Confident wrong answers. Without a reranker score threshold and an explicit 'I could not find this', the system invents plausible text and the user cannot tell.

Design an ML Inference & Classification Service (language detection, image recognition, audio denoising, X-ray triage)

Difficulty: Hard (Staff Expectation)  .  Target: 45 min
[list] 1. Requirements
❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
Is this online inference or batch scoring?
The single biggest fork. Batch lets you queue and amortise; online puts a model on the request path with a latency budget and a capacity floor.
What is the cost of a wrong answer, and in which direction?
For X-ray triage a false negative is a missed diagnosis and a false positive is a wasted review — wildly asymmetric. That asymmetry sets the decision threshold, not accuracy.
Is a human in the loop?
If yes, the system is a ranking and routing problem — get the right cases in front of a reviewer — not an autonomous decision system. This changes the whole design.
How often does the model change?
Weekly retraining needs versioning, shadow traffic and rollback as first-class features rather than an afterthought.
What is the input size and modality?
A 30-second audio clip, a 20 MB medical image and a 40-character text string have completely different preprocessing and batching characteristics.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.

Functional:

  • Accept an input (text, image or audio), run a model, return a label with a confidence score
  • Return “uncertain” rather than a forced label when confidence is below threshold
  • Support multiple model versions concurrently, with traffic splitting for canaries
  • Log every inference with its input reference, output, model version and latency

Non-Functional:

  • p95 under 300 ms for text, under 2 s for image and audio
  • Cost per inference is a first-class constraint — GPUs are the dominant line item
  • A model rollback must take effect in under a minute without a redeploy
  • The system must degrade to a cheaper model rather than fail
[chart] 2. Capacity Estimation
⚖ Assumptions — and what breaks if each is wrong
10M inferences/day, peaking at 3× average
At 100× this volume the batching design stays but the fleet becomes large enough that model-specific hardware sizing dominates.
GPU inference takes ~40 ms per item unbatched, ~4 ms amortised at batch 32
If the model were CPU-friendly the entire GPU scheduling layer disappears and this becomes an ordinary stateless service.
Inputs are retained for retraining
If they cannot be retained — medical or regulated data — the feedback loop that improves the model has to be redesigned around federated or on-premise training.

Assumptions: 10M inferences/day, 3× peak, average payload 200 KB for images.

~116/s
average inference QPS
~350/s
peak QPS
~4 ms
amortised GPU time at batch 32
~1.4 GB/s
peak payload ingest
~2 TB/day
retained inputs
8–12
GPU replicas at peak

The number that decides the architecture: unbatched, 350 QPS × 40 ms means 14 GPU-seconds per second — 14 GPUs sitting at 100% with no headroom. Batched at 32, the same load needs roughly 1.4 GPU-seconds per second. Batching is not an optimisation here; it is the difference between an affordable system and an unaffordable one. Everything in the serving design exists to fill batches without blowing the latency budget.

[plug] 3. API Design
POST /v1/predict Body: { model, input_ref | inline_input, threshold?, explain? } Response: 200 { label, confidence, model_version, latency_ms, alternatives:[{label, confidence}] } 200 { label: null, reason: "below_threshold", confidence } // NOT an error -- "I am not sure" is a valid, required answer Errors: 413 payload too large, 429 shedding, 503 no healthy model POST /v1/predict:batch // async, for bulk scoring Response: 202 { job_id } -> results written to object storage POST /v1/feedback Body: { inference_id, correct_label, reviewer_id } // the label that becomes tomorrow's training data, and today's // measurement of whether the model is still working GET /v1/models -> versions, traffic split, health
[db] 4. Schema Design
-- Every inference is logged. This table IS the evaluation dataset, -- the drift monitor and the audit trail -- do not treat it as a log. TABLE inferences { inference_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, model_version VARCHAR, input_ref TEXT, -- object-storage key, never the bytes input_hash BYTES, -- dedup + cache key label VARCHAR, -- NULL when below threshold confidence FLOAT, latency_ms INT, created_at TIMESTAMP } -- INDEX: (model_version, created_at) for per-version drift analysis TABLE labels { -- ground truth, arriving late and sparsely inference_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, true_label VARCHAR, source ENUM(reviewer, user_correction, audit), labelled_at TIMESTAMP } -- The JOIN of these two tables is your live accuracy measurement. -- If you cannot write that query, you cannot tell that the model broke. TABLE model_registry { version VARCHAR PRIMARY KEY, artifact_key TEXT, traffic_pct INT, threshold FLOAT, state ENUM(shadow, canary, live, retired) }
[build] 5. High-Level Architecture
Inference path — and why the batcher is the entire economics
inputtensor / resultbatchunbatched calls
What is moving: raw inputs are decoded and normalised on a cheap CPU tier, then held by the batcher for up to ~10 ms or until 32 accumulate, and run through the GPU as one call. Preprocessing is deliberately off the GPU so the expensive resource is never idle waiting on the cheap one.
What goes wrong: take the batcher out and each request occupies the GPU alone. At 350 QPS × 40 ms that is 14 GPU-seconds per second — roughly ten times the hardware for identical traffic and no better latency. Batching is not an optimisation here; it is the difference between an affordable system and an unaffordable one.
client | v API GATEWAY auth, size cap, rate limit, shed early | v PREPROCESS decode, resize/resample, normalise (CPU, scales cheaply) | deliberately separated from inference: preprocessing is CPU-bound | and would otherwise waste the GPU it is sitting on v RESULT CACHE keyed by (input_hash, model_version) | hit -> return v miss BATCHER wait up to N ms OR until batch is full, whichever first | this queue is where the latency/cost trade actually lives v GPU MODEL SERVERS v3 (live, 90%) | v4 (canary, 10%) | v4 (shadow, 0%) | shadow gets a copy of live traffic, returns nothing v threshold check -> label, or "uncertain" -> HUMAN REVIEW QUEUE | v INFERENCE LOG -> drift monitoring, evaluation, next training set
The three separations that matter: preprocessing off the GPU, a cache before the batcher, and shadow traffic that exercises a new model on real inputs while returning nothing to anyone.
[search] 6. Component Deep Dives

Dynamic batching is the whole serving design. The batcher holds a request for up to a fixed window — say 10 ms — or until the batch fills, whichever comes first. That window is a direct, tunable trade: a longer wait means fuller batches, better GPU utilisation and lower cost per inference, at the price of added tail latency for every request. The mistake is treating it as a constant. Under light load the window should shrink toward zero, because a half-empty batch costs nothing to run and waiting only hurts; under heavy load it should grow. State it as “I would make the batch window adaptive to queue depth” and you have said something most candidates do not.

The threshold is a product decision, not a model decision. A classifier emits a score; turning that score into an action requires choosing a cut-off, and the right cut-off depends entirely on the asymmetry of the errors. For X-ray triage a false negative is a missed diagnosis and a false positive is a few wasted minutes of a radiologist’s time, so the threshold should be set to catch nearly everything and route aggressively to human review. For a landmark-recognition feature, a wrong label is a mild embarrassment and the threshold can be much higher. Never answer this question with “we would optimise accuracy” — accuracy weights both errors equally, which is almost never what anyone wants.

Caching works better here than people expect. Inference is a pure function of (input, model version), so results are perfectly cacheable by content hash. Real workloads are Zipfian — the same image, the same audio clip, the same phrase get submitted repeatedly — and a cache hit costs microseconds against tens of milliseconds of GPU. Note the versioning subtlety: the model version must be part of the key, or a model rollout silently serves stale predictions from the previous model.

Shadow deployment is how you avoid shipping a worse model. Offline evaluation tells you how a model performs on the data you have; it says nothing about the data you will get. Run the new version on a copy of live traffic, discard its output, and compare its predictions with the live model’s. Disagreements are where you look. Only after the disagreement rate is understood do you move to a canary that actually serves users.

Drift is the failure that has no error message. Nothing crashes, latency is fine, and the answers slowly stop being right — the input distribution moved. Detect it without waiting for ground truth by monitoring the prediction distribution and the confidence histogram: if the share of “uncertain” results jumps, or the class mix shifts, something changed even before any label arrives. This is why the inference log is part of the design rather than an operational afterthought.

[balance] 7. Trade-off Analysis
DecisionChosen ✓Alternative ✗Reasoning
BatchingDynamic, adaptive windowFixed size, or noneNo batching needs roughly 10× the GPUs. A fixed window is wrong at both ends of the load curve: it wastes latency when idle and under-fills when busy.
PreprocessingSeparate CPU tierOn the GPU nodeDecode and resize are CPU-bound. Doing them on the GPU node leaves the expensive resource idle while it waits for the cheap one.
Below thresholdReturn “uncertain”Always return the top labelA forced label at 51% confidence looks identical to one at 99% to every downstream consumer. Surfacing uncertainty is what makes human review possible.
RolloutShadow, then canaryOffline evaluation onlyOffline metrics measure the data you already had. Shadow traffic measures the data you actually get, which is the only one that matters.
Result cacheKeyed by content hash + model versionNo cacheInference is a pure function, workloads are Zipfian, and a hit is microseconds against tens of milliseconds of GPU.
[shield] 8. Fault Tolerance
GPU fleet saturated
Shed at the gateway with 429 before the request consumes preprocessing, and fail over to a smaller distilled model that runs on CPU. Degraded predictions beat no predictions, provided the response says which model answered.
A model version is bad
Traffic split lives in the registry, not in a deployment, so rollback is a percentage change that takes effect in seconds. This is the reason not to bake the model into the container image.
Model artifact fails to load
The server refuses to report healthy and stays out of rotation. A node serving a partially loaded model silently returns nonsense, which is far worse than a node that is visibly down.
Poisoned or adversarial input
Hard caps on decoded dimensions and duration before the model sees anything — a decompression bomb is a resource attack disguised as an image. Rate-limit per caller on inference cost, not on request count.
Silent accuracy collapse (drift)
Monitor the prediction and confidence distributions continuously, not just latency. Alert on a shift in the uncertain-rate; it moves before any ground-truth label arrives to tell you.
[flag] 9. Conclusion — what I would say in the last three minutes
The dominant constraint

Batching economics. Unbatched, this needs roughly ten times the GPUs; every serving decision — the adaptive window, the CPU preprocessing tier, the cache — exists to fill batches without breaking the latency budget.

What I would build first

The preprocessing tier, the batcher and the inference log. The log is not optional: without it you cannot measure drift, and drift is the failure mode with no error message.

What I deliberately did not build

Training and the feature store. Serving and training are separable, and conflating them is how ML systems become impossible to reason about.

The biggest risk

Silent accuracy decay. Nothing alerts, latency stays flat, and the answers quietly stop being right. That is why prediction-distribution monitoring is in the design rather than in a follow-up.

Design an ML Experiment & Pipeline Platform (experiment tracking, lineage, and pipeline health metrics)

Difficulty: Hard (Staff Expectation)  .  Target: 40 min
[list] 1. Requirements
❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
Are we tracking experiments, or orchestrating them?
Tracking is a metadata store — comparatively easy. Orchestration is a distributed scheduler with retries and dependencies, which is D6’s problem wearing different clothes. Scope this explicitly.
Must a result be exactly reproducible?
Reproducibility forces you to version code, data, environment and hyperparameters together. Without it you only need to record metrics, which is a far smaller system.
How large are the artifacts?
Metrics are kilobytes; model checkpoints are gigabytes. They belong in different stores, and conflating them is the classic mistake.
How many concurrent experiments, and how chatty?
A training run logging a metric every step at 1 kHz across thousands of runs is a high-rate ingest problem, not a CRUD app.
Who consumes this — researchers, or production?
If production models are promoted from here, the registry becomes a control plane with access control and audit, not a notebook companion.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.

Functional:

  • Record runs: parameters, metrics over time, artifacts, code version, dataset version
  • Compare runs side by side and query across them (“best F1 where lr < 0.01”)
  • Full lineage: from a deployed model back to the exact data and code that produced it
  • Pipeline health: freshness, volume, schema drift and failure rates per stage

Non-Functional:

  • Logging must never slow or fail a training run — the tracker is not on the critical path
  • Handle 10K concurrent runs each logging at up to 100 Hz
  • Metadata retained for years; large artifacts on a lifecycle policy
  • Queries across runs return in under a second for a dashboard to be usable
[chart] 2. Capacity Estimation
⚖ Assumptions — and what breaks if each is wrong
10K concurrent runs, 100 metric points/sec each
At 10× this the write path stays but metric storage must become a proper TSDB rather than a relational table.
Artifacts average 500 MB, metrics are kilobytes
If artifacts were small, one store would do and the split would be unnecessary complexity.
Researchers tolerate seconds of lag in the UI
If live training curves had to be real-time, the buffered async write path would need replacing with a streaming one.

Assumptions: 10K concurrent runs, 100 points/sec each, 500 MB average artifact.

1M/s
metric points at peak
~2 bytes
per point compressed
~170 TB/yr
metrics, compressed
~500 MB
average artifact
~50 TB/day
artifact writes at 100K runs
<1 s
cross-run query budget

The number that shapes the design: 1M metric points per second is time-series ingest, not database inserts. Writing each point as a row through an ORM would need thousands of database connections and would fall over. This is the same problem as D11 — and the correct answer is to reuse D11 rather than build a second one. Recognising that two problems are the same problem is worth more than a novel design.

[plug] 3. API Design
POST /v1/runs Body: { experiment, params{}, code_ref, dataset_ref, env_ref } Response: 201 { run_id } // code_ref/dataset_ref/env_ref are content hashes -- this is // what makes a result reproducible rather than merely recorded POST /v1/runs/{id}/metrics // batched, fire-and-forget Body: { points:[{ key, value, step, ts }] } Response: 202 // client buffers and never blocks training on this call. // A tracker outage must not kill a 40-hour training run. POST /v1/runs/{id}/artifacts -> { upload_url } // direct to object store POST /v1/runs/{id}/finish Body: { status, summary_metrics{} } GET /v1/runs?experiment=&filter=params.lr<0.01&sort=-metrics.f1 GET /v1/models/{version}/lineage -> run, code, dataset, parent models GET /v1/pipelines/{id}/health -> freshness, volume, schema drift
[db] 4. Schema Design
-- Metadata is relational; metrics are time series; artifacts are blobs. -- Three stores, because these three have nothing in common. TABLE runs { run_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, experiment VARCHAR, params JSONB, -- GIN index: query across runs by param code_ref BYTES, -- git sha dataset_ref BYTES, -- content hash of the snapshot env_ref BYTES, -- container digest summary JSONB, -- final metrics, denormalised for sorting status ENUM(running, finished, failed, killed), started_at, ended_at TIMESTAMP } -- Summary metrics are denormalised on purpose: "best F1 in this -- experiment" must not require scanning a time series per run. SERIES metrics { -- in the TSDB, keyed like any other series labels: { run_id, key }, points: (step | ts, value) } TABLE lineage_edges { -- a DAG, not a tree: models beget models child VARCHAR, parent VARCHAR, kind ENUM(trained_from, distilled_from, finetuned_from), PRIMARY KEY (child, parent) }
[build] 5. High-Level Architecture
Experiment tracking — and the outage where dropping data is the right answer
metric pointsbatched writemetadatafailed flush
What is moving: metric points at up to 100 Hz per run, buffered in the client and flushed asynchronously; run metadata and the four reproducibility hashes; and gigabyte checkpoints, which the client uploads directly to object storage rather than through the API.
What goes wrong — and why it is fine: the ingest service is down. The client buffers, then drops the points and keeps training. A gap in a loss curve costs nothing; killing a 40-hour run on expensive hardware because a metadata service returned 503 is unacceptable. This is the same inversion as D11: the observability system must never be able to take down the thing it observes.
TRAINING JOB (thousands, running for hours) | | client library buffers in memory, flushes every few seconds, | drops on the floor if the tracker is down v INGEST API stateless, validates, fans out by kind | +---------------+------------------+ v v v METADATA METRICS ARTIFACTS Postgres TSDB object storage runs, params 1M points/sec checkpoints, plots lineage DAG (reuse D11) (client uploads direct) | | | +---------------+------------------+ v QUERY / COMPARE UI cross-run filters, curve overlay, lineage walk PIPELINE HEALTH (a separate concern sharing the same metrics store) freshness -- how old is the newest row? volume -- row count vs the same hour last week schema -- column types and null rates vs the last run These three catch most data incidents. The model is usually fine; the data that reached it is not.
Three stores because the three data kinds have nothing in common, and a client that buffers and drops rather than blocking — an observability system must never be able to kill the thing it observes.
[search] 6. Component Deep Dives

The tracker must never be on the critical path. A training run can last forty hours on expensive hardware; losing it because a metadata service returned 503 is an unacceptable failure. So the client library buffers in memory, flushes asynchronously, and drops metrics rather than blocking or retrying indefinitely. Losing a few points from a training curve costs almost nothing; losing the run costs a day and a large bill. Say this explicitly — it is the same inversion as D11’s “monitoring must not take down production”, and interviewers notice when a candidate applies a principle across problems.

Reproducibility is four hashes, not one. To reproduce a result you need the code, the data, the environment and the parameters, and it is the data that people forget. “Trained on the users table” is not a reference — that table has changed since. The dataset reference must be an immutable snapshot: a content hash, a table version, or a time-travel timestamp. Without it, lineage is decorative and no result can actually be rerun.

Lineage is a DAG and it is queried backwards. The question that matters is never “what did this run produce?” It is “a model in production is behaving badly — what data produced it, and what else came from that data?” That is a reverse traversal, and it is the query to design for. Model-begets-model relationships — fine-tuning, distillation — make it a DAG rather than a tree, so a bad dataset can taint a whole subgraph of descendants that must be found and retired together.

Pipeline health is three cheap checks that catch most real incidents. Freshness: how old is the newest row? Volume: row count against the same window last week. Schema: column types and null rates against the previous run. Almost every “the model got worse” incident is really an upstream data incident, and these three catch it far earlier than model metrics do — because model metrics need ground-truth labels, which arrive days later if at all.

On what metrics to track for pipeline performance — a question asked directly in the bank — the answer has three layers, and naming all three is the signal. System: stage latency, throughput, failure and retry rates, cost per run. Data: freshness, volume, null rate, schema drift, feature distribution shift. Model: prediction distribution, confidence histogram, and — once labels arrive — precision and recall sliced by segment. Most candidates give only the first layer, which is the one that tells you least about whether the pipeline is doing its job.

[balance] 7. Trade-off Analysis
DecisionChosen ✓Alternative ✗Reasoning
Metric ingestReuse the D11 metrics storeA new bespoke store1M points/sec is a time-series problem that is already solved here. Building a second one is duplicated operational burden for no gain.
Client behaviourBuffer and dropBlock and retryA tracker outage must never kill a 40-hour training run. Losing points from a curve is cheap; losing the run is not.
ArtifactsDirect client upload to object storageThrough the APIStreaming gigabytes through a metadata service makes it a bandwidth bottleneck and couples its availability to every checkpoint write.
Summary metricsDenormalised onto the run rowComputed from the series“Best F1 in this experiment” is the most common query. Scanning a time series per run to answer it makes the UI unusable.
ScopeTracking only; orchestration is separateOne combined systemOrchestration is a distributed scheduler with retries and dependencies. Merging them produces a system that does neither well.
[shield] 8. Fault Tolerance
Tracking service is down
Clients buffer, then drop. Training continues and the curve has a gap. This is the correct trade and it should be a stated design property rather than an accident.
Metric write storm from one run
Per-run rate limits at ingest, plus aggregation in the client (log every N steps, not every step). One badly instrumented run must not degrade everyone else’s tracking.
Object storage unavailable
Checkpoint writes fail and the run retries with backoff. Metadata and metrics continue, so the run is still observable even though its artifacts are not being saved.
Dataset snapshot deleted by a lifecycle policy
Lineage records the reference, so this is detectable rather than silent — but reproducibility is lost. Pin datasets referenced by any promoted model, and make deletion of a pinned snapshot fail loudly.
Lineage graph has a cycle or missing edge
Validate on write: a run may only reference artifacts that already exist. A broken lineage graph is discovered exactly when you need it most, during an incident.
[flag] 9. Conclusion — what I would say in the last three minutes
The dominant constraint

Three data kinds with nothing in common. Metadata is relational and small, metrics are a 1M-point-per-second time series, artifacts are gigabyte blobs. One store cannot serve all three, and the metrics half is a problem this guide has already solved in D11.

What I would build first

The run metadata store with the four reproducibility hashes, and the buffer-and-drop client. Those two decide whether the platform is trustworthy and whether it is safe.

What I deliberately did not build

Orchestration, and a feature store. Both are frequently bolted on here and both are separate systems that deserve their own design.

The biggest risk

Lineage that is recorded but never exercised. It looks complete until an incident, when you discover the dataset reference points at a mutable table that has since changed.

Design Google Maps for an Uncovered Region (imagery ingestion, map tiles, routing, IP→geo lookup)

Difficulty: Hard (Staff Expectation)  .  Target: 45 min
[list] 1. Requirements
❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
Are we building the map, or serving it?
Wholly different systems. Capture and conflation is an offline data pipeline; serving tiles and routes is a read-heavy low-latency system. I would scope to both but design them separately.
What is the source of truth for geometry?
Vehicle capture, satellite imagery, or crowd-sourced edits? Each has a different trust model, and crowd-sourcing makes moderation a first-class component rather than an afterthought.
Does routing need live traffic?
Static routing is a precomputable shortest-path problem. Live traffic makes edge weights change every minute and invalidates precomputation.
Offline use on-device?
Users in an uncovered region very likely have poor connectivity, so tile and routing-graph packs must be downloadable — which changes the client design entirely.
What accuracy is required — street level or building level?
Drives capture density, storage, and whether a single pass by one vehicle is sufficient.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.

Functional:

  • Ingest imagery and GPS traces from capture vehicles; produce road geometry and imagery tiles
  • Serve map tiles by (z, x, y) and panoramic imagery by location
  • Route between two points, with turn-by-turn directions
  • Resolve a coordinate to an administrative region, and an IP range to a region

Non-Functional:

  • Tile serve p99 under 100 ms; routing under 500 ms
  • Map data is immutable once published and versioned, so clients can cache aggressively
  • Ingestion is throughput-bound and may lag by days; serving may not
[chart] 2. Capacity Estimation
⚖ Assumptions — and what breaks if each is wrong
1,000 capture vehicles, 8 hours/day, imagery at ~15 MB/s each
Halving the fleet halves ingest but doubles time to coverage. This is the schedule/cost trade the whole capture plan turns on.
Tiles are pre-rendered, not rendered per request
Vector tiles rendered on the client would cut storage enormously and move cost to the device; a reasonable alternative for modern clients.
Routing is static, without live traffic
Live traffic makes edge weights mutable and rules out full precomputation of shortest paths.

Assumptions: 1,000 vehicles × 8 h/day × 15 MB/s of raw imagery; tiles to zoom 20.

~432 TB
raw imagery per day
~15 GB/s
peak ingest if streamed live
~4.4 T
tiles at z0–z20 worldwide
~10 KB
average tile
~100 ms
tile p99 budget
<1%
tiles ever requested

The number that decides ingestion: 432 TB/day cannot be uploaded over mobile networks — that is roughly 40 Gbps sustained. Vehicles write to physical disks that are shipped or offloaded at depots. Saying this out loud is the point: the highest-bandwidth link in a planet-scale capture system is a van full of drives, and recognising when the network is not the answer is a staff-level instinct.

The number that decides serving: a full tile pyramid to zoom 20 is trillions of tiles, and almost none are ever requested — population is Zipfian on the map too. Render the low zooms eagerly and the deep zooms lazily on first request, then cache. This turns an impossible storage bill into a manageable one.

[plug] 3. API Design
GET /v1/tiles/{version}/{z}/{x}/{y}.{fmt} Response: 200 image/webp | application/vnd.mapbox-vector-tile Headers: Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable // version is in the PATH, so a new map release is a new URL. // Immutable tiles need no invalidation -- the same trick as // content-hashed asset URLs. This is why the CDN can hold everything. GET /v1/pano?lat=&lng=&heading= -> { pano_id, tiles[], links[] } POST /v1/route Body: { origin, destination, mode, depart_at? } Response: { distance_m, duration_s, legs[], polyline, alternatives[] } GET /v1/geocode/reverse?lat=&lng= -> { country, admin1, locality } GET /v1/geoip?ip= -> { country, region, confidence } POST /internal/ingest/manifest // a depot registers an offloaded drive
[db] 4. Schema Design
-- ROUTING GRAPH: nodes are intersections, edges are road segments. TABLE edges { edge_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, from_node, to_node BIGINT, length_m INT, speed_kph SMALLINT, road_class TINYINT, -- motorway .. residential; drives hierarchy geometry LINESTRING, cell_id BIGINT -- S2/H3 cell: the partition key } -- Partitioned by cell so a route query touches few partitions. -- Long-distance routes cross partitions, which is what the -- hierarchy below exists to avoid. -- IP -> REGION: ranges, not points. The lookup is "which interval -- contains this integer", not an equality match. TABLE ip_ranges { start_ip NUMERIC(39), end_ip NUMERIC(39), -- v4 and v6 as integers region VARCHAR, confidence FLOAT, PRIMARY KEY (start_ip) } -- Ranges are disjoint and sorted, so the lookup is a binary search: -- the largest start_ip <= query. ~500K rows fits in memory; no -- database round trip is needed at all.
[build] 5. High-Level Architecture
Build and serve the map — and the cold CDN every new version creates
raw captureprocessed data / tilesmap buildorigin fetches
What is moving: 432 TB/day of imagery arrives on physical drives, because that volume cannot go over the air. Conflation turns noisy GPS traces into centrelines, and a build publishes an immutable, versioned tile set that the CDN can cache for a year with no invalidation logic at all.
What goes wrong: immutability has a sting. Because the version is in the URL path, publishing vN+1 changes every tile URL at once — so the CDN is instantly cold and the origin takes the full load. Roll out by region and pre-warm the low zoom levels, which are the overwhelming majority of requests. Ch 9
OFFLINE: BUILD THE MAP ONLINE: SERVE IT capture vehicles client imagery + GPS + LiDAR | | v | physical drives shipped CDN immutable, versioned tiles | (432 TB/day cannot go | ~99% hit rate: tiles never change | over the air) v v TILE SERVICE INGEST at depot lazy render on miss, then cache | | v v ALIGN + CONFLATE ROUTING SERVICE GPS traces -> centrelines hierarchical: local roads near imagery -> blur faces/plates the ends, motorway graph in the merge with existing geometry middle | | v v VERSIONED MAP BUILD ------------> GEO LOOKUP (in-memory interval published atomically as vN search for coord and IP ranges) The two halves share nothing but the published artefact. Ingestion may lag by days; serving may not. Coupling them would make a capture backlog into a user-facing outage.
Immutable versioned tiles are the load-bearing decision: they make the CDN able to hold everything, and they remove cache invalidation from the design entirely.
[search] 6. Component Deep Dives

Routing does not search the whole graph. A naive Dijkstra from London to Rome explores millions of residential streets that no sensible route uses. Real systems exploit hierarchy: a long route uses local roads only near its two endpoints and a much smaller motorway-class graph in between. Contraction hierarchies formalise this by precomputing shortcut edges, turning a continental route into a search over a graph orders of magnitude smaller. The trade to state: precomputation assumes static edge weights, so live traffic and contraction hierarchies are in tension — production systems recompute periodically and apply live weights only near the route.

Conflation is the genuinely hard part of building the map. Ten vehicles driving the same road produce ten noisy GPS traces that must become one centreline, and next month’s pass must merge into the existing geometry rather than create a parallel road. This is a clustering and map-matching problem, it is where the quality of a map actually comes from, and it is the part candidates skip. Mentioning it — even briefly — distinguishes someone who has thought about building a map from someone who has thought about serving one.

Immutable versioned tiles remove an entire problem. Because the map version is in the URL path, a tile is never updated in place; a new build is a new set of URLs. That means Cache-Control: immutable with a one-year lifetime, a CDN hit rate approaching 100%, and no invalidation logic anywhere. It is the same move as content-hashed asset URLs in Ch 9: make the identity change when the content changes, and staleness becomes impossible by construction.

IP→region is an interval problem, not a lookup problem. The naive design — a row per IP, or a WHERE start <= ip AND ip <= end scan — is either impossibly large or unindexable. Because the ranges are disjoint and sorted, the correct structure is a sorted array searched by binary search for the largest start below the query. At roughly 500K ranges the whole table is a few megabytes and lives in process memory, so the lookup never touches the network. Recognising “this is interval search over a static sorted array” turns a database question into an in-memory one.

Privacy is a hard requirement in capture, not a feature. Faces and number plates must be blurred before imagery is published, which means the blur pipeline sits on the critical path of publication and its failure mode must be to block the build. A missed blur is a legal incident, not a bug, so the correct behaviour on model uncertainty is to over-blur.

[balance] 7. Trade-off Analysis
DecisionChosen ✓Alternative ✗Reasoning
Imagery uploadPhysical drive shipmentNetwork upload432 TB/day is ~40 Gbps sustained from vehicles on mobile networks. The bandwidth does not exist; a van of drives is the higher-throughput link.
Tile identityVersion in the URL path, immutableMutable tiles + purgeImmutable tiles give a near-100% CDN hit rate and delete cache invalidation from the design. Purging trillions of URLs is not a thing you want to operate.
Deep-zoom tilesRender lazily on first requestPre-render everythingUnder 1% of tiles are ever requested. Pre-rendering the full pyramid is a vast bill for data nobody reads.
RoutingHierarchical / contracted graphPlain DijkstraA continental route over the full graph explores millions of irrelevant residential edges and cannot meet a 500 ms budget.
IP→regionSorted array + binary search, in processDatabase range queryDisjoint sorted intervals make this a few megabytes and a memory access. A database round trip per request is pure waste.
[shield] 8. Fault Tolerance
A capture drive is lost or corrupt
Vehicles checksum on write and retain data until the depot acknowledges ingestion. The affected road segments are simply re-queued for a future pass — capture is idempotent by design because roads do not move.
A bad map build is published
Versions are immutable and published atomically, so rollback is repointing clients at the previous version. Gate publication on automated checks: total road length within a few per cent of the prior build, no region losing connectivity, zero unblurred faces in a sample.
Routing service unavailable
Serve tiles regardless — a map you can look at is still useful. Clients that downloaded an offline routing pack keep routing locally, which is why the offline pack is a resilience feature and not only a connectivity one.
Conflation merges two roads wrongly
Detect with topology invariants: a build that creates a dead end where a through road existed, or doubles the road length in a cell, is rejected. Geometry errors are far easier to catch as invariant violations than by inspection.
CDN origin overload after a new version publishes
A new version invalidates every cached tile at once, which is a cold-cache stampede. Stagger the rollout by region and pre-warm the low zooms, which are the overwhelming majority of requests. Ch 9
[flag] 9. Conclusion — what I would say in the last three minutes
The dominant constraint

Building the map and serving it are different systems. Ingestion is throughput-bound and may lag days; serving is latency-bound and may not. They share only an immutable published artefact, and coupling them would turn a capture backlog into a user-facing outage.

What I would build first

Immutable versioned tiles behind a CDN. That single decision gives a near-100% hit rate and removes cache invalidation from the design entirely.

What I deliberately did not build

Live traffic, which makes edge weights mutable and fights the precomputation routing depends on, and crowd-sourced edits, which make moderation a whole subsystem.

The biggest risk

Conflation quality. Nothing crashes when traces merge badly; the map is simply wrong, and wrong maps are discovered by users rather than by monitoring. Topology invariants on each build are the only cheap defence.

Design a Fleet Upgrade System (“upgrade 5,000 servers” — and the same question on the Moon)

Difficulty: Hard (Staff Expectation)  .  Target: 40 min
[list] 1. Requirements
❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
Can the service tolerate any capacity loss during the upgrade?
If yes, rolling batches work. If not, you need spare capacity or blue-green, which roughly doubles hardware cost for the duration.
Is the upgrade reversible?
A binary rollback is easy; a schema migration or a disk-format change often is not. Irreversible steps must be identified before the first machine is touched, because they remove the safety net everything else assumes.
Are the machines stateful?
Stateless replacement is trivial. Stateful nodes need data to be drained or re-replicated first, and the upgrade rate is then bounded by re-replication bandwidth, not by machine count.
What is the round-trip latency to the fleet?
This is the Moon variant, and it is a real question. At a 1.3-second one-way delay, no synchronous orchestration protocol works and the agent must be autonomous.
What is the maintenance window, and is there one at all?
A global service has no quiet hour, which forces the design toward continuous safe rollout rather than a scheduled event.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.

Functional:

  • Roll a new version across N machines with a controlled, observable blast radius
  • Halt automatically on a health regression, and roll back without human intervention
  • Track per-machine state: pending, draining, upgrading, verifying, done, failed
  • Resume correctly after the orchestrator itself restarts mid-rollout

Non-Functional:

  • Never take more than a configured fraction of capacity out of service at once
  • Complete 5,000 machines within a working day; tolerate weeks for a high-latency fleet
  • The orchestrator must be crash-safe — its own failure must not strand machines mid-upgrade
[chart] 2. Capacity Estimation
⚖ Assumptions — and what breaks if each is wrong
5,000 machines, ~4 minutes per machine end to end
If a machine took an hour — a large database re-replicating — batch size stops being the limit and data movement does.
Stateless services; capacity is fungible
Stateful nodes make the rate bound re-replication bandwidth, and the whole plan changes.
The fleet can lose 5% of capacity safely
If it can only lose 1%, the rollout takes five times as long, which may exceed the window and force blue-green instead.

Assumptions: 5,000 machines, 4 min per machine, 5% concurrent budget.

250
machines per wave at 5%

~80 min

~4 h

1.3 s

~2.6 s
minimum RPC round trip there

The number that changes everything in the Moon variant: a 2.6-second minimum round trip makes any synchronous control loop unusable — a health check, a lock renewal or a heartbeat that assumes millisecond RTT will time out constantly. The correct response is not a longer timeout. It is to invert control: the orchestrator publishes a desired state, and autonomous agents on each machine pull it, act, verify locally, and report back asynchronously. The Moon question is a test of whether you notice that latency changes the architecture, not the configuration.

[plug] 3. API Design
POST /v1/rollouts Body: { target_selector, artifact, strategy:{ batch_pct, bake_s, halt_on:{ error_rate_delta, latency_p99_delta } } } Response: 201 { rollout_id, state:"planning" } POST /v1/rollouts/{id}:pause | :resume | :abort // abort rolls back completed batches; pause freezes in place GET /v1/rollouts/{id} -> { state, waves_done, in_flight, failed[], health_delta } // AGENT-FACING -- pull, not push. This is what makes the design work // across a high-latency link and survive an orchestrator restart. GET /v1/agent/desired?machine_id= -> { version, action, token } POST /v1/agent/report Body: { machine_id, state, version, health, token }
[db] 4. Schema Design
TABLE rollouts { rollout_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, artifact TEXT, strategy JSONB, state ENUM(planning, running, paused, halted, rolled_back, done), started_at TIMESTAMP } -- One row per machine. THIS is the crash-safety mechanism: the -- orchestrator holds no rollout state in memory, so it can be -- killed at any moment and resume by reading this table. TABLE machine_state { machine_id VARCHAR PRIMARY KEY, rollout_id UUID, desired_ver VARCHAR, actual_ver VARCHAR, state ENUM(pending, draining, upgrading, verifying, done, failed), wave INT, fencing_token BIGINT, -- monotonic; agent rejects stale orders updated_at TIMESTAMP } -- INDEX: (rollout_id, state) -- "how many are in flight?" is the -- query the concurrency budget is enforced with, every tick.
[build] 5. High-Level Architecture
Staged rollout — and the halt that stops 10 machines becoming 5,000
desired versionagent reports OKpullingfailure report
What is moving: the orchestrator writes a desired version into a table and agents pull it — nothing is ever pushed. Waves grow exponentially (1, then 10, then 100) with bake time between them, because the first machine buys the cheapest information you will ever get.
What goes wrong — and is caught: wave 2 shows an error-rate regression against the concurrently running old version. The rollout halts automatically and rolls back the completed waves; wave 3 never starts. Ten machines were affected instead of five thousand — which is the entire purpose of the design. Note the comparison must be against a live baseline, not yesterday, or a diurnal dip reads as a regression.
ORCHESTRATOR (stateless; all state is in the table) | | every tick: | 1. count machines not in {done, failed} -- the budget | 2. if under budget, promote N pending -> desired_ver | 3. compare canary health vs baseline; halt if regressed v DESIRED STATE TABLE one row per machine, fencing token per order ^ | agents PULL (never pushed to) | +---+-----------+-----------+-----------+ | | | | agent agent agent agent ... x5000 drain -> upgrade -> verify locally -> report | +-- if verification fails: roll back ITSELF, report failed The agent does not wait to be told. On a 2.6 s round trip, an agent that asks permission before rolling back is an agent that stays broken. WAVE SHAPE 1 -> 10 -> 100 -> 250 -> 250 ... exponential, then capped The first machine catches "the binary does not start". The first ten catch "it starts and is broken". Only then is it worth going fast.
Pull-based agents with local verification and self-rollback. The orchestrator expresses intent; it never drives a machine, which is what makes it crash-safe and latency-tolerant.
[search] 6. Component Deep Dives

Exponential wave sizing is the whole safety story. Upgrading in equal batches of 250 means the first 250 machines carry the same risk as the last 250, which wastes the cheapest information you will ever get. Start with one machine, then ten, then a hundred: the first catches “the binary does not start”, the first ten catch “it starts and is broken”, the first hundred catch problems that only appear under real traffic mix. Each stage buys confidence proportional to what it risks, and the total time cost of the small early waves is minutes against a rollout measured in hours.

Bake time is not a delay, it is the measurement. A machine that has been running the new version for thirty seconds has told you almost nothing; many regressions — memory leaks, connection-pool exhaustion, cache warm-up effects, a slow-growing queue — take minutes to appear. A rollout with no bake time between waves is a fast way to break the entire fleet with confidence. The comparison must also be against a concurrent baseline, not against yesterday: compare upgraded machines with not-yet-upgraded ones serving the same traffic at the same moment, so a diurnal pattern or an unrelated incident cannot be mistaken for a regression.

Pull beats push, and not only for the Moon. A push-based orchestrator must track connections to 5,000 machines, retry the ones that are down, and cope with the fact that a timeout tells it nothing about whether the command was executed (Ch 1). A pull-based agent asks “what should I be running?”, acts, and reports. Machines that were offline pick up the desired state when they return. The orchestrator becomes stateless and its own crash becomes a non-event — it restarts and reads the table. The fencing token matters here: an agent that was paused mid-upgrade and resumes must not act on a superseded order, exactly the stale-actor problem from Ch 6.

The Moon variant is a latency question in costume. At 2.6 seconds round-trip, three things break: synchronous health checks, lock leases, and any protocol that assumes a timely acknowledgement. The design must move verification to the machine — the agent decides locally whether the upgrade worked and rolls itself back if not — and tolerate reports arriving seconds or minutes late. It also raises a question worth asking aloud: with that delay, is a human able to intervene at all? If not, the automatic halt criteria are the only safety mechanism, and they need to be conservative.

Identify the irreversible steps first. Rolling back a binary is easy. Rolling back a schema migration, a disk reformat or a protocol change that peers have already adopted often is not. Those steps must be separated, ordered so that the reversible parts ship first, and protected by expand-and-contract: add the new column, dual-write, migrate readers, and only drop the old column in a later, separate rollout.

[balance] 7. Trade-off Analysis
DecisionChosen ✓Alternative ✗Reasoning
Control directionAgents pull desired stateOrchestrator pushes commandsPull makes the orchestrator stateless and crash-safe, handles offline machines for free, and is the only thing that works at multi-second RTT.
Wave sizingExponential: 1, 10, 100, 250Equal batchesEqual batches risk as much on the first wave as the last, and discard the cheapest information available.
VerificationLocal, on the agentCentral health checkA central check needs a round trip per machine and cannot act during a network partition. Local verification lets a machine roll itself back unattended.
Rollout stateIn a database, one row per machineIn orchestrator memoryIn-memory state means an orchestrator crash strands machines mid-upgrade with no record of intent.
Regression baselineConcurrent not-yet-upgraded machinesYesterday’s metricsComparing against history confuses diurnal patterns and unrelated incidents with a real regression, in both directions.
[shield] 8. Fault Tolerance
Orchestrator crashes mid-rollout
It holds no state, so a replacement reads machine_state and continues. Agents in flight finish and report; the fencing token stops a resumed agent acting on a superseded order.
A machine fails to come back
It is marked failed, counts against the concurrency budget, and the rollout halts once failures exceed a threshold rather than grinding through the whole fleet. Halting on an absolute count is a common bug: it should be a rate.
The new version is subtly worse
Automatic halt on a health delta against the concurrent baseline, then automatic rollback of completed waves. This is why bake time exists; without it the fleet is upgraded before the regression is visible.
Network partition to a subset of the fleet
Pull-based agents simply do not receive new desired state and keep running the current version, which is the safe outcome. Machines mid-upgrade verify locally and self-roll-back on failure.
An irreversible step has already run
Rollback cannot help, so the design must prevent it: irreversible steps are separated into their own rollout, gated on the reversible one having fully baked, and use expand-and-contract so the old and new forms coexist.
[flag] 9. Conclusion — what I would say in the last three minutes
The dominant constraint

The blast radius has to be bounded before speed matters. Everything here — exponential waves, bake time, a concurrency budget, automatic halt — exists to make sure a bad version reaches ten machines rather than five thousand.

What I would build first

The desired-state table with pull-based agents. It makes the orchestrator stateless, survives its own crash, handles offline machines for free, and is the only shape that works at multi-second latency.

What I deliberately did not build

A push-based orchestrator and central health verification. Both are the obvious designs and both fail exactly when the network is the thing that is broken.

The biggest risk

Irreversible steps. Rollback is the safety net the whole design assumes, and a schema change or disk reformat quietly removes it — which is why identifying those first is a clarifying question, not an implementation detail.

Design a Reservation & Booking System (airline seats, parking bays, tickets — inventory under contention)

Difficulty: Hard (Staff Expectation)  .  Target: 40 min
[list] 1. Requirements
❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
Is overbooking allowed?
This is the first question and it reframes everything. If overbooking is permitted the invariant is soft and eventual consistency is viable; if a seat may never be double-sold, you need a hard constraint enforced in one place.
How long may a hold last before payment?
The hold window is the entire concurrency design. A 10-minute hold means inventory is reserved but unpaid, which needs expiry, and expiry is where the bugs live.
Is payment synchronous with booking?
Third-party payment takes seconds and can fail or time out ambiguously, which is why booking and payment must be separate steps with an idempotency key between them.
What is the contention shape?
A parking garage is uniform demand on fungible bays. A concert on-sale is 100,000 people contending for the same 50 seats in one second — a completely different problem needing a queue.
Are units fungible or individually chosen?
“Any bay” allows a counter and is trivially scalable. “Seat 14A” forces per-unit rows and per-unit locking.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.

Functional:

  • Search availability for a resource over a time range
  • Hold a specific unit for a bounded window, then confirm with payment or expire
  • Cancel and refund, returning inventory to the pool
  • Never sell the same unit twice — the one invariant that cannot bend

Non-Functional:

  • Search is read-heavy and may be slightly stale; booking may not be
  • Survive a flash sale: 100K concurrent attempts on a few hundred units
  • Money and inventory must never diverge, including across a payment timeout
[chart] 2. Capacity Estimation
⚖ Assumptions — and what breaks if each is wrong
Inventory per resource is small — hundreds of units
Millions of units per resource would make per-unit rows expensive and push toward counters plus a reconciliation process.
Reads outnumber writes by roughly 100:1
If writes dominated, caching search results would stop paying and the design would be write-bound.
A payment provider may take seconds and time out ambiguously
If payment were instant and reliable, the hold-then-confirm state machine could collapse into a single transaction.

Assumptions: 100K search QPS, 2K booking attempts/sec, flash peaks of 100K/sec on one resource.

100K/s
search QPS
~2K/s

100K/s
