rows the invariant lives on

The number that decides the design: in a flash sale, 100,000 requests contend for a few hundred units, and every one of them wants to write the same rows. No amount of horizontal scaling helps, because the contention is on the data, not the compute. The only real answers are to serialise access to that inventory — a queue in front of it — or to shard the inventory itself into independent buckets. Recognising that this is a single-row hot-write problem rather than a throughput problem is most of the answer.

[plug] 3. API Design
GET /v1/availability?resource=&from=&to= Response: 200 { units:[{unit_id, state, price}], as_of } // explicitly stale: as_of tells the client how much to trust it. // Availability search is a CACHE; it is never the source of truth. POST /v1/holds Headers: Idempotency-Key: <client uuid> Body: { resource, unit_id | any, from, to, user_id } Response: 201 { hold_id, unit_id, expires_at } 409 unit_unavailable // the honest, common answer // The hold is the ONLY place the invariant is enforced. POST /v1/holds/{id}/confirm Headers: Idempotency-Key: <same key retried safely> Body: { payment_token } Response: 200 { booking_id, state:"confirmed" } 410 hold_expired 402 payment_failed // hold is released immediately DELETE /v1/bookings/{id} -> 200 { refund_id } // idempotent
[db] 4. Schema Design
-- The invariant lives on ONE ROW per unit. Not in application code, -- not in a distributed lock -- in a uniqueness constraint the -- database cannot be talked out of. TABLE units { unit_id VARCHAR PRIMARY KEY, -- e.g. "FL123-2026-04-01-14A" resource_id VARCHAR, state ENUM(available, held, booked), hold_id UUID, -- NULL unless held hold_expires TIMESTAMP, -- NULL unless held version BIGINT -- optimistic concurrency } -- The claim is a single conditional UPDATE, which is atomic: -- UPDATE units SET state='held', hold_id=?, hold_expires=now()+10min, -- version=version+1 -- WHERE unit_id=? AND (state='available' -- OR (state='held' AND hold_expires < now())) -- lazy expiry -- 0 rows updated => somebody else won. No lock, no coordination. TABLE bookings { booking_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, unit_id VARCHAR UNIQUE, -- ^ UNIQUE on unit_id is the belt-and-braces: even a bug in the -- hold logic cannot produce two confirmed bookings for one unit. user_id UUID, idempotency_key VARCHAR UNIQUE, state ENUM(confirmed, cancelled), payment_ref TEXT }
[build] 5. High-Level Architecture
Hold, pay, confirm — and the timeout where doing nothing is correct
booking requestinventory / resultpaymentambiguous
What is moving: the request takes a hold via a single conditional UPDATE on one row — that one statement settles every race atomically — then calls the payment provider with an idempotency key, and only confirms once payment succeeds.
What goes wrong: the payment call times out. You do not know whether the card was charged (Ch 1). Confirming risks giving away a seat nobody paid for; releasing risks charging someone who gets nothing. The correct action is to do neither — leave the hold to expire and reconcile against the provider afterwards. If the charge did land, refund it: a refund is recoverable, a double-sold seat is not.
SEARCH PATH (read-heavy, may be stale) client -> CDN/cache -> availability read replica stale by seconds; the 409 on hold is what corrects it BOOKING PATH (must be correct) client | Idempotency-Key v HOLD SERVICE ---- conditional UPDATE on ONE row ----> PRIMARY DB | 0 rows = lost the race = 409. No distributed lock, | no consensus, no coordination. The constraint is local. v hold granted, expires in 10 min | v PAYMENT (external, slow, can time out ambiguously) | success -> confirm: state=booked + insert booking row | failure -> release hold immediately | TIMEOUT -> do nothing; let the hold expire | never guess. Reconcile against the provider later. v EXPIRY lazy (checked on the next claim) + a sweeper for cleanliness Lazy expiry is what makes this correct without a timer per hold. FLASH SALE -> virtual waiting room in front, admitting N/sec the queue converts 100K concurrent writers into a rate
Search is a cache and may lie; the hold is the only place truth is decided. That separation is what lets the read path scale without endangering the invariant.
[search] 6. Component Deep Dives

Put the invariant on one row and the problem stops being distributed. “This seat is sold at most once” is a uniqueness constraint. If the row for that seat lives in one place, a single conditional UPDATE ... WHERE state = 'available' settles every race atomically: exactly one writer sees one row affected, everyone else sees zero and gets a 409. No distributed lock, no consensus, no two-phase commit. This is the guide’s recurring spine — make the constraint local instead of coordinating — and it is the same move as partitioning by conversation in D4 and by host in D10. Candidates who reach for Redis locks or 2PC here have made a local problem distributed for no reason.

Lazy expiry beats a timer. The tempting design gives every hold a scheduled job to release it. That is millions of timers, and a missed timer silently strands inventory. Instead, make expiry a predicate in the claim itself: a unit is claimable if it is available or if it is held and the hold has expired. Now expiry costs nothing, cannot be missed, and is correct even if every background sweeper is down. Keep a sweeper anyway, but only to keep dashboards honest — correctness must not depend on it.

An ambiguous payment timeout is the hard case, and the answer is to do nothing. When the payment provider times out you do not know whether the charge happened (Ch 1). Confirming risks giving away a seat that was never paid for; releasing risks charging someone who gets nothing. The correct behaviour is to leave the hold alone and let it expire, then reconcile against the provider’s record of truth asynchronously. If the charge did land, refund it — a refund is a recoverable business outcome, whereas a double-sold seat is not. Idempotency keys on both hold and confirm mean the client can retry the whole flow safely without creating a second booking.

A flash sale is a rate problem wearing a concurrency costume. 100,000 people hitting the same few hundred rows will convoy on the database regardless of how many application servers you run. The fix is a virtual waiting room: admit users at a rate the inventory can absorb, give them a queue position so the experience is honest, and let the rest wait. This trades a worse experience for a system that stays up — and it is far better than everyone getting a timeout. The alternative, sharding inventory into buckets, works when units are fungible (any parking bay) and fails when they are not (seat 14A exists in exactly one place).

Search may lie, and that is fine. Availability is read at 100K QPS and cached; it will show seats that were taken a second ago. The 409 on hold is the correction, and the UI must treat it as a normal outcome rather than an error. Trying to make search strongly consistent would put every read on the primary and destroy the read path for no correctness gain, because the seat can be taken between the response and the click anyway.

[balance] 7. Trade-off Analysis
DecisionChosen ✓Alternative ✗Reasoning
Concurrency controlConditional UPDATE on one rowDistributed lock / 2PCThe invariant is naturally local to one row. Introducing a distributed lock adds a failure domain and a liveness problem to solve something the database already does atomically.
Hold expiryLazy, as a predicate in the claimA timer per holdMillions of timers, and a missed one strands inventory silently. A predicate cannot be missed and costs nothing.
Payment timeoutDo nothing; let the hold expire, reconcileAssume success or failureGuessing either way produces a double-sold seat or a charge with nothing behind it. A later refund is recoverable; a double sale is not.
Search consistencyStale cache, 409 on conflictStrongly consistent availabilityStrong consistency puts 100K QPS on the primary and still cannot stop the seat being taken between render and click.
Flash saleVirtual waiting roomScale application serversContention is on rows, not CPU. More servers convoy harder on the same rows; a queue converts concurrency into a rate the inventory can absorb.
[shield] 8. Fault Tolerance
Two users claim the same unit simultaneously
The conditional UPDATE settles it atomically — one row affected, one 409. The UNIQUE constraint on bookings.unit_id is the second line of defence in case the hold logic is ever wrong.
Client retries a booking after a network timeout
The idempotency key returns the original booking rather than creating a second one. Without it, a retry on an ambiguous response is how one user ends up with two seats and two charges.
Payment provider is down
Holds are granted but cannot confirm, so they expire and inventory returns automatically. Degrading to “cannot complete purchase” is acceptable; losing inventory is not.
Primary database failover mid-hold
Holds are durable rows, so they survive. In-flight claims fail and clients retry with the same idempotency key. Nothing is stranded because expiry is lazy rather than scheduled.
Expiry sweeper stops running
Nothing breaks: the claim predicate already treats an expired hold as claimable. The sweeper only tidies rows so dashboards are accurate — correctness never depended on it.
[flag] 9. Conclusion — what I would say in the last three minutes
The dominant constraint

The one invariant that cannot bend is “sold at most once”. Every decision follows from putting that invariant on a single row, where a conditional UPDATE settles all races atomically and no distributed coordination is required.

What I would build first

The hold state machine with lazy expiry and idempotency keys on both steps. That is the correctness core; search, caching and the waiting room are all optimisations layered on top.

What I deliberately did not build

Distributed locking, and strongly consistent availability search. Both are the instinctive answers and both add cost and failure modes without buying correctness.

The biggest risk

The ambiguous payment timeout. It is rare, it is the one case where doing nothing is right, and it is where systems quietly double-sell inventory or charge for seats nobody received.

Design Collaborative Editing (Google Docs, and the same engine for a shared canvas or photo editor)

Difficulty: Hard (Staff Expectation)  .  Target: 45 min
[list] 1. Requirements
❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
Text, or a spatial canvas?
This changes the data model completely. Text is a sequence where concurrent inserts must not scramble order; a canvas is a set of objects where concurrent moves are usually independent and far easier.
Must offline editing merge, or is live-only acceptable?
Live-only lets a server serialise everything, which is dramatically simpler. Offline merge is what forces CRDTs or a robust transform, and it is the hardest requirement in the design.
How many concurrent editors per document?
Five is a different system from five hundred. Above roughly fifty, broadcasting every keystroke to everyone becomes the bottleneck and updates must be batched.
Is full edit history required?
Undo needs recent operations; legal or compliance history needs all of them forever, which changes storage from a buffer into an archive.
Does the server need to read the content?
Server-side search, spell-check and thumbnails all require plaintext, which rules out end-to-end encryption. This is a product decision with a large architectural consequence.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.

Functional:

  • Multiple users edit one document simultaneously and converge to the same state
  • Show remote cursors and selections live
  • Undo affects only your own edits, not whatever happened most recently
  • Reconnect after disconnection and merge without losing work

Non-Functional:

  • Local edits apply instantly — typing must never wait for a round trip
  • Remote edits appear within ~200 ms
  • Convergence is non-negotiable: no sequence of concurrent edits may leave two clients with different documents
[chart] 2. Capacity Estimation
⚖ Assumptions — and what breaks if each is wrong
Typical document has fewer than 10 concurrent editors
Hundreds of editors forces update batching and a fan-out tier, which this design does not need.
Live collaboration; offline merge is supported but rare
If most editing were offline, CRDTs become clearly correct and the server-authority design stops being viable.
The server may read document content
End-to-end encryption would remove server-side search, thumbnails and transform, and force all merging onto clients.

Assumptions: 1M active documents, ~10 editors each at peak, ~5 ops/sec per active editor.

~50/s
ops per busy document
~500/s
fan-out messages per document
~200 ms
remote-edit budget
~100 B
per operation
~1 KB/s
per active editor
1
authoritative sequencer per doc

The number that shapes the design: a document is a very small, very hot object. Ten editors at five operations per second is only ~50 writes/sec — trivial in absolute terms — but they all target the same document, and they must be totally ordered. So the scaling axis is not operations per second; it is documents. Shard by document ID and give each document a single authoritative sequencer, and the hard part becomes local to one process.

[plug] 3. API Design
// WebSocket per open document. HTTP only for load and snapshot. GET /v1/docs/{id} -> { snapshot, version, participants[] } WS /v1/docs/{id}/stream -> { type:"op", client_id, base_version, ops:[...] } <- { type:"ack", client_seq, server_version } <- { type:"op", from, server_version, ops:[...] } // transformed <- { type:"cursor", from, range } // ephemeral, never persisted <- { type:"resync", snapshot, version } // client too far behind // base_version is what makes this work: the server knows exactly // which document state the client was looking at, and therefore // which concurrent ops it must transform against. POST /v1/docs/{id}/snapshot // internal: compact the op log
[db] 4. Schema Design
-- The op log is the source of truth; snapshots are an optimisation. TABLE operations { doc_id UUID, version BIGINT, -- server-assigned, gapless, per document client_id UUID, client_seq BIGINT, -- dedup on client retry op JSONB, -- {insert, pos, text} | {delete, pos, len} | {move,...} created_at TIMESTAMP, PRIMARY KEY (doc_id, version) } -- (doc_id, version) is a total order per document. That total order -- IS the definition of the document -- everything else is derived. TABLE snapshots { doc_id UUID, version BIGINT, content BYTES, PRIMARY KEY (doc_id, version) } -- Load = latest snapshot + ops after it. Without snapshots, opening -- a year-old document means replaying millions of operations. -- Cursors are NOT stored. They are ephemeral presence state, they -- are worthless one second later, and persisting them would be a -- far higher write rate than the edits themselves.
[build] 5. High-Level Architecture
Concurrent edits — and the split brain that silently forks a document
local editsordered oprebased op
What is moving: two edits authored against the same document state. Each applies locally first — typing never waits for a round trip — then the session owner assigns a sequence number, transforms the second against the first, and broadcasts the rebased operation. One sequencer per document turns a distributed consensus problem into a single-threaded one.
What goes wrong: a network blip and two nodes both believe they own the document. Now there are two total orders, and clients converge to different documents with no error anywhere. This is why ownership needs a fenced lease rather than a best-effort lock: the stale owner’s writes must be rejected at the log, not merely discouraged. Ch 6
client A client B | edit applies LOCALLY first (0 ms) | | and is queued as pending | v v WEBSOCKET GATEWAY ------------------- WEBSOCKET GATEWAY \ / v v DOCUMENT SESSION (one per doc_id, sharded) - assigns the next version number - transforms incoming ops against concurrent ones - broadcasts the transformed op to everyone else This single-writer-per-document property is what makes ordering trivial. Consensus is only needed to decide WHO owns a document, not for the edits themselves. | v OP LOG (append-only, per doc) --> periodic SNAPSHOT | v document is defined as: snapshot + ops since FAILURE: session owner dies -> another node acquires the doc lease (fencing token), replays from the last snapshot, resumes. Clients reconnect and resync from their last known version.
One authoritative sequencer per document turns a distributed consensus problem into a single-threaded one. The hard part is not ordering the edits; it is owning the document.
[search] 6. Component Deep Dives

The core problem is that concurrent edits are not commutative. Two users inserting at position 5 of the same paragraph cannot both simply apply their operation — whichever lands second is now inserting at a position that means something different. There are two families of solution. Operational Transformation keeps operations as position-based edits and transforms an incoming operation against every concurrent one before applying it; it is compact and it is notoriously easy to get subtly wrong, which is why it works best with a single server sequencing everything. CRDTs give every character a unique, immutable identity so that inserts are defined relative to neighbours rather than positions, which makes operations commutative and merge without a server — at the cost of metadata per character and a document that grows even as text is deleted (tombstones).

Choose by the offline requirement. If editing is live and the server sequences everything, OT is simpler and lighter. If clients must merge after being offline for days, or edit peer-to-peer, CRDTs are the honest answer because there is no single sequencer to appeal to. Saying “I would use OT because we have a server and live editing, and I would switch to CRDTs the moment serious offline merge is required” is a much stronger answer than naming either one on its own.

A spatial canvas is genuinely easier, and it is worth saying so. For a photo editor or a drawing surface, most concurrent operations touch different objects and commute naturally — moving object A and recolouring object B do not interact at all. The only real conflicts are two users changing the same property of the same object, where last-writer-wins with a per-object version is usually acceptable. The trap is ordering: a z-order list is a sequence and has exactly the text problem again, and grouped or nested objects create structural conflicts a flat model does not. So: per-object LWW for properties, and a CRDT-style ordered set only for the layer stack.

Local-first application is what makes it feel instant. Every edit applies to the local document immediately and joins a pending queue; the server’s acknowledgement arrives later and may carry a transformed version of what you sent. The client must therefore be able to rebase its pending operations onto the server’s history — the same problem as a git rebase, running on every keystroke. This is where most implementation bugs live, and it is why the client keeps base_version: without knowing exactly what state an operation was authored against, correct transformation is impossible.

Undo must be per-user, which is subtler than it sounds. Undo does not mean “revert the last operation in the log” — that would undo a colleague’s work. It means “construct the inverse of my last operation, transformed against everything that has happened since”. If a colleague deleted the sentence you are undoing an edit to, the inverse must be transformed into a no-op rather than resurrecting text.

[balance] 7. Trade-off Analysis
DecisionChosen ✓Alternative ✗Reasoning
Merge algorithmOT with a server sequencerCRDTWith a live server there is a natural total order, and OT’s operations are far smaller. The moment strong offline merge is required this flips to CRDTs.
Ordering authorityOne session owner per documentConsensus across replicasSingle-writer-per-document makes ordering trivial. Consensus is needed only to decide ownership, which changes rarely, not for every keystroke.
Local editsApply immediately, rebase on ackWait for server confirmationA round trip per keystroke is unusable. The cost is client-side rebase complexity, which is the price of the feature existing at all.
CursorsEphemeral, never persistedStored with the documentCursor updates are a higher write rate than edits and are worthless a second later. Persisting them buys nothing and costs everything.
LoadingSnapshot + tail of opsReplay the full logA long-lived document has millions of operations. Replaying them all to open a file is an unbounded cost that grows with the document’s age.
[shield] 8. Fault Tolerance
Session owner node dies
Another node acquires the document lease with a fencing token, replays from the last snapshot plus the op log, and resumes. Clients reconnect and resync from their last acknowledged version, replaying their pending queue. Ch 6
Client reconnects after being offline
It sends its pending operations with their base_version; the server transforms them against everything that happened meanwhile. If it is too far behind to transform economically, the server sends a full resync instead — correct, and occasionally visible as a jump.
Two nodes both believe they own a document
This is split-brain, and it is the failure that silently corrupts documents by producing two divergent orderings. The fencing token makes the stale owner’s writes rejected at the log rather than merely discouraged.
Op log write fails after broadcasting
Ordering must be decided by the log, not by the broadcast: assign the version and persist before fanning out. Broadcasting first is faster and lets clients converge on state the server cannot reproduce after a crash.
A malformed op corrupts the document
Validate operations against the current document state before assigning a version, and keep snapshots immutable so any point in history can be recovered. The op log is the audit trail that makes corruption diagnosable rather than mysterious.
[flag] 9. Conclusion — what I would say in the last three minutes
The dominant constraint

Concurrent edits do not commute. Everything in the design exists to impose a total order on operations that were authored against different states, and then to make each client’s local view converge to that order.

What I would build first

One authoritative session per document with an append-only op log and periodic snapshots. That converts a distributed consensus problem into a single-threaded one and makes ordering trivial.

What I deliberately did not build

Offline-first merge and end-to-end encryption. Either would force CRDTs and move all merging onto clients — a legitimate design, and a different one.

The biggest risk

Split-brain on document ownership. Two sequencers means two orderings and silently divergent documents, which is why ownership needs a fenced lease rather than a best-effort lock.

Design a Denylist / Request Blocking Service (deny service to banned IPs from a third-party feed)

Difficulty: Medium-Hard  .  Target: 35 min
[list] 1. Requirements
❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
How fast must a new ban take effect?
Seconds versus minutes is the whole design. Seconds means pushing updates to every edge; minutes allows ordinary polling and a much simpler system.
Fail open or fail closed?
If the denylist service is unavailable, do we admit everything or reject everything? For abuse prevention, fail open. For a sanctions or fraud list, possibly closed — and that is a business decision, not an engineering one.
How large is the list, and is it ranges or individual addresses?
A million individual IPs is a set membership problem. CIDR ranges are an interval problem and need a different structure entirely.
Is the third-party feed trusted?
An upstream feed that suddenly contains 0.0.0.0/0 would take the site down. Feed changes need sanity limits before they are applied.
Do we need to explain or appeal a block?
Auditability turns a stateless filter into a system that must record why each decision was made, which is a meaningfully larger design.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.

Functional:

  • Ingest a third-party feed of banned addresses and CIDR ranges, plus internal manual bans
  • Decide allow/deny for every inbound request, at the edge
  • Support temporary bans with expiry, and an allowlist that always overrides
  • Record every block for audit and appeal

Non-Functional:

  • The check must add under 1 ms — it runs on 100% of traffic
  • New bans propagate globally within 30 seconds
  • The service must never be able to take the site down
[chart] 2. Capacity Estimation
⚖ Assumptions — and what breaks if each is wrong
~1M denylist entries, mostly CIDR ranges
Tens of millions of individual addresses would push from an in-memory structure toward a probabilistic filter with a confirmation lookup.
Feed updates arrive every few minutes, not continuously
A high-frequency feed would need streaming updates rather than periodic snapshot rebuilds.
Blocking is best-effort abuse prevention, not a legal control
If it were a sanctions list, fail-open would be unacceptable and the availability calculus reverses.

Assumptions: 1M denylist entries, 500K req/sec across the edge fleet, 200 edge nodes.

500K/s
requests checked
~1M
denylist entries
~8 MB
compressed trie in memory
<1 µs
per lookup, in process
~30 s
global propagation target
0
network hops on the hot path

The decision that makes this trivial instead of hard: a million entries compress to roughly 8 MB as a prefix trie, which fits comfortably in every edge process’s memory. So the check is a local memory lookup, not a network call. The naive design — query a denylist service per request — adds a round trip to 100% of traffic and creates a dependency that can take the whole site down. Recognising that the dataset is small enough to replicate everywhere is the entire answer.

[plug] 3. API Design
// CONTROL PLANE -- low volume, ordinary REST POST /v1/bans Body: { cidr, reason, expires_at?, source } DELETE /v1/bans/{cidr} POST /v1/allowlist Body: { cidr, reason } // always wins over a ban GET /v1/bans/check?ip= -> { blocked, matched_rule, source } // for support and appeals, NOT the hot path // DATA PLANE -- edges pull versioned snapshots, they are never pushed to GET /v1/snapshot/latest -> { version, url, sha256, entry_count } GET /v1/delta?from= -> { version, added[], removed[] } // Pull means an edge that was offline catches up on its own, and // the control plane holds no per-edge state. // The hot path has NO API. It is a function call into local memory.
[db] 4. Schema Design
TABLE rules { cidr CIDR PRIMARY KEY, -- v4 and v6 action ENUM(deny, allow), -- allow always wins reason TEXT, source ENUM(feed, manual, automated), expires_at TIMESTAMP, -- NULL = permanent created_at TIMESTAMP } -- EDGE REPRESENTATION: a binary radix trie over address bits. -- Longest-prefix match, so a /32 allow beats an enclosing /8 deny -- for free -- specificity is structural, not a rule engine. -- root -- +- 0... -> ... -- +- 1... -> 10.0.0.0/8 DENY (feed) -- +- 10.1.2.3/32 ALLOW (manual override) -- Lookup walks at most 32 (v4) or 128 (v6) bits: constant time. TABLE block_events { -- sampled, not every block: 500K/s of audit ts TIMESTAMP, ip INET, matched_rule CIDR, edge VARCHAR } -- rows would dwarf the traffic being protected
[build] 5. High-Level Architecture
Denylist distribution — and the upstream feed that could ban everyone
feed dataaccepted deltasnapshotrejected
What is moving: a feed of banned ranges is validated, diffed and compiled into a signed radix trie of about 8 MB, which every edge pulls. The hot path never appears here at all — the actual check is a local memory lookup with zero network hops.
What goes wrong: the upstream feed malfunctions and publishes an over-broad range. Applied faithfully, that blocks everyone. Treat the feed as untrusted input: reject any delta banning more than a small fraction of address space, or removing most existing rules, and never accept a prefix broader than a configured maximum. Edges keep the last good snapshot indefinitely, so a rejected feed is an alert, not an outage.
third-party feed internal signals (abuse detection, manual) | | v v FEED INGEST -- validate, diff, SANITY-CHECK ------> RULES DB | | +- reject if the delta bans > 5% of the v address space, or removes > 50% of SNAPSHOT BUILDER existing rules. A bad feed is the most builds a signed radix trie likely way this system causes an outage. every ~30 s, versioned | v OBJECT STORE / CDN ^ edges PULL every 30 s | +--------------+--------------+--------------+---+ | | | | edge 1 edge 2 edge 3 ... edge 200 8 MB trie in process memory; lookup is a function call | v allow / deny (< 1 microsecond, zero network hops) If the control plane is entirely down, edges keep serving the last good snapshot indefinitely. The blocking decision never depends on anything being reachable.
The entire hot path is a local memory lookup. The control plane can be down for hours and no request is affected — bans simply stop getting fresher.
[search] 6. Component Deep Dives

A radix trie gives longest-prefix matching for free. The requirement “an allowlist entry overrides an enclosing ban” sounds like it needs a priority system, but it falls out of the structure: walking the address bit by bit, the deepest node that matches is by definition the most specific rule. There is no rule engine, no ordering to get wrong, and lookup is bounded by the address length — 32 steps for IPv4, 128 for IPv6 — regardless of how many rules exist. This is the same insight as the IP→region lookup in D17: the right data structure turns a policy question into a constant-time memory access.

Fail open, and say why. If the snapshot cannot be fetched, the edge keeps the last good one; if it has none, it allows traffic. The reasoning is blast radius: failing closed means a bug or an outage in an auxiliary protective component takes down the entire service, which is a far larger harm than a window of unblocked abuse. The exception worth naming is a legal control — a sanctions list — where serving a blocked party is the greater harm and the calculus reverses. This is a business decision and it should be surfaced as one, not assumed.

The third-party feed is the most likely cause of an outage. A feed that malfunctions and publishes an over-broad range would, applied faithfully, block everyone. So ingestion is not a copy; it is a validation step with hard limits: reject any delta that would ban more than a small fraction of address space, reject one that removes most existing rules, never accept a rule broader than a configured maximum prefix length, and always subtract the allowlist last. Treat upstream data as untrusted input, exactly as you would a user request.

Do not log every block. At 500K requests per second, even a 1% block rate is 5,000 audit rows per second, which is a larger data problem than the traffic being protected. Sample aggressively for volume, but keep every block that resulted from a manual rule, because those are the ones a human will be asked to justify. Aggregate counters per rule give the operational picture without the row-per-event cost.

Push versus pull, again. Pushing updates to 200 edges means tracking 200 connections, retrying failures and knowing which edges are stale. Pulling a versioned snapshot from a CDN means the control plane holds no per-edge state, offline edges catch up automatically, and propagation is bounded by the poll interval rather than by the slowest connection. The 30-second target is met comfortably by a 10-second poll of a small delta.

[balance] 7. Trade-off Analysis
DecisionChosen ✓Alternative ✗Reasoning
Check locationIn-process, local memoryCall a denylist serviceA network call on 100% of traffic adds latency and creates a dependency that can take the site down. 8 MB replicates everywhere for free.
StructureRadix trie, longest-prefix matchHash set of addressesA hash set cannot express CIDR ranges or specificity. The trie gives override semantics structurally rather than through rule ordering.
DistributionEdges pull versioned snapshotsControl plane pushesPull removes per-edge state, handles offline edges automatically, and keeps working when the control plane is down.
On failureFail open, keep the last snapshotFail closedA protective component must not be able to cause a larger outage than the abuse it prevents. A legal control is the deliberate exception.
AuditSample high-volume, keep manual blocksLog every decision5,000 rows/sec of audit is a bigger data problem than the traffic being protected, and almost none of it is ever read.
[shield] 8. Fault Tolerance
Control plane entirely down
Edges keep serving the last good snapshot indefinitely. Bans stop getting fresher, which is a degradation nobody notices for hours — the correct behaviour for an auxiliary system.
Third-party feed publishes garbage
Sanity limits reject the delta before it is built into a snapshot, and the previous snapshot stays live. Alert loudly: a rejected feed is a real incident even though nothing broke.
A legitimate large network is banned
The allowlist overrides by longest-prefix match and propagates in one poll interval, so the remedy is fast. This is why manual allow entries exist separately from feed data and are never overwritten by it.
Snapshot is corrupt or truncated
Snapshots are content-hashed and the edge verifies before swapping. A failed verification means keeping the current trie — never load a partially parsed denylist, which would silently allow or block arbitrarily.
Edge memory pressure from IPv6 growth
IPv6 tries are deeper and larger. Cap entries, prefer aggregated prefixes over individual /128s, and alert on snapshot size growth — an OOM on the edge is an outage caused by the protective system itself.
[flag] 9. Conclusion — what I would say in the last three minutes
The dominant constraint

The dataset is small enough to live everywhere. A million rules compress to about 8 MB, so the check is a local memory lookup rather than a network call — which removes both the latency and the dependency that the obvious design would add to 100% of traffic.

What I would build first

The radix trie and the pull-based snapshot distribution. Together they make the hot path zero-hop and make control-plane availability irrelevant to serving.

What I deliberately did not build

Per-request auditing and real-time streaming updates. Both sound thorough and both add cost far out of proportion to their value here.

The biggest risk

The upstream feed. It is untrusted input with the power to block everyone, and the sanity limits on ingestion are the only thing standing between a bad publish and a total outage.

Design a Distributed Sort (“the data set does not fit in memory and you have many workers”)

Difficulty: Medium-Hard  .  Target: 35 min
[list] 1. Requirements
❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
Does the whole result need to be globally sorted, or only partitioned?
A globally ordered single output is much stricter than “each output file is sorted and files are in order”. Downstream consumers usually only need the latter, and it is far cheaper.
What is the key distribution?
Uniform keys make range partitioning trivial. Skewed keys — and real keys are always skewed — are the entire difficulty, because one reducer gets everything.
Is this one-off or recurring?
A recurring job justifies sampling, tuning and a stored partition map. A one-off should use the simplest thing that finishes.
Where does the data live and where must the output go?
If input and output are the same object store, network shuffle is the cost. If workers have local disks, spilling changes the arithmetic.
Are duplicate keys significant, and must the sort be stable?
Stability constrains how you merge and rules out some parallel shortcuts.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.

Functional:

  • Sort a data set far larger than any single machine’s memory, by a specified key
  • Produce output that is globally ordered across partitions
  • Tolerate a worker dying mid-job without restarting from scratch

Non-Functional:

  • Scale roughly linearly with worker count until the network saturates
  • Skewed keys must not make one worker the whole job’s runtime
  • Bounded memory per worker — the job must never depend on fitting in RAM
[chart] 2. Capacity Estimation
⚖ Assumptions — and what breaks if each is wrong
10 TB input, 100 workers with 16 GB RAM each
Total RAM is 1.6 TB against 10 TB of data, so the data cannot be held in memory even collectively. That is what forces external sorting.
Keys are skewed, as real keys always are
Uniform keys would make fixed-range partitioning correct and sampling unnecessary.
The network is the bottleneck, not the CPU
On very fast interconnects, comparison cost can dominate instead and merge strategy matters more.

Assumptions: 10 TB input, 100 workers, 16 GB RAM each, 10 Gbps per node.

10 TB
input size
1.6 TB
total cluster RAM
~100 GB
per worker share
~6×
spill passes at 16 GB
10 TB
bytes crossing the network once
~2.2 h
shuffle floor at 10 Gbps

The number that frames the whole problem: 10 TB of data against 1.6 TB of total RAM means the data cannot be resident even across the entire cluster. So this is an external sort: sort what fits, spill sorted runs to disk, then merge. And because every record must reach the worker that owns its key range, at least 10 TB crosses the network exactly once — roughly 2.2 hours at 10 Gbps per node. The shuffle is the job. Everything else is an optimisation around that floor.

[plug] 3. API Design
POST /v1/sorts Body: { input_prefix, output_prefix, key_spec, order, workers, sample_rate } Response: 201 { job_id, state:"sampling" } GET /v1/sorts/{id} Response: { state, phase:"sample|map|shuffle|merge", partitions:[{ id, bytes, state, worker }], skew_ratio } // max partition / mean partition // skew_ratio is the number to watch: above ~3 the job is // waiting on one straggler and the partition map was wrong. // WORKER-FACING POST /internal/tasks/claim -> { task_id, kind, inputs[], attempt } POST /internal/tasks/report Body: { task_id, state, output_refs[] } // tasks are idempotent and write to attempt-scoped paths, so a // duplicate execution is harmless -- see the fault table
[db] 4. Schema Design
-- The partition map is the artefact that decides whether this job -- finishes in two hours or twenty. It is built by SAMPLING, not -- by assuming a uniform key space. TABLE partition_map { job_id UUID, partition INT, key_start BYTES, -- inclusive key_end BYTES, -- exclusive est_bytes BIGINT, -- from the sample PRIMARY KEY (job_id, partition) } -- Boundaries are chosen so est_bytes is roughly EQUAL per partition, -- not so the key ranges are equal. Equal key ranges on skewed data -- is exactly how one reducer ends up with 80% of the rows. TABLE tasks { job_id UUID, task_id INT, kind ENUM(map, merge), attempt INT, worker VARCHAR, state ENUM(pending, running, done, failed), output_prefix TEXT, -- includes attempt: .../task7/attempt2/ PRIMARY KEY (job_id, task_id, attempt) } -- Attempt-scoped output paths are what make retries safe: a -- zombie worker writes to a path nobody will ever read.
[build] 5. High-Level Architecture
External sort — and the key skew that makes one reducer the whole job
boundariesshuffled datamerged outputskewed partition
What is moving: a small random sample first, to choose partition boundaries with roughly equal bytes per range; then the data itself, sorted in memory, spilled as runs, and shuffled to the reducer that owns its range. Ordering falls out of the boundaries — no reducer ever compares against another.
What goes wrong: skip the sample and split the key space evenly, and a skewed distribution sends most rows to one reducer. The job’s runtime becomes that single worker’s runtime. Worse, if a single key value exceeds a partition’s budget, no boundary choice helps — it cannot be split without breaking the sort, and needs special handling or an accepted straggler.
PHASE 0 -- SAMPLE read ~0.1% of records at random | build the partition map so each range holds | roughly EQUAL BYTES, not equal key width v this phase costs minutes and saves hours PHASE 1 -- MAP / SORT each worker reads its input split | sort in memory until the buffer is full | spill a sorted run to local disk | repeat; partition each run by the partition map v PHASE 2 -- SHUFFLE every partition's data moves to its owner | 10 TB crosses the network exactly once -- the job's floor v PHASE 3 -- MERGE owner k-way merges its sorted runs | streaming, bounded memory: one buffer per run | never materialises the partition in RAM v OUTPUT part-00000 .. part-00099, each internally sorted, partitions in key order = globally sorted result Globally sorted WITHOUT any global comparison: ordering comes from the partition boundaries, and each partition is sorted independently.
Range-partition then sort locally. That is the whole trick: it makes the global order fall out of the partition map rather than out of any cross-worker coordination.
[search] 6. Component Deep Dives

Sampling is the difference between a good job and a stuck one. The obvious approach — divide the key space into equal ranges — assumes a uniform distribution that real data never has. If 40% of your keys start with the same prefix, one reducer receives 40% of the data and the job’s runtime is that one worker. Reading a small random sample first and choosing boundaries at the sample’s quantiles gives partitions of roughly equal size, which is what actually matters. This phase costs minutes and routinely saves hours, and skipping it is the single most common way this problem is answered badly.

Even with sampling, a single hot key can defeat you. If one key value alone exceeds a partition’s budget, no boundary choice helps — that key cannot be split across partitions without breaking the sort. The honest answers are to handle that key specially (sort its records separately and concatenate, since they are all equal on the sort key anyway), or to accept the straggler. Naming this limitation is better than pretending sampling solves everything. It is the same hot-key problem as Ch 5, and it has the same shape: partitioning distributes keys, not load.

External merge is where the memory bound is actually held. A worker sorts what fits in its buffer, writes that sorted run to disk, and repeats until its input is consumed. Then it merges the runs with a heap, holding one small read buffer per run — so peak memory is number of runs × buffer size, not data size. If there are too many runs to merge at once, merge in multiple passes. Each pass rereads the data, which is why buffer size matters: the number of passes is roughly log-base-(runs per pass) of the total runs.

Retries must be idempotent, and the trick is the output path. A worker that is slow may not be dead, so a scheduler that reassigns its task can end up with two workers writing the same output. Give every attempt its own output prefix and have the coordinator record which attempt won; the loser’s bytes are simply never read and are garbage-collected later. This turns an exactly-once problem into an at-least-once one with a commit step — the same move as fencing in D6.

Speculative execution is how you beat stragglers. Near the end of a phase, when most tasks are done and a few are lagging, start duplicate copies of the slow ones and take whichever finishes first. Because the tasks are already idempotent, this costs only wasted compute and it protects against the far more common cause of a slow task: a degraded machine rather than skewed data.

[balance] 7. Trade-off Analysis
DecisionChosen ✓Alternative ✗Reasoning
PartitioningRange partition from a sampleEqual key ranges, or hashEqual ranges collapse on skewed data. Hash partitioning balances beautifully but destroys order, so the output is not globally sorted.
Sort strategyExternal merge sort with spillsSort in memoryThe data is larger than total cluster RAM. Any design that assumes it fits is answering a different question.
Global orderFalls out of partition boundariesA final merge of all partitionsA single final merge is a serial bottleneck through one machine. Ordered partitions give the same result with no coordination.
RetriesAttempt-scoped output pathsLocking a task to one workerA slow worker is indistinguishable from a dead one. Idempotent output makes duplicate execution harmless instead of dangerous.
StragglersSpeculative duplicate tasksWaitThe last few tasks dominate tail runtime, and duplication is cheap once tasks are idempotent.
[shield] 8. Fault Tolerance
A worker dies mid-task
Its task is reassigned and rerun from the input split. Only that task’s work is lost, not the job — which is the whole reason for splitting work into independently retryable units.
A worker is slow but alive
Speculative execution starts a duplicate; the first to finish commits. Attempt-scoped outputs mean the loser’s bytes are inert rather than corrupting.
Partition skew discovered mid-job
Monitor the skew ratio during shuffle. A badly skewed map is worth aborting and resampling early; discovering it at the merge phase means the job has already paid the shuffle cost.
Disk fills during spilling
Bound the number of runs per worker and merge intermediate runs early to reclaim space. Running out of disk mid-merge fails the task late, after the most expensive phase.
Coordinator fails
Task state is in a durable store, so a replacement resumes from it. In-flight tasks complete and report; the coordinator holds no state that cannot be rebuilt.
[flag] 9. Conclusion — what I would say in the last three minutes
The dominant constraint

The data is bigger than the cluster’s total memory. That forces an external sort — spill sorted runs, then merge with bounded buffers — and it means at least one full pass of the data across the network, which is the floor on runtime.

What I would build first

The sampling phase and the partition map. Minutes of work that decide whether the job finishes in hours or hangs on one straggler for a day.

What I deliberately did not build

A globally strict single output file, and hash partitioning. The first serialises the job through one machine; the second balances perfectly and destroys the ordering the job exists to produce.

The biggest risk

Key skew that sampling cannot fix. A single value larger than a partition budget cannot be split, and no amount of boundary tuning helps — it needs special handling or an accepted straggler.

Design Degrees of Connection (“is this profile 1st, 2nd or 3rd degree?” at LinkedIn scale)

Difficulty: Hard (Staff Expectation)  .  Target: 40 min
[list] 1. Requirements
❓ Clarify first — and what each answer changes
How many degrees do we need — and is 3 the maximum?
This is the whole design. Degrees 1 and 2 are cheap; degree 3 is where the neighbourhood explodes and precomputation stops being possible.
Is this shown on a profile view, or on a search results page?
One profile is a single query. A results page needs the degree for 25 profiles at once, which is a batch problem with a much tighter per-item budget.
Is the answer allowed to be slightly stale?
A connection made five seconds ago not yet showing as 1st degree is almost always acceptable, and that tolerance is what makes caching viable.
Do we need the connecting path, or just the number?
“You are connected via Priya” is a much more expensive query than “2nd degree”, because it needs an actual path, not just its existence.
What is the degree distribution at the top end?
A user with 30,000 connections has a second-degree neighbourhood in the tens of millions. Those users break every naive approach and must be handled explicitly.
At L6 the interviewer is watching which question you ask first. Naming the dominant constraint before being steered is the cheapest available staff signal — see T6 for the rubric.

Functional:

  • Given viewer V and profile P, return 1, 2, 3 or “out of network”
  • Answer for a page of ~25 profiles in one request
  • Reflect new connections within seconds

Non-Functional:

  • p99 under 50 ms for a batch of 25 — it renders inline with search results
  • Handle 1B members with an average of 500 connections
  • Slight staleness acceptable; a wrong answer that is one degree too far is tolerable, one that is too close is not
[chart] 2. Capacity Estimation
⚖ Assumptions — and what breaks if each is wrong
1B members, ~500 connections average
At 50 average the second-degree set fits comfortably and the whole design simplifies.
Answers may be seconds stale
Strict freshness would remove caching and force every query to hit the graph store.
Degree 3 is the maximum required
Degree 4 makes the neighbourhood approach the whole graph and the question stops being answerable this way.

Assumptions: 1B members, ~500 connections each, 25 profiles per search page.

1B

The arithmetic that decides everything: at 500 connections, second degree is roughly 500 × 500 = 250,000 members — large but storable. Third degree is 500³ = 125 million, which is an eighth of the network and cannot be precomputed or cached per user. So the design must be asymmetric: precompute or cache the second-degree set, and answer third degree by a bounded search rather than by materialising anything.

[plug] 3. API Design
POST /v1/degrees:batch Body: { viewer_id, target_ids:[ ...up to 100... ] } Response: 200 { results:{ target_id: { degree: 1|2|3|null, via?: [member_id] } } } // batch by construction: a search results page needs 25 at once, // and 25 separate round trips cannot fit a 50 ms budget GET /v1/connections/{member}?cursor= -> paged 1st-degree list POST /v1/connections Body: { a, b } // creates an undirected edge // invalidates the 2nd-degree cache for a, b and all their // 1st-degree neighbours -- the expensive part of a write
[db] 4. Schema Design
-- Adjacency, sharded by member. Both directions are stored, because -- "who is connected to X" must be answerable without a scan. TABLE edges { member_id BIGINT, peer_id BIGINT, created_at TIMESTAMP, PRIMARY KEY (member_id, peer_id) } -- Partition key is member_id, so one member's whole adjacency list -- is a single-shard read. This is the one access pattern that must -- never fan out. -- 2nd-degree set, cached as a compressed bitmap / roaring set. -- ~250K member IDs compress to a few hundred KB, which is small -- enough to fetch and intersect in single-digit milliseconds. CACHE second_degree { key: member_id value: RoaringBitmap(member_ids), built_at, edge_version ttl: hours, invalidated on connection change } -- No 3rd-degree cache exists. 125M IDs per member is ~500 MB per -- user even compressed; storing it for 1B members is absurd. -- Degree 3 is COMPUTED, never stored.
[build] 5. High-Level Architecture
Degree lookup — and the high-degree member who breaks the arithmetic
batch of profilesadjacency / resultcached 2-hop setuncacheable
What is moving: the viewer’s cached second-degree set — ~250K IDs as a compressed bitmap, a few hundred kilobytes — intersected against each target’s ~500 first-degree connections. Third degree is 2 + 1, computed by meeting in the middle rather than by expanding three hops to 125 million members.
What goes wrong: a viewer with 30,000 connections has a second-degree neighbourhood in the tens of millions — too large to cache and constantly invalidated. Because the relation is symmetric, the fix is to expand from whichever side is smaller: compute from the target instead. Without that check, a handful of users dominate the cluster’s load.
search results page: viewer V, 25 targets | v DEGREE SERVICE (batch of 25 resolved together) | | 1. degree 1: is target in V's adjacency list? | single-shard read, then a set lookup < 1 ms | | 2. degree 2: is target in V's cached 2nd-degree bitmap? | one cache fetch (~hundreds of KB), 25 lookups ~5 ms | | 3. degree 3: NOT precomputed. Instead: | fetch each TARGET's 1st-degree list, and test | whether it intersects V's 2nd-degree bitmap. | Meet in the middle: expand 2 hops from V (cached) and | 1 hop from each target (small), then intersect. This turns | 125M into 25 small reads plus 25 bitmap intersections. v RESULT 1 | 2 | 3 | out of network HIGH-DEGREE MEMBERS (30K+ connections): 2nd-degree set approaches tens of millions -> do not cache it. Fall back to intersecting from the OTHER side, which is small.
Bidirectional search is the whole design: expanding two hops from the viewer and one hop from each target meets in the middle and never materialises the third-degree neighbourhood.
[search] 6. Component Deep Dives

Meet-in-the-middle turns an impossible query into a cheap one. Testing “is P within 3 hops of V?” by expanding three hops from V means touching 125 million members. But 3 = 2 + 1, so expanding two hops from V — a set you already have cached — and one hop from P — a single adjacency read of about 500 entries — and testing whether the two sets intersect gives exactly the same answer. The work drops from hundreds of millions to a few hundred, and the asymmetry is deliberate: put the expensive expansion on the side you can cache and reuse across all 25 targets on the page.

Roaring bitmaps are why the second-degree set is affordable. 250,000 member IDs as a list of 64-bit integers is 2 MB; as a compressed bitmap it is often a few hundred kilobytes, and — more importantly — intersection is a bitwise operation over compressed runs rather than a hash-set probe per element. That is what makes 25 intersections fit inside a 50 ms budget alongside everything else on the page.

High-degree members break the symmetry, and the fix is to flip it. A member with 30,000 connections has a second-degree neighbourhood in the tens of millions; caching that is both expensive and constantly invalidated. But the relation is symmetric — if V is within 3 hops of P then P is within 3 hops of V — so when the viewer is a high-degree member, compute from the target’s side instead, where the neighbourhood is ordinary. Choosing which end to expand from based on degree is the single most valuable optimisation here, and it is the same “expand the cheaper side” instinct as query planning in a database.

Invalidation is the expensive part of a write. When A and B connect, the second-degree set changes not only for A and B but for everyone connected to A or B — a thousand cache entries per new connection. Eagerly recomputing them is wasteful, because most will never be read before they change again. Instead, invalidate lazily with a version stamp: store the edge-set version the bitmap was built from and rebuild on read when it is stale. This trades a slower first read for enormously less write amplification, and it is acceptable precisely because the requirement allowed staleness.

Be honest about the error direction. A cached second-degree set that is a few seconds stale can produce an answer one degree too far — showing 3rd where the truth is now 2nd. That is harmless. The reverse — claiming a closer connection than exists — would be a privacy problem, because degree gates what profile information is visible. So the cache must only ever be able to miss new edges, never invent them, which means additions may lag but removals must be applied immediately.

[balance] 7. Trade-off Analysis
DecisionChosen ✓Alternative ✗Reasoning
Degree 3Meet in the middle (2 from viewer + 1 from target)Expand 3 hops from the viewerThree hops is ~125M members. Bidirectional search gives the identical answer for a few hundred operations.
2nd-degree setCached compressed bitmapComputed per requestRecomputing 250K members per query cannot meet 50 ms, and the same set is reused across all 25 targets on the page.
High-degree membersExpand from the smaller sideCache everything uniformlyA 30K-connection member has a tens-of-millions neighbourhood. Symmetry of the relation lets you choose the cheap end instead.
InvalidationLazy, version-stampedEager recompute on every edgeOne new connection dirties ~1,000 cached sets, most of which will never be read before changing again.
FreshnessStale additions, immediate removalsUniform TTLDegree gates profile visibility, so being one degree too far is harmless and being too close is a privacy incident.
[shield] 8. Fault Tolerance
2nd-degree cache is cold or unavailable
Fall back to computing from adjacency lists for the batch, with a reduced target set and a slower response. Degrading to “connection degree unavailable” on a search page is acceptable; failing the page is not.
A viewer has an enormous connection count
Detect by degree at query time and switch to expanding from the target side. Without this check, one member’s query can consume orders of magnitude more resources than everyone else’s combined.
A connection is removed
Removals must invalidate immediately rather than lazily, because a stale bitmap would show a closer degree than the truth and expose profile data the viewer should no longer see.
Graph shard unavailable
Adjacency is partitioned by member, so an outage affects a subset of members rather than everyone. Return “unknown” for affected targets instead of guessing a degree.
Cache stampede on a popular member
Many viewers connected to the same hub can miss the same bitmap simultaneously after an invalidation. Coalesce the rebuild so one request computes and the rest wait. Ch 9
[flag] 9. Conclusion — what I would say in the last three minutes
The dominant constraint

Third degree is 125 million members and cannot be materialised. Everything follows: cache what is affordable at two hops, and answer three hops by meeting in the middle rather than by expanding further.

What I would build first

The compressed second-degree bitmap and the bidirectional intersection. Together they turn the expensive query into a handful of set operations and let one cached set serve all 25 targets on a page.

What I deliberately did not build

Returning the connecting path, and any degree beyond three. The path needs an actual traversal rather than a set intersection, and degree 4 approaches the whole graph.

The biggest risk

High-degree members. They break the neighbourhood arithmetic the whole design rests on, and without an explicit switch to expand from the smaller side, a handful of users can dominate the cluster’s load.

Part 3
Google Staff (L6) Interview Framework & Master Toolkit
Strategic execution guides, capacity estimation mental math, trade-off matrices, and behavioral leadership frameworks calibrated specifically for Staff Software Engineer evaluations at top-tier tech companies (Google L6, Meta E6, Amazon L7).

1. The 45-Minute Staff (L6) System Design Pacing Guide

At Google L6, the interviewer does not want to prompt you. They expect you to own the room, proactively drive the architecture, state assumptions clearly, and pivot between high-level macro trade-offs and micro-level algorithmic deep dives.

Time Phase Staff-Level Execution Strategy What Interviewers Evaluate
0:00 - 0:05 Scope & Requirements Clarify core Functional Requirements (3-4 max). Define crisp Non-Functional SLAs (Availability 99.99%, latency targets p99 < 50ms, data durability). State explicit out-of-scope items. Ability to ruthlessly prioritize and avoid over-engineering trivial features.
0:05 - 0:10 Capacity Estimation Calculate DAU, write QPS, read QPS, network ingress/egress bandwidth, and 5-year storage requirements. Convert storage into hardware count (RAM vs NVMe vs Object Store). Practical engineering instinct; grounding architectural decisions in hardware physics.
0:10 - 0:18 High-Level Architecture Sketch end-to-end data flow: Client -> DNS/CDN -> Load Balancer -> API Gateway -> Microservices -> Message Queues -> Primary/Replica DB & Cache. Establish data contracts (APIs). Breadth of knowledge; clean separation of concerns and clear system boundaries.
0:18 - 0:35 Deep Dives & Hard Problems Dive deep into the 2-3 most technically complex bottlenecks (e.g. Celebrity fan-out, cross-DC consensus, exactly-once transactions, geospatial matching, data synchronization). The Core L6 Differentiator: Depth in distributed algorithms, concurrency, and DB internals.
0:35 - 0:42 Fault Tolerance & Bottlenecks Walk through failure modes: "What if the Redis master crashes?", "What if a network partition isolates Region B?", "How do we handle a thundering herd during Super Bowl?". Resilience thinking, self-correction, graceful degradation, and operational excellence.
0:42 - 0:45 Summary & Extensibility Summarize the system's operational guarantees. Proactively mention future scale enhancements (e.g. machine learning rankers, cost optimizations). Executive communication and holistic strategic vision.

2. Latency Numbers & Capacity Mental Math Every Staff Engineer Must Know

Jeff Dean's latency numbers adjusted for modern hardware (NVMe SSDs, 100GbE data center networks, cloud infrastructure):

Rule-of-Thumb Conversion Factors:

  • Seconds in a day: 86,400 ≈ 100,000 (makes mental math 10x faster: 10M requests/day ≈ 100 QPS; 1 Billion requests/day ≈ 10,000 QPS).
  • Storage conversions: 1 Million records × 1 KB = 1 GB; 1 Billion records × 1 KB = 1 TB; 1 Billion records × 1 MB = 1 PB.
  • Network throughput: 1 Gbps link ≈ 125 MB/sec; 10 Gbps link ≈ 1.25 GB/sec.
  • Redis throughput: Single thread Redis node ≈ 50,000 - 100,000 QPS. Cluster of 10 nodes handles ~1M QPS easily.
  • Postgres / MySQL throughput: Single primary handles ≈ 5,000 - 10,000 writes/sec (with SSD WAL); Read replicas handle ~20,000 - 50,000 reads/sec each.

3. The Grand Architecture Trade-off Matrix

Staff engineers never say "Technology X is the best." They say: "Under constraints A and B, Technology X is superior because of trade-off Y."

Architectural Decision Option A Option B Staff-Level Decision Rule
Data Model Relational (PostgreSQL, Spanner) NoSQL / Document (Cassandra, DynamoDB, MongoDB) Use Relational when you need complex JOINs, ACID guarantees, or schema evolution. Use NoSQL when you need petabyte-scale horizontal writes, simple key-based access patterns, and schema flexibility.
Data Ingestion Synchronous RPC (gRPC / REST) Asynchronous Messaging (Kafka / SQS / PubSub) Use Sync RPC when the client strictly needs the immediate return value to continue (e.g. Auth, Checkout validation). Use Message Queues for fire-and-forget, buffering high spikes, and decoupling consumer systems.
Client Push Protocol WebSockets Server-Sent Events (SSE) / HTTP Long-Polling Use WebSockets for bidirectional real-time communication (Chat, Collaborative Whiteboards, Multiplayer Games). Use SSE for unidirectional server-to-client streaming (AI text generation, live stock ticker).
Cache Invalidation Write-Through Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading) Use Write-Through when read latency must always be minimal (zero cache miss penalty) and data cannot tolerate staleness. Use Cache-Aside when write volume is high and only a fraction of data is frequently read.
Distributed Transactions Two-Phase Commit (2PC) Saga Pattern (Choreographed / Orchestrated) Use 2PC within homogeneous, low-latency NewSQL clusters (Spanner). Use Sagas across disparate microservices where long-running locks are intolerable and compensating actions are feasible.
Search Indexing Elasticsearch / OpenSearch PostgreSQL Full-Text Search (GIN Index) Use Postgres FTS when data volume is < 10M rows and you want zero operational overhead. Use Elasticsearch when you need fuzzy matching, typo tolerance, multi-faceted filtering, and scale across billions of documents.

4. Google L6 Staff Leadership & Engineering Scenarios

In Google Staff interviews (System Design & Leadership / Googlyness), evaluators look for specific L6 behaviors: driving consensus among conflicting senior engineers, managing technical debt vs velocity, preventing catastrophic post-mortems, and designing scalable organizational architectures.

How do you handle two Principal Engineers with opposing architectural visions?
Staff Answer Strategy: "I do not arbitrate based on seniority or debate in endless meetings. I establish a shared Decision Framework based on business constraints (Latency SLA, operational cost, team ramp-up time). I ask each engineer to write a 1-page design proposal addressing the matrix, run a time-boxed 3-day proof of concept (POC) benchmarking the critical path under synthetic load, and align the team around empirical data. If trade-offs remain evenly matched, I favor reversible decisions (Type 2) over irreversible ones (Type 1) and establish a clear escalation path."
Describe how you lead a high-severity (SEV-0) cascading outage post-mortem.
Staff Answer Strategy: "I enforce a Blameless Post-Mortem culture focused on systemic prevention. I lead the investigation using the '5 Whys' root-cause methodology. We isolate why the blast radius was not contained (e.g. missing circuit breaker, lack of load shedding, synchronous dependency cycles). I convert learnings into concrete P0 Action Items with assigned owners: adding deadline propagation, automated canary analysis (ACA), chaos engineering drills, and updating playbooks before declaring the post-mortem closed."
How do you manage massive technical debt that threatens system scalability?
Staff Answer Strategy: "I never ask product management for a '6-month complete rewrite'—that almost always fails. Instead, I quantify the business risk of technical debt (e.g. 'each release carries a 15% rollback rate and infrastructure costs grow super-linearly with user growth'). I use the Strangler Fig Pattern: progressively decomposing the legacy monolith by routing 1% -> 5% -> 100% of traffic to isolated microservices behind an API gateway, delivering incremental value while reducing operational risk."

5. The Mental Model — How All of This Fits Together

Fifteen chapters is a lot of parts. This is the single diagram that connects them. Read it top to bottom: each layer's decisions are constrained by the layer above, and the bottom half exists only because the physical world refuses to cooperate.

REQUIREMENTS │ what are we actually being asked to build? ▼ WORKLOAD & SLOs ← Ch 1, 14 load parameters (usually a DISTRIBUTION, not an average) percentiles, not means │ what must never break ▼ DATA MODEL ← Ch 12 relationship shape picks relational / document / graph ▼ STORAGE ENGINE ← Ch 12 B-tree vs LSM — decided by the read/write ratio above │ ┌───────── ONE MACHINE IS NO LONGER ENOUGH ────────┐ ▼ REPLICATION ↔↔↔ PARTITIONING ← Ch 4, 5 SAME data, DIFFERENT data, many nodes different nodes → availability → capacity → read scale → write scale ▼ ORTHOGONAL. Composed, not sequenced. The hard problems live in their INTERACTION. ▼ TRANSACTIONS ← Ch 7 the guarantee you WANT across all of that ▼ ######################################################### # THE TROUBLE WITH DISTRIBUTED SYSTEMS ← Ch 1, 8 # # asynchronous network + lying clocks + pauses # # # # ⇒ you cannot tell "slow" from "dead" # # ⇒ every guarantee above is now an ASSUMPTION # ######################################################### ▼ CONSISTENCY & CONSENSUS ← Ch 2, 3, 6 the PRICE LIST │ linearizability → costs latency, always, not just in partitions │ causality → the strongest model that stays fast + available │ total order broadcast ≡ consensus ≡ leader election ≡ linearizable compare-and-set ▼ "Buy the MINIMUM coordination that makes your invariant hold."
💡 The three relationships people miss

1. Replication and partitioning are orthogonal, and their interaction is where the hard problems are. Rebalancing a shard that has three replicas; global vs local secondary indexes; routing a request when both the partition map and the leader can change. Neither chapter alone prepares you for those.

2. The “trouble” layer is a refutation, not a list of war stories. Read it as: everything above assumed you can tell whether a node is alive. You cannot. Fencing tokens are the punchline — the lease you thought you held may have expired during a GC pause, and only the storage layer rejecting a stale token saves you.

3. The bottom line is an equivalence, not four definitions. Once you see that total order broadcast, consensus, leader election and linearizable compare-and-set are one problem, “do we need consensus here?” becomes answerable: you need it exactly when you need a total order, and you need a total order exactly when an invariant spans nodes.

When You See This in a Design Problem, Think This

The point of the guide is that when you meet an unfamiliar problem, you recognise its shape. This is the lookup table.

When the problem says…The real question is…Reach for
“must never lose data”What is the acceptable RPO, and against which failure?Sync replication, WAL + fsync, quorum writes Ch 4, 12
“high write throughput”Are the writes random or can they be sequential?LSM, partitioning, batching, log-structured design Ch 5, 12
“globally distributed”Which operations must cross regions? Speed of light is 150ms.Geo-partitioned ownership, causal consistency, follower reads Ch 4, 2
“booking / reservation / seats”Is this a phantom? Can the invariant live on one row?Materialize the conflict, or SERIALIZABLE + retry Ch 7
“must be unique globally”Uniqueness, or ordering? They are different.Unique constraint if single-leader; consensus if sharded. IDs need neither — use disjoint ranges Ch 6
“exactly once”Exactly-once delivery is impossible. Do you mean effect?At-least-once + idempotency key + dedupe store Ch 1, 15
“social feed / timeline”Fan-out on write or read? What about celebrities?Hybrid fan-out; a timeline is a materialized view Ch 11, 12
“real-time / live updates”Server → client only, or bidirectional?SSE if one-way; WebSocket + pub/sub backplane if not Ch 11
“search / filter by anything”Is the filter the partition key? If not, you are scattering.Local index + scatter/gather, or a CDC-fed search store Ch 5, 12
“analytics on live data”OLTP and OLAP are opposite machines.CDC into a columnar store. Never the OLTP primary Ch 12
“run exactly once per hour”The lock is not enough — pauses outlive leases.Consensus election + fencing token + idempotent job Ch 6, 8
“across multiple services”Can I redraw the boundary so it becomes local?First try co-location. Then saga + outbox. Never 2PC Ch 7, 13
“one customer is huge”Hot key. More shards will not help.Salt, tier, or isolate into a dedicated cell Ch 5
“update DB and notify others”That is a dual write — it will drift.Transactional outbox, or CDC off the WAL Ch 13
“p99 is fine but users complain”Where are you measuring, and over what population?Client-side SLI, slice by tenant, fan-out amplification Ch 14
“deploy without downtime”Old and new run together — and rollback must work.Expand/contract, forward compatibility, field numbers Ch 15
“survive a region failure”What is the RTO, and how do clients reconverge?Geo-replication, fencing, rehearsed failover Ch 4
