Twenty Design Mistakes Caused by Misunderstanding This Material

Each of these is a real, recurring failure — and each traces to a specific misconception in the chapters above.

⚠ The recurring twenty
1. Retrying without idempotency
A timeout does not mean it did not happen. Double charges. Ch 1
2. “We're ACID so we're safe”
Default isolation permits write skew. Name your level. Ch 7
3. SELECT FOR UPDATE on absence
You cannot lock rows that do not exist. Phantoms get through. Ch 7
4. W+R>N called “strong”
A probability dial, not a guarantee. Sloppy quorums void it. Ch 4
5. Distributed lock without fencing
A paused holder still writes. Enforce at the resource. Ch 8
6. Auto-failover on async replication
A silent decision to lose acknowledged writes. Ch 4
7. Partitioning by timestamp
100% of writes hit the newest partition. Ch 5
8. More shards to fix a hot key
The hot value hashes to one place regardless. Ch 5
9. Dual-writing DB + cache/index
Guaranteed drift. Use outbox or CDC. Ch 13
10. 2PC across microservices
Blocking, and availability is the product of all participants. Ch 7
11. Application data in etcd/ZK
Coordination services, not databases. A known way to kill a cluster. Ch 6
12. Dependency checks in liveness probes
One DB blip restarts the whole fleet. Ch 13
13. Retries at every layer
3×3×3 = 27× load during an incident. Budget them at one layer. Ch 13
14. Unbounded queues
Converts a throughput problem into an OOM. Bound every queue. Ch 13
15. Averaging latency
Describes nobody. And percentiles do not average either. Ch 14
16. LWW on wall clocks
Clock skew silently discards correct writes. Ch 8
17. Analytics on the OLTP primary
Buffer-pool eviction, I/O contention, blocked vacuum. Ch 12
18. Renaming a column in one deploy
Breaks un-upgraded nodes and makes rollback impossible. Ch 15
19. Auto-rebalance + auto-failure-detection
A cascading-failure generator. Keep a human in the loop. Ch 5
20. “Eventual consistency is fine”
Unfalsifiable without a number. Measure lag or you have not chosen it. Ch 4
🌱 The six sentences worth memorising
  • You cannot distinguish a slow node from a dead one. Everything else follows from this.
  • A timeout tells you nothing about whether the work happened. So make the work safe to repeat.
  • Do not prevent the stale actor from acting — make its action harmless. Idempotency and fencing are both this.
  • Consensus, total order broadcast, leader election and linearizable CAS are one problem. Buy the minimum.
  • Making a constraint local beats coordinating. Co-locate the data, or move the invariant onto one row.
  • Every guarantee has a price, and the price is usually latency — all the time, not just during failures.

6. What Google Actually Asks — The Question Bank

Every other section of this guide teaches mechanisms. This one is about targeting: which mechanisms you are most likely to be asked to assemble under time pressure, and where in this document the answer already lives. It is built from a 78-question sample of Google system-design reports, cross-checked against seven other public question banks. The questions themselves live on their own page — the Question Bank — and this card is the analysis of them. Read the provenance note at the end before you treat any of it as gospel.

💡 The single fact that should reshape your preparation

At L6 you are preparing for two design rounds, not one. An L5 loop contains a single system design interview. An L6 loop contains two — sometimes three — and they are deliberately different in kind: one product / applied design, and one infrastructure / architecture design.

Almost all popular preparation material is the product round, and this guide originally was too — nine of its first ten designs. D11–D14 and the enrichment of Ch 9 and Ch 10 exist specifically to close that half of the loop. The infra round is the one candidates under-prepare, because it does not look like the questions in the videos.

🔗 The full question bank is a separate page
  • Open the System Design Question Bank → — all 78 Google-tagged questions, filterable by company, by type and by topic, sorted newest first, with each one linked to the chapter or design here that answers it.
  • Filter to “Engineering” before you read it. The source bank filters by “system design” across every role, so 18 of the 78 are product-manager questions (“Design the US flag”, “How would you price the Amazon Kindle?”) and 5 are Fermi estimation. 55 are engineering questions — that is the set that matters for an L6 software loop.
  • 39 of the 78 map to a section of this guide. The Gaps filter shows the 21 engineering questions that do not, which is the honest picture of what is still missing here.
Sorted by recency deliberately: it is the only ordering in the data that is not shaped by how long a question has been sitting there collecting answers — and it filters most of the product-sense questions out for free.
⚠ Common misconception
“The popular list of system design questions is the Google list.”

It substantially is not. The public canon — Twitter, Uber, Netflix, Instagram — is consumer product design, because that is what makes legible video content. Google’s reported pool leans much harder toward infrastructure and operations, because that is the problem domain of a company that runs its own fleet, its own storage layer and its own network.

The 78-question sample makes this concrete. Alongside the familiar prompts sit “How would you upgrade 5,000 servers?”, “Design a system to log messages in order”, “Design a monitoring system for 1,000 web servers”, “Design a cache controller”, “Design a system to deny service to requests from banned IPs” and “Design a system to upgrade hundreds of thousands of machines on the Moon.” That last one is not a joke: it is a latency-constraint question wearing a costume. A 1.3-second one-way light delay makes every synchronous protocol you know unusable, and the interviewer wants to watch you notice.

Clusters — where the same problem keeps reappearing in different clothes

Individual questions are weak evidence. A cluster of near-duplicates asked over several years is much stronger, and it tells you what to be able to derive rather than recall.

ClusterCountThe variants askedCoverage
AI / ML systems11LLM Q&A · RAG over private data · Gemini query serving · Gemini email summariser · ML experiment tracking · ML pipeline metrics · language detection · sound denoising · landmark recognition · X-ray triage · image classificationPartly — D14 covers the LLM/RAG half; the classic-ML half is a gap
Fleet & operations6Upgrade 5,000 servers · upgrade machines on the Moon · monitor 1,000 web servers · metrics and logging service · collect logs from many sources · troubleshoot after a deployD11 · Ch 14
Caching3Distributed LRU cache · cache controller · cache consistencyD12 · Ch 9
Typeahead / prediction3Sentence autocomplete suggestions · predict the next word being typed on a phone · autocomplete search results pageD13
Collaborative editing3Concurrent user flows in Google Docs · Docs-like photo-editing collaboration · a Doc with an MS-Paint surfaceGap — CRDT theory in Ch 4, no design
Reservation & payment3Airline booking · payment system · parking-garage reservation and paymentGap — the invariant-on-one-row idea is in Ch 7
Geospatial3Google Maps for an uncovered area · Street View capture with 1,000 cars · map IP ranges to regionsGap — H3 indexing appears in D9 only
Storage & KV4Key-value store · distributed file system · move data between Cassandra clusters · external sort across workersD3 · D8 · Ch 12

The derivation chains matter more than the list. Counter → leaderboard → trending topics is one problem with three coats of paint. So is crawler → indexer → typeahead. A distributed counter is partitioning plus a decision to give up read-your-writes. If you can derive them at the table, you do not need to memorise them.

The rubric — the same prompt, three different bars

The most consistent finding across every source is that the L4/L5/L6 distinction is not about which mechanisms you know. It is about who speaks first.

THE SAME PROMPT, THREE DIFFERENT BARS L4 the interviewer states the requirements -> the candidate builds to them "here is a design that satisfies what you told me" L5 the candidate surfaces the missing requirements before being asked "you have not mentioned retention -- I will assume 30 days, which is what decides the storage tier" L6 the candidate names the DOMINANT CONSTRAINT before the interviewer steers "everything here is downstream of one number: the 40:1 read/write skew. I am designing around that, and I will justify every other choice against it." ^ at L6 the highest-signal moments of the round are started by the CANDIDATE. An interviewer who has to pull the trade-offs out of you has already written "solid L5" on the feedback form.
The ladder is about initiative, not vocabulary. This is why a clean, correct, well-scaled architecture is one of the most common paths to a down-level: it is a complete answer to a question nobody asked you to answer alone.

That last point deserves stating plainly, because it is counter-intuitive and it is the single most-cited down-level cause: a technically excellent design can read as L5. A clean architecture with sensible trade-offs is a strong L4 result. What converts it into an L6 result is that you decided what the problem was, said which constraint dominates, named what you were deliberately not building, and volunteered the failure modes before anyone asked.

⚠ Where this list comes from, and how much to trust it

None of this is confirmed by Google. The 78-question sample is a public bank of self-reported candidate questions, cross-checked against seven preparation vendors. Both have known biases: candidates disproportionately report what they found memorable or difficult, vendors list what they already sell content for, and — as the composition table above shows — the bank mixes product-manager questions into the same filter.

Counts here are how many times a thing appears in this sample, not measured interview frequency. Treat the clusters as solid, single questions as weak signal, and the recency ordering as the most reliable cut, since it is the only column that is not a popularity artefact.

Use it to allocate study time, not to predict your loop. The value of the analysis is that it tells you where the infrastructure round lives — and that finding is robust across every source, even where individual questions are not.

🌱 Takeaway — how to use this bank

Do not grind the list. Seventy-eight memorised designs lose to six derivable ones.

  • Prepare two rounds, split by kind. One product, one infrastructure. If your practice is all product designs, half your loop is unrehearsed.
  • Sort by recency, not popularity. It is the only ordering in the data that is not shaped by how long a question has been sitting there collecting answers — and it filters out the product-sense questions for free.
  • The infra round is fleet, observability and admission control. Upgrading a fleet, ordering a log, capping a caller, caching at scale — not feeds.
  • Trust clusters over questions. Three ways of asking about collaborative editing is a signal. One question about a smart refrigerator is not.
  • Say the dominant constraint out loud in the first five minutes. It is the cheapest available L6 signal and most candidates never spend it.
  • Volunteer the failure modes. If the interviewer has to ask “what happens when that node dies”, you have already handed away the point.
  • Budget time for the end. The highest-signal discussion is late-round trade-offs and failure analysis. Candidates who over-invest in the first architecture diagram never reach it.

7. Further Study — Video & Lecture References

Every chapter and most designs in this guide now end with a ▶ Watch alongside block pointing at specific lectures. This card is the consolidated index: what each source is, who it is for, and where it stops being useful. Every link was checked before it was added.

💡 How to actually use these

Do not watch a course. Twenty-six hours of lectures is a worse use of your time than four targeted ones. The per-chapter blocks exist so you can watch the single lecture that covers the thing you are shaky on, then come back. Use video to repair a specific gap, not to feel productive.

Where video runs out

Worth knowing, because it tells you where to stop searching. For three topics this guide covers, there is no video at this depth and the written source is the better use of your time:

  • Metastable failure (Ch 10) — no recorded talk found. Read the HotOS 2021 paper; it is five pages. Then Marc Brooker’s post and the USENIX ;login; follow-up.
  • Retries, timeouts and backoff (Ch 10, Ch 13) — Amazon Builders’ Library, and Marc Brooker’s talks and papers.
  • Observability at high cardinality (Ch 14, D11) — nothing good found. The Google SRE books and the Prometheus TSDB documentation are the substitutes.
⚠ On link rot and on what video is for

Every link here returned HTTP 200 when it was added, and the lecture IDs were pulled from the live playlists rather than from memory. That still decays — channels reorganise and courses re-record. If one is dead, search the lecture title; these are all stable, well-known series.

The more important caveat: watching is the least effective way to prepare. It feels like progress because it is comfortable. The exercises in this guide, and drawing a design on a blank page before reading the answer, are worth several times as much per hour. Use these to fix a specific gap you have identified, then close the tab.

8. Scenario Drills — 24 Situations With Worked Answers

The designs in Part 2 test whether you can build a system. These test something different and harder to practise: the judgement calls a staff engineer is actually asked to make — in an incident, in a design review, in a room where someone has proposed something reasonable-sounding and wrong. Several are drawn directly from the reported question bank, where “a production service started erroring after a deployment, how would you troubleshoot it?” is a real Google prompt.

💡 How to use these

Answer out loud before you click. Reading a good answer produces the comfortable feeling of understanding without any of the retrieval that makes it stick. Say your answer, then open the drill and look specifically for what you did not say — that gap is the entire value of the exercise.

Most of these have no single right answer. What is being assessed is whether you name the trade-off, ask what the answer changes, and say what you would do first.

Incident & on-call judgement
1p99 latency has tripled. p50 is unchanged. Dashboards are green on every service. Where do you look first?Show answer

An unchanged p50 with a tripled p99 rules out most causes immediately. A genuinely overloaded service slows everything, so the median would move too. What moves only the tail is something a minority of requests touch: a cache that has partially cooled, one degraded replica in a pool, a hot partition, GC pauses on a subset of hosts, or a dependency called only on certain code paths.

Look at the distribution rather than the average: latency per host, per shard, and per endpoint. If one host is bad, it is hardware or GC. If one shard is bad, it is a hot key. If one endpoint is bad, it is a code path and its dependency. Service-level dashboards are green precisely because they aggregate away the thing you are hunting.

The principle: averages hide the tail, and the tail is the user experience. Always disaggregate before theorising.
2A dependency was down for 20 minutes. It has been healthy for an hour, but your service is still failing. Why?Show answer

You are in a metastable failure. During the outage, clients timed out and retried; the retry backlog is now itself enough load to keep your service saturated. The original cause is gone and the effect sustains itself — the system has two stable states and you are in the bad one.

The server is also doing more work than before, computing responses for requests whose callers already gave up. That work is pure waste crowding out requests that could still be served.

Recovery requires shedding, not patience: drain traffic or reject aggressively so queues empty, then reopen gradually. Adding capacity often fails because the retry volume scales with the number of clients, not with your capacity.

The principle: fixing the trigger is not the same as recovering. See the animation in Ch 10.
3At 3am you can restore service by failing over to a replica that is 30 seconds behind. Do you?Show answer

It depends entirely on what those 30 seconds contain, and that is a question you must be able to answer before the incident. Thirty seconds of profile-picture updates is nothing. Thirty seconds of payments is a reconciliation project and possibly a regulatory one.

Ask three things: are the lost writes recoverable from another source — a queue, an upstream log, the client? Will the old primary come back and try to re-apply them, creating a split brain? And can you detect which writes were lost, or will they be silent?

If the writes are unrecoverable and undetectable, staying down is often the better call — downtime is visible and reversible, silent data loss is neither.

The principle: prefer failures you can see over failures you cannot. Decide the acceptable data loss before you are on the call.
4Your team wants to add a retry to fix intermittent 500s from a downstream service. Do you approve it?Show answer

Not as stated. Ask two questions first. Is anyone else already retrying? If the client and the gateway both retry three times, adding a third layer means 27× amplification against a service that is already failing. Retry at exactly one layer — the one closest to the user that can make a meaningful decision.

Is the operation idempotent? Retrying a non-idempotent write turns intermittent errors into duplicate side effects, which is a worse problem than the one you are solving.

If a retry is genuinely right, it needs jitter (or clients synchronise), a budget (or volume is unbounded), and a circuit breaker (or you keep paying the timeout after the outage is established). Backoff alone closes one axis of five.

The principle: a retry is a load multiplier applied at the worst possible moment.
5Error rate is 0.5% and your SLO allows 0.1%. A product launch is scheduled for tomorrow. What do you do?Show answer

This is what error budgets are for — it converts an argument into arithmetic. You are burning budget at five times the allowed rate; the question is not whether the launch is important but whether there is budget left to spend on it.

Say it in those terms: “we have consumed X% of this quarter’s budget and at the current rate it is exhausted in N days. Launching adds risk on top of that.” That reframes it from engineering-versus-product into a shared decision with a number attached.

Then offer options rather than a veto: launch behind a flag to a small percentage, launch after the specific regression is fixed, or launch and accept a feature freeze afterwards. An L6 brings the trade-off, not the refusal.

The principle: reliability arguments are won with budgets, not with adjectives.
6A single customer's traffic is degrading the service for everyone else. What is the fix, in order?Show answer

Isolate first, optimise later. The immediate action is a per-tenant concurrency limit or rate limit so one caller cannot consume shared capacity — a bulkhead, applied at the edge where rejection is cheap.

Then find out why they are expensive: a hot key, an unbounded query, a missing index on their data shape, a retry loop on their side. The answer changes the durable fix — a hot key needs replication or client-side caching, an unbounded query needs a hard limit in the API contract.

The structural fix, if this recurs, is cellular architecture: partition tenants across independent cells so the blast radius of any one tenant is one cell rather than the fleet.

The principle: noisy-neighbour problems are isolation failures before they are performance problems.
Design review & technical judgement
7A team proposes moving from a monolith to 40 microservices. How do you respond?Show answer

Ask how many teams there are. Microservices are an organisational solution with a technical cost: they buy independent deployability and team autonomy, and they charge you distributed transactions, eventual consistency, network failure modes on every call, and versioned interfaces forever.

If three engineers are shipping a product, 40 services means 40 deploy pipelines and 40 sets of timeouts maintained by people who are also trying to build features. If eight teams are blocking each other on a shared release train, the trade is obviously worth it.

The middle path is usually right: extract the two or three components with genuinely different scaling or ownership, keep the rest together, and revisit. Splitting is easy to do and very hard to undo.

The principle: match the architecture to the org chart, not to the fashion.
8Someone proposes a distributed lock via Redis to prevent double-processing. What do you say?Show answer

Ask whether the constraint can be made local instead. Most double-processing problems are a uniqueness constraint in disguise, and a uniqueness constraint on one row in the database you are already writing to is atomic, free, and cannot fail independently.

If a distributed lock is genuinely needed, it has a specific hazard: a lock lease can expire while its holder is paused — a GC pause, a hypervisor stall — and that holder will wake up believing it still holds the lock. Redis locks do not prevent this. The mitigation is a fencing token: a monotonically increasing number the resource checks and rejects if stale.

So the answer is: prefer a conditional write on one row; if you must lock, demand fencing; and never rely on a lock for correctness of something a database constraint could enforce.

The principle: do not prevent the stale actor from acting — make its action harmless.
9A design proposes strong consistency across three regions. What do you probe?Show answer

The latency floor, and whether it was chosen or inherited. Strong consistency across regions means a write is not acknowledged until a quorum in other regions has it — that is a round trip measured in tens or hundreds of milliseconds, paid on every write, forever, not just during incidents.

Ask which specific operations need it. Usually it is a small minority — the ledger, the inventory decrement — and the rest are being dragged along by a decision made once at the database level. Classifying per operation rather than per system is the actual design work.

Then ask what happens during a partition, because the answer is forced: the minority side stops serving. If nobody has agreed that a region going read-only is acceptable, they have not actually chosen CP.

The principle: consistency is paid in latency on the happy path and in availability on the bad one.
10An engineer wants to cache a permission check to cut latency. Do you agree?Show answer

Be careful: this one has a security edge. Caching an authorisation decision means that when permission is revoked, the stale “allow” keeps working for the length of the TTL. That is not a staleness inconvenience, it is a window in which a removed employee can still read data.

The asymmetry is the key insight: caching a deny is safe, caching an allow is not. So bound it hard — seconds, not minutes — and add an explicit revocation channel that invalidates on permission change rather than waiting for expiry.

Also ask whether the latency actually matters. A permission check against a local replica is often already sub-millisecond, and the cache is being added to a path that was never the bottleneck.

The principle: a cache is a replica you chose not to keep consistent — decide what a wrong answer costs before you add one.
11A proposal says “we will use Kafka exactly-once semantics so duplicates are impossible.” Your response?Show answer

That guarantee stops at the boundary of the system that issued it. Exactly-once mode gives you idempotent producers and a transaction that commits the consumer offset together with writes back into the same system. Within that boundary it is real and useful.

It says nothing about external effects. If the consumer charges a card, sends an email or calls a partner API, that call cannot join the broker’s transaction and a retry will do it again.

So the correct design is at-least-once delivery plus idempotency at the point of effect: commit the side effect and the record that it happened in one transaction, and push an idempotency key across every boundary you do not control. Exactly-once delivery is impossible; exactly-once processing is achievable, and it is something you build in the consumer.

The principle: guarantees do not cross system boundaries unless you carry them across explicitly.
12A team wants to add a new required field to a message consumed by six services. How should they ship it?Show answer

Never as one change. You cannot deploy every producer and consumer simultaneously, so for some window old and new code coexist — and a required field breaks any consumer that has not been updated.

Use expand-and-contract. First make the field optional and have producers start writing it. Wait until every consumer has been updated to read it and handle its absence. Only then, once no old readers remain, make it required and remove the fallback. Each step is independently deployable and independently reversible.

The underlying requirement is that the encoding is backward and forward compatible: old readers must skip fields they do not recognise, and new readers must tolerate fields that are missing.

The principle: every schema change is a distributed deployment problem, not a data-modelling one.
Scaling & capacity
13Traffic will grow 10× in six months. Where do you look for what breaks first?Show answer

Look for the things that do not scale horizontally, because everything else is a budget conversation rather than an engineering one.

The usual list: a single-primary database taking all writes; anything with global coordination on the request path — a shared counter, a distributed lock, a strongly-consistent config read; connection-pool ceilings, which are often reached long before CPU; and any component sized by total data rather than by request rate, such as an in-memory index.

Then check the non-linear ones. Cache hit rate is the big one: a hit rate that drifts from 99% to 95% is a 5× increase in origin load, so growth can break the database without the database itself changing at all.

The principle: find the components whose cost curve is not a straight line, because they fail before the obvious ones.
14Your database is at 80% CPU. Someone proposes a read replica. Is that the right move?Show answer

Only if the load is reads. Replicas offload reads and add nothing for writes — in fact each replica adds replication work to the primary. If the 80% is write-driven, replicas make it slightly worse.

So first disaggregate: what fraction is reads, and are those reads cacheable? A cache in front is usually cheaper and faster than a replica, and does not introduce replication lag. If reads dominate and are not cacheable — varied, personalised, freshly written — then replicas are right.

Then confront the consequence nobody mentions in the proposal: reads from a replica are stale. You now need to decide, per query, which ones tolerate that, and add read-your-writes routing for the ones that do not.

The principle: adding a replica is choosing a consistency model, not adding hardware.
15One shard holds 60% of your traffic. What are your options?Show answer

Diagnose the shape before choosing a fix, because the three causes have different answers.

If it is a bad partition key — say partitioning by country when one country dominates — the fix is to repartition on something with better distribution, which is expensive but permanent.

If it is a hot key, no partition scheme helps: a single key cannot be split. Replicate that key across nodes with salted names and pick one at random, or cache it client-side with a short TTL, which collapses enormous read volume into almost nothing.

If it is temporary — a celebrity, a launch — consider handling it as a special case rather than reshaping the whole system for an event that ends next week.

The principle: partitioning distributes keys, not load. Zipfian traffic guarantees the two diverge.
16You need to migrate 10 TB from one database to another with no downtime. Outline the approach.Show answer

Dual-write with backfill, then verify, then cut over — and the verification step is the one people skip.

Start writing to both systems while continuing to read from the old one. Backfill history in batches, watching that the backfill does not saturate the source. Then run a comparison job continuously: read from both, compare, alert on divergence. You will find bugs here, and finding them now is the entire point.

Cut reads over gradually — 1%, 10%, 100% — with a fast path back. Only once reads have been fully on the new system for a meaningful period do you stop writing to the old one, because until then rollback is free and afterwards it is not.

The principle: keep rollback cheap for as long as possible, and let a comparison job find your bugs rather than your users.
17Cost has doubled while traffic grew 20%. Where do you look?Show answer

Something is scaling super-linearly, and there is a short list of usual suspects.

Cross-AZ or cross-region network transfer is the classic invisible one — a chatty service pair placed in different zones, or a replication topology that fans traffic across zones. Storage that was never expired: logs, metrics at full resolution, orphaned snapshots, soft-deleted rows.

Then retries and fan-out: a service added to the call path multiplies work by its own fan-out, and a retry policy under mild degradation can double request volume without any traffic change. Finally, cardinality — observability bills grow with distinct label combinations, not with request rate, so a single new label can double a monitoring bill overnight.

The principle: cost is a signal about architecture. A super-linear bill means a super-linear dependency.
18A synchronous call chain is five services deep. What is your concern?Show answer

Availability multiplies and latency accumulates. Five services at 99.9% each is 99.5% end to end — roughly five times the downtime of any single one. Latency is the sum of all five plus five network hops, and the p99 is far worse than the sum of the p99s because a slow call anywhere shows up in every request.

The questions to ask: do all five need to be synchronous? Anything that does not affect the response should be an event, not a call. Is there a deadline propagated from the edge, so no service is computing a reply whose caller has already given up? And is each hop bulkheaded, so one slow service cannot exhaust the thread pools of the ones above it?

The principle: every synchronous hop is a multiplication of failure probability. Make the chain shallower before you make it faster.
Data, consistency & correctness
19Two users click “buy” on the last item simultaneously. Walk through preventing a double sale.Show answer

Put the invariant on one row and let the database settle it. The claim is a single conditional update — UPDATE items SET state='held' WHERE id=? AND state='available'. Exactly one writer sees one row affected; the other sees zero and gets a clean rejection. No distributed lock, no consensus, no coordination.

Add a uniqueness constraint on the confirmed order’s item ID as a second line of defence, so even a bug in the hold logic cannot produce two sales.

Reaching for a distributed lock here is the common mistake: it takes a problem that is naturally local to one row and makes it distributed, adding a failure domain and a liveness problem to solve something the database already does atomically.

The principle: make the constraint local instead of coordinating. See D19.
20A user updates their profile and immediately reloads. They see the old data. What is happening and what do you do?Show answer

The write went to the primary and the read went to a replica that has not caught up. This is replication lag, and it is the single most common consistency complaint in any system with read replicas.

The cheapest fix is read-your-writes: after a user writes, route their reads to the primary for a short window — or track the write’s position and require the replica to have reached it before serving. Sticky routing by user achieves most of this.

Note what you should not do: making all reads strongly consistent removes the point of having replicas and puts full read load back on the primary. The problem is not that replicas are stale in general — it is that they are stale for the person who just wrote, and only that case needs fixing.

The principle: pick the weakest consistency model that makes the observed behaviour correct, not the strongest available.
21A payment API call times out. You cannot tell whether the charge happened. What do you do?Show answer

Nothing — and that is the correct engineering answer, not an evasion. A timeout tells you the reply did not arrive; it says nothing about whether the work happened. Assuming success risks delivering goods that were never paid for; assuming failure risks charging someone who receives nothing.

So leave the state as-is, let any hold expire naturally, and reconcile asynchronously against the provider’s record of truth, which is authoritative. If the charge did land, refund it — a refund is a recoverable business outcome, whereas a double-sold seat or an unpaid delivery is not.

The thing that makes this safe is the idempotency key sent with the original request: the client can retry the whole flow and the provider will recognise it rather than charging twice.

The principle: when you cannot know, do not guess — make the operation safe to repeat and reconcile against the source of truth.
22Your event consumer processed 400 messages twice after a restart. What went wrong and what is the fix?Show answer

Nothing malfunctioned. This is at-least-once delivery behaving exactly as specified: the consumer was restarted before committing its offset for those messages, so on restart it resumed from the last committed position and replayed them.

The fix is not a broker setting. Make the effect and the record of the effect commit together: write the business row and the processed-message ID in one transaction, with a uniqueness constraint on the message ID. The replay then violates the constraint, is recognised as a duplicate, and is skipped.

Then decide this per consumer, not per system: a duplicate email is mildly annoying, a duplicate charge is a financial incident. The two deserve different amounts of machinery.

The principle: the right delivery guarantee is a function of what a duplicate costs, not of what the broker supports.
23Someone asks you to explain, in one minute, why your system uses eventual consistency. What do you say?Show answer

Lead with the trade, not the mechanism. Something like: “During a network partition we can either refuse to answer, or answer with data that may be seconds out of date. For a feed, refusing is a visible outage and being seconds stale is invisible — so we answer. For payments we make the opposite choice, and that path refuses.”

That answer does three things an interviewer is listening for: it names the choice as forced rather than preferred, it ties the decision to user impact rather than to a database feature, and it makes clear the choice is per operation, not a property of the whole company.

What to avoid: “we are an AP system.” That is a category error, and it tells the listener you learned CAP as a slogan.

The principle: state the trade in terms of what the user experiences, then name the exception.
24An analytics query is locking rows and slowing the transactional path. What are your options?Show answer

Recognise the shape first: OLTP and OLAP have fundamentally different access patterns and should not share a store. Transactional work is many small row-level reads and writes; analytics is a few queries scanning enormous ranges of a few columns.

Short-term: move the query to a read replica so it cannot block the write path, and check the isolation level — many analytical queries do not need repeatable reads and are holding locks they do not require.

Durable fix: replicate into a columnar store via change data capture. Columnar storage reads only the columns needed and compresses far better on homogeneous data, so the same query often runs orders of magnitude faster and stops touching the transactional system at all.

The principle: when two workloads have opposite access patterns, the answer is usually two stores, not better tuning.
🌱 Takeaway — what these drills are really testing

Notice how few of these are answered with a technology. Almost all are answered with a question, a trade-off, or an ordering.

  • Disaggregate before theorising. Per host, per shard, per endpoint, per tenant. Aggregate dashboards hide exactly what you are hunting.
  • Ask what the answer changes. “How many teams do you have?” decides the microservices question; “what is in those 30 seconds?” decides the failover.
  • Say what you would do first. Isolate, then optimise. Stop the bleeding, then find the cause. Ordering is most of the judgement.
  • Prefer failures you can see. Visible downtime beats silent data loss; a fast rejection beats a slow timeout.
  • Make the constraint local. It answers the double-sale, the double-processing, the distributed lock and the rate limiter — four drills, one idea.
  • Bring the trade-off, not the refusal. “We have burned 80% of the budget; here are three options” lands where “that is unsafe” does not.
